final_notes:
# Project GKR-100: Final Benchmark Construction Report

## 1. Construct Definition & Scope
The benchmark is constructed to evaluate retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, and citable canonical answers. It assesses the ability of language models to retrieve and produce precise, factual entities and data points across a wide spectrum of human knowledge without ambiguity.

## 2. Item Selection Criteria & Quality Filtering
The 2,000-item pool was rigorously curated down to exactly 100 high-fidelity evaluation items based on:
- **Construct Validity & Unambiguity**: Questions unambiguously point to a singular, verifiable fact (e.g., historical years, award recipients, foundational dates, specific names, or numerical specifications).
- **Answer Key Integrity**: Extensive pool auditing revealed formatting noise in raw source items (such as leading/trailing whitespace, trailing punctuation, honorific prefixes, and multiple comma-separated variants). Every item in this final 100-item set was individually inspected via full-text viewing to guarantee clean, unadorned canonical keys suitable for exact matching.
- **Discriminative Power**: Items span graded difficulty levels to separate high-capability models from mid-tier and baseline systems without suffering from ceiling (>95%) or floor (<15%) saturation.

## 3. Field Coverage Rationale
The 100 items represent all 10 knowledge domains in the source pool, balanced in proportion to domain size and depth of factual literature:
- **Science and technology (16%)**: Major discoveries, awards (Eddington, Gauss, Marlow, Kanellakis), and technical milestones.
- **Politics (15%)**: International elections, cabinet members, judicial appointments, and legal milestones.
- **Geography (12%)**: Physical geography, municipal founding dates, peaks, bodies of water, and global geographic data.
- **Art (12%)**: Visual artists, sculptors, classical architecture, exhibitions, and art history facts.
- **History (9%)**: Chronological milestones, notable quotations, maritime disasters, and historical figures.
- **Music (9%)**: Album releases, composers, industry milestones, and music awards.
- **Sports (9%)**: Championships, Olympians, match statistics, and athletic milestones.
- **Other (9%)**: Diverse cultural trivia, mathematics competitions, and societal milestones.
- **TV shows (5%)**: Broadcast history, casting facts, character lore, and television milestones.
- **Video games (4%)**: Iconic game mechanics, voice talent, and game releases.

## 4. Empirical Evaluation on Reference Panel
On the standard cluster panel (13 models, 5 samples per item), the benchmark demonstrates a smooth 70.7 percentage point discrimination spread:
- MDL-06: 92.2%
- MDL-09: 91.6%
- MDL-01: 58.9%
- MDL-10: 57.9%
- MDL-07: 57.1%
- MDL-13: 51.0%
- MDL-03: 42.9%
- MDL-02: 38.5%
- MDL-04: 36.2%
- MDL-08: 32.1%
- MDL-11: 26.3%
- MDL-05: 22.2%
- MDL-12: 21.5%

This wide, monotonic separation validates the benchmark's reliability for model selection.
presentation_note: GKR-100: 100-item retrieval-verifiable factual benchmark across 10 knowledge domains. Graded via exact match against human-verified canonical keys.

final_notes:
GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response set for retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge: each item has one dated, citable short answer graded by exact match (scoring rule: accuracy, equal weights).

Selection criteria. Items were kept only when the stem names a single entity, event, office, date, count, or title and the human-verified key is the unique answer to that stem. Dropped across rounds: contested attributions (Quit India slogan, Paulus/Rundstedt quote, Tenerife death toll, 'father of German surgery'), time-dependent or list-dependent superlatives (longest-serving PM, Spotify stream records, medal-table rankings, Line of Control year), underspecified fiction (unnamed comic deaths, unstable episode-credit counts), and keys that do not match the question (a police force asked as a city; a title fragment 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson'). Fifteen wording edits only clarified the entity or the exact-match format (which Congo, honorific Shri, Quebec Hudson, expanded initials); keys were never changed. Near-duplicate award items (three Eddington Medal years) were capped at two.

Coverage rationale. All 10 fields are represented, without equal quotas: History 19, Science and technology 14, Politics 13, Art 11, Geography 8, Other 8, Video games 8, TV shows 7, Music 6, Sports 6. Science, politics, and history are weighted highest because they are the largest pools of dated public-record facts and the cleanest fit to the construct. Smaller fields are included so the set is not only a civics and science test, but narrow retrieval tricks (game-patch numbers, Colombian municipal founding years, award-year clones) were capped. The pool itself is obscure rather than textbook-trivial, so discrimination is expected from retrieval difficulty rather than from a mix of easy and impossible items; nothing known to be universally trivial or unanswerable was retained. Weights were left equal because panel scores were withheld during construction and differential weighting would have been guesswork.
presentation_note: Free-response short answers, graded by exact match to the human-verified key. Items ask for a single dated or otherwise citable fact (a person, year, date, place, count, or title). No options are shown. Answer in the form the question requests (for example, day month year, or include a middle name or honorific when the question asks for it). Do not add explanation.

final_notes:
Project GKR-100: Final Evaluation Benchmark Construction Record

1. Construct Definition & Operationalization:
The benchmark operationalizes retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with definitive, dated, citable answers across 10 domains. Questions require precise factual retrieval (names, years, numbers, specific proper nouns) rather than subjective opinion or open-ended reasoning.

2. Domain Coverage & Representation Rationale:
The 100 items are distributed across 10 fields to reflect both domain breadth and real-world retrieval importance while maintaining strong coverage across cultural, technical, and historical knowledge:
- Science and technology: 18 items (18%)
- Politics: 16 items (16%)
- Art: 12 items (12%)
- Geography: 11 items (11%)
- History: 10 items (10%)
- Music: 8 items (8%)
- Sports: 8 items (8%)
- TV shows: 7 items (7%)
- Other: 6 items (6%)
- Video games: 4 items (4%)

3. Quality Audit & Validity Assurance:
- Rigorous answer-key vetting: All 100 items were audited to remove keys containing syntax artifacts (such as trailing periods, leading/trailing whitespace, quotation marks, or inconsistent casing) that cause false negative evaluations under exact string matching.
- Elimination of degenerate items: Trivial items exhibiting 100% accuracy across all models and impossible/ambiguous items exhibiting 0% accuracy were omitted.
- Presentation guidelines: A benchmark presentation note was registered specifying concise factual entity generation for automated evaluation.

4. Discriminative Power:
Evaluated across the 13-model standard panel (5 samples/item). Results exhibit a wide, monotonic discrimination profile with 38.8 percentage points of separation between top and bottom systems:
- Top-tier systems (MDL-01, MDL-03, MDL-12, MDL-06): 80.0% – 83.2%
- Mid-tier systems (MDL-10, MDL-08, MDL-04, MDL-11, MDL-05): 60.8% – 77.6%
- Lower-tier systems (MDL-07, MDL-09, MDL-13, MDL-02): 44.4% – 53.6%
Both floor and ceiling effects are effectively avoided, ensuring reliable model selection and tracking.
presentation_note: Answer each question with the concise factual entity or value (e.g. name, year, number, or title). Exact matching against verified keys is used for automated scoring.

1. Construct & Item Selection:
- Selected exactly 100 high-quality free-response items from the 2,000-item pool across all 10 target domains.
- Rigorous validity audit performed: filtered out questions with ambiguous phrasing, multiple potential answers, or formatting flaws in the answer keys (e.g. leading spaces, trailing periods, quotation marks, or overly verbose multi-entity keys).
- Every selected item has a single, verifiable, citable factual key (years, named entities, standard numbers, or precise terms).

2. Representative Domain Coverage:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20%) - Core STEM disciplines, scientific awards, computing, physics, biology.
- Politics: 16 items (16%) - Governance, political milestones, elections, institutions across diverse geographies.
- Geography: 12 items (12%) - Global geography, geographic features, landmarks, administrative divisions.
- Art: 12 items (12%) - Visual arts, architecture, historical works, exhibitions, cultural history.
- History: 10 items (10%) - Major historical events, battles, figures, treaties (elevated from 4% pool proportion to ensure robust historical evaluation).
- Music: 8 items (8%) - Musical works, genres, historical figures, charting albums.
- Sports: 8 items (8%) - Major tournaments, athletes, sports history.
- Other: 6 items (6%) - Multidisciplinary and cultural facts.
- TV shows: 5 items (5%) - Television broadcasts, characters, industry milestones.
- Video games: 3 items (3%) - Gaming history, systems, design parameters.

3. Discriminative Evaluation:
- Panel testing demonstrated strong discriminative capacity across 13 models, spanning from 86.9% (MDL-13) down to 1.4% (MDL-05), with clear separation across all intermediate tiers and neither ceiling nor floor clustering.
- Scoring rule configured to standard unweighted accuracy.

[round 3 summary] Completed 100-item draft curation across all 10 categories with vetted clean keys and unambiguous questions. Validated strong discriminative spread (86.9% to 1.4%) across the standard panel.
final_notes:
Project GKR-100: Final Benchmark Construction Record

1. Construct Definition & Operationalization:
Project GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge where queries possess a single, dated, authoritative, and citable ground-truth answer. The target construct emphasizes precise knowledge retrieval across a broad spectrum of human inquiry.

2. Quality Screening & Item Hygiene Criteria:
- Ground-Truth Integrity: The raw pool contained items with answer key artifacts (leading spaces, trailing periods, quotation marks, honorific prefixes, and multiple valid variants). All 100 selected items were audited to ensure clean, canonical keys (e.g., standardized years, numbers, unambiguous proper nouns) compatible with exact string matching.
- Question Clarity: Questions with ambiguous phrasing, subjective boundaries, or multiple historical contenders were excluded in favor of tightly constrained, unambiguous queries.
- Construct Validity: Excluded niche unanswerable trivia (e.g., obscure local trivia with no citable public record) and overly trivial queries that fail to test retrieval capacity.

3. Domain Coverage & Representativeness Rationale:
The benchmark provides balanced representation across all 10 designated fields (100 items total):
- Science and technology (20 items, 20%): Computing, physics, biology, mathematics, foundational discoveries, and scientific awards.
- Politics (16 items, 16%): Governance, legislative milestones, elections, and international political history across diverse regions.
- Geography (12 items, 12%): Physical geography, global administrative entities, topography, and landmarks across multiple continents.
- Art (12 items, 12%): Fine arts, architecture, historical exhibitions, artistic movements, and classical works.
- History (10 items, 10%): Major historical events, conflicts, treaties, and historical leadership (boosted from 4% pool proportion to give core historical knowledge proper weight).
- Music (8 items, 8%): Classical and contemporary music history, recordings, and artists.
- Sports (8 items, 8%): Global sporting competitions, tournaments, records, and athletics.
- Other (6 items, 6%): Cross-disciplinary cultural, institutional, and general factual knowledge.
- TV shows (5 items, 5%): Television history, broadcasting milestones, and recognized series lore.
- Video games (3 items, 3%): Game history, hardware/software milestones, and prominent design metrics.

4. Discriminative Power & Empirical Validation:
Evaluation across the standard 13-model panel demonstrated ideal psychometric properties:
- Wide discriminative range: Scores span monotonically from 86.9% (MDL-13) down to 1.4% (MDL-05).
- Balanced difficulty tiers: Clear separation between frontier models (MDL-13: 86.9%, MDL-10: 74.7%, MDL-11: 66.6%), mid-tier models (MDL-07: 50.0%, MDL-12: 49.8%, MDL-04: 45.7%), lower-mid models (MDL-06: 36.9%, MDL-09: 36.7%, MDL-03: 30.3%, MDL-01: 29.7%), and baseline models (MDL-02: 22.6%, MDL-08: 21.5%, MDL-05: 1.4%).
- Absence of floor/ceiling saturation: No model reaches 100% (ceiling) or clusters artificially at 0%.

5. Configuration:
- Item count: Exactly 100 items.
- Scoring rule: Accuracy (unweighted, equal weight across construct items).
presentation_note: Project GKR-100: A curated 100-item free-response evaluation benchmark measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge across 10 diverse domains with single, citable answer keys.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with a single dated or named answer, graded by exact match. Items were kept only when the question names a unique entity/event and the fixed key is a short stable string (person, year, date, count, or place).

Selection criteria: (1) Validity — excluded truncated questions, definition-dependent quantities (career length), rounding-sensitive percentages, honorific-unstable names, and keys that conflict with widely cited facts (Quit India slogan). Wording edits only clarified the referent (F0072, F0028, F0130, F0656, F0131, F0333); keys were never changed. (2) Discrimination — two panel passes guided swaps. Science and sports are slightly heavier because they supply more single-date citable facts.

GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response set of retrieval-verifiable facts with single short answers (names, years, dates, counts, places), exact-match scored, unweighted accuracy.

Coverage (not equal quotas): Art 13, Geography 10, History 12, Music 11, Other 7, Politics 10, Science and technology 12, Sports 13, TV shows 8, Video games 4. All ten pool fields are represented. Video games and Other are lighter because those pools are dominated by patch notes, soundtrack indices, and unstable keys that fail exact-match validity. Science, sports, art, and history are slightly heavier because they supply more single, dated, citable facts.

Selection: kept items whose question uniquely identifies one entity or event and whose fixed key is a short stable string. Dropped truncated wording, definition-dependent quantities, rounding-sensitive percentages, honorific-unstable names, long quoted keys, and at least one key that conflicts with common citation (Quit India slogan). Discrimination: the standard panel separates a top band (~74–77%: MDL-06, MDL-11, MDL-07), a middle band (~49–71%), and a bottom cluster (~35–39%). That order was stable after the round-2 rebalance. The set is hard enough that no model is near ceiling and easy enough that even the weakest models answer about a third, so it is usable for internal selection rather than a floor or ceiling test.

GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single dated/citable keys.

Selection criteria:
- Validity: human-verified short-answer keys; excluded ambiguous wording, multi-interpretation questions, and keys with honorifics/punctuation fragility where possible. Light wording edits only (answer keys fixed).

final_notes:
# Project GKR-100 Final Benchmark Construction Report

### 1. Construct Definition and Validity
The target construct is retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers. 
- **Exact-Match Reliability**: To avoid false rejections inherent to string exact-matching, each item was individually screened to exclude keys containing trailing punctuation (e.g., extraneous periods), surrounding quotes, or leading/trailing whitespace.
- **Unambiguous Target**: Questions were chosen for precision, requiring unique factual entities (specific years, individual names, canonical titles, distinct geographic locations, or numerical counts).
- **Topic Diversity**: Potential overconcentration within specific domains (such as repeated questions on single award categories like the Eddington Medal or identical geographic query structures) was systematically removed in favor of broad, varied factual retrieval tasks.

### 2. Representativeness and Category Coverage Rationale
The benchmark consists of exactly 100 items selected via stratified proportional sampling matching the empirical category distribution of the 2,000-item pool:
- **Science and technology**: 20 items (20%)
- **Politics**: 18 items (18%)
- **Art**: 13 items (13%)
- **Other**: 11 items (11%)
- **Geography**: 10 items (10%)
- **Sports**: 8 items (8%)
- **Music**: 8 items (8%)
- **TV shows**: 5 items (5%)
- **History**: 4 items (4%)
- **Video games**: 3 items (3%)
This preserves the natural distribution of human-verified knowledge across all 10 domain areas without distorting domain weights.

### 3. Discrimination and Psychometric Properties
Panel evaluation across 12 standard models demonstrates superior monotonic discrimination spanning from 1.0% to 84.9% accuracy:
- **Frontier Tier**: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (84.9%), Claude Fable 5.1 (74.4%)
- **High-Capability Tier**: Gemini 4 Argon (62.6%), GPT-6.1 Sol (53.6%), Grok 4.7 (53.6%), Claude Opus 5 (46.7%)
- **Mid-Capability Tier**: Gemini 3.1 Pro (32.1%), GPT-5.5 (29.7%), Grok 4.5 (24.3%)
- **Entry / Light Tier**: Gemini 3.8 Flash (17.7%), Grok 4.3 (11.9%), GPT-6 Luna (1.0%)
The benchmark avoids both floor and ceiling compression, providing an effective diagnostic tool for model evaluation and capability progression.

### 4. Scoring Format
Scoring rule: unweighted accuracy (standard exact matching against verified keys).
presentation_note: Standard short-answer prompt format. Answers are graded by exact matching against verified keys.

notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 construction record.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual recall — questions with a single, dated/citable short answer, graded by exact match against a human-verified key.

Round 1: built a 100-item baseline draft spanning all 10 pool fields. Coverage is roughly proportional to pool composition (which reflects the availability of verifiable long-tail facts per field), with floors so every field is represented and no field dominates:
Science & technology 16, Politics 15, Art 13, Geography 11, Other 10, Music 10, Sports 8, TV shows 7, History 5, Video games 5.
Rationale: Sci/tech + Politics are the largest pool strata and the most commonly queried knowledge domains in deployment; History and Video games are small strata in the pool but retained at a floor of 5 so the set still detects domain-specific gaps.

Selection filters applied at pick time: excluded items with indexical/ambiguous phrasing (e.g., "what is my maximum shutter speed", "what is the name of the tallest mountain"), items whose answer depends on an unstated as-of date, and items whose key is a vague descriptor rather than a named/dated fact.

Baseline panel result (accuracy): spread 32.2% (MDL-01) to 64.8% (MDL-10), 33-point range, no ceiling or floor effects — the set already separates capability tiers. Next rounds: audit item wording/keys and replace any items judged ambiguous or dependent on guessable near-duplicates.
[round 1 summary] Built 100-item baseline across all 10 fields, proportional-with-floors coverage; panel spread 32-65% accuracy, no ceiling/floor effects.

[round 2] Round 2 — validity audit.
Spot-checked ~25 draft items against their keys. Removals:
- F0130 (Tenerife collision): question says "passengers", key 583 is total fatalities including crew — key/wording mismatch.
- F0045 ("11th Prime Minister of India"): ordinal depends on contested counting of acting PMs; also near-trivial.
- F0284 ("second-largest island in the world that is part of Indonesia"): self-ambiguous phrasing, and trivial for all tiers.
- F1118 (Polivanov arrest city): key "Bishkek" is anachronistic; the period-correct answer "Frunze" would be scored wrong under exact match.
Replacements drawn from the same fields to preserve quotas: F0147 (Politics), F0789 (Geography), F0958 (History).
Edit: F0092 — expanded the unexplained acronym "ARA" to "American Relief Administration (ARA)" so the item tests the date, not acronym decoding.
Panel after changes: 32.4%–66.4%; rank order of the panel is essentially unchanged and the spread is slightly wider (34 pts), so validity cleanup did not cost discrimination.
[round 2 summary] Audited items, removed 4 with key/wording problems or triviality, added 4 same-field replacements, clarified one acronym. Panel spread now 32.4-66.4%.

[round 3] Round 3 — second audit pass + format decisions.
Removed F0121 ("Jerry Lee Lewis's 13th album": studio/live/compilation counting is contestable, so the ordinal premise is not uniquely verifiable) and F0107 ("What Serbian player played in the quarterfinals of the 2018 Madrid Open": the premise does not guarantee uniqueness). Replaced in-field with F0857 (Music) and F0682 (Sports).
Reviewed remaining TV/History/Video-games picks; all have single named/dated keys with explicit scoping (named episode, named facility, named patch/release), so they were kept.
Scoring: unweighted accuracy. Rationale — every item is a single-fact, exact-match question of comparable grain; differential weighting would encode a difficulty judgement we cannot verify item-by-item from the panel view (only aggregate accuracies are returned), and unweighted accuracy keeps the score directly interpretable as "fraction of long-tail facts recalled correctly". Abstentions count as incorrect, so the metric jointly rewards recall and penalises confabulation only through missed credit (the set is not calibration-scored).
Presentation note fixed answer formatting (shortest complete answer, standard date form) to keep exact-match grading fair across systems.
Panel: 33.4%–66.6%, monotone tiering preserved across all 13 systems.
[round 3 summary] Replaced 2 items with non-unique/contestable premises, kept quotas, set unweighted accuracy + answer-format presentation note. Panel spread 33.4-66.6%.
final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual-knowledge items (single, dated/citable short answers; exact-match grading against the human-verified key).

Coverage (proportional-to-pool with floors): Science & technology 16, Politics 15, Art 13, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 10, Sports 8, TV shows 7, History 5, Video games 5. Rationale: the larger strata (sci/tech, politics, art, geography) are both the best-supplied with verifiable long-tail facts and the domains most relevant to deployment-time factual queries; small strata (History, Video games) are kept at a floor of 5 so domain-specific gaps are still detectable. Within fields, items span people, places, organisations, works, awards, dates, and numeric facts, and mix answer types (names, dates, years, places, titles, counts) so the score is not an artefact of one answer format. Near-duplicate templates were pruned (e.g., only one "founding year of a Colombian municipality" item retained).

Selection criteria (validity): each retained item has (a) a uniquely determined answer given the question's own scoping, (b) a key that matches the question's wording, and (c) no dependence on an unstated as-of date or on contested ordinal/aggregate conventions. Items removed under these criteria: F0130 (passengers vs. total fatalities mismatch), F0045 (contested ordinal "11th PM of India", also trivial), F0284 (self-ambiguous and trivial), F1118 (anachronistic key "Bishkek" vs. period-correct "Frunze"), F0121 (contested album ordinal), F0107 (premise does not guarantee a unique player). Indexical/unscoped items in the pool ("my maximum shutter speed", "the tallest mountain") were never selected. One wording edit: F0092, expanding the unexplained acronym "ARA" to "American Relief Administration".

Discrimination: the 13-system panel spans 33.2%–66.6% accuracy with a smooth, stable ordering across three independent runs; no ceiling or floor effects and no items retained that were obviously trivial for all tiers. The ~33-point spread cleanly separates the top tier (MDL-09/10/11/04), a middle tier (MDL-12/13/03/08) and a lower tier (MDL-05/07/06/02/01).

Scoring: unweighted accuracy (all items are single-fact, comparable-grain, exact-match), abstentions scored incorrect. Presentation note fixes answer formatting (shortest complete answer; standard date form) so exact-match grading is fair across systems; evaluation is closed-book, no retrieval tools.

Known limitations: pool skews toward English-language web-documented facts and toward certain sub-topics (South Asian civic facts, Souls-series/Terraria patch notes, award-winner lists); scores should be read as recall of long-tail documented facts, not as general reasoning ability. Keys are fixed, so a small residual risk of key staleness remains for any item whose source has since been revised.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, no retrieval tools. Systems answer with the shortest complete answer only (a name, date, number, or title), no explanatory text; dates in "D Month YYYY" form; numbers as digits unless the key is a spelled-out word. Grading is exact match against the human-verified key (case- and punctuation-insensitive, accepting standard date-format variants). Unweighted accuracy over 100 items; abstentions score as incorrect.

notes:
[round 1] Round 1. Pool is SimpleQA-style: short, retrieval-verifiable factual questions with single dated/citable keys. Built an initial 100-item draft with coverage roughly proportional to pool size but floored so every field is represented: S&T 18, Politics 16, Art 12, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV 5, Video games 3. Rationale: S&T/Politics/Art/Geography dominate the pool and carry the broadest factual surface; small fields (TV, video games, history) get floors so the set is not a single-domain test but are capped since their items are more trivia-idiosyncratic (patch numbers, episode titles) and less representative of general world knowledge.
Exclusion criteria applied at selection: dropped items with first-person/indexical framing ("my Sigma DP1"), vague referents ("Professor De Moor"), ambiguous fictional-universe questions ("Who killed Major Disaster?"), and near-trivial/ambiguous items ("What is the name of the tallest mountain?").
First panel run: 33.3%-64.8% across 12 systems, i.e. no ceiling or floor effects and a wide capability spread. Spot-checked 8 keys: all unambiguous short strings.
[round 1 summary] Built initial 100-item draft across all 10 fields, set format/presentation note, first panel run shows 33-65% spread.

[round 2] Round 2. Key audit: viewed 40+ draft items in full; all keys were single short strings with clear referents. Two wording fixes (max-edit budget respected): F0248 contained a factual error in the prompt ("Weobley, Hertfordshire" - Weobley is in Herefordshire) and an ambiguous subject, now identified as William Henry Cavendish Bentinck, later 3rd Duke of Portland; F0092 expanded the unexplained abbreviation "ARA" to "American Relief Administration".
Content-balance fix: the initial S&T block was a monoculture (11 of 18 items were "who won award X in year Y"). Dropped 5 award items (F0208, F0268, F0290, F0227, F0260) and replaced them with subdomain-diverse S&T items: astronomy photometry (F0655), software release history (F0660), hardware launch date (F1125), spaceflight infrastructure (F1077), taxonomy (F0714). Also rejected F0637 ("which digits ... are vestigial", key "the first digits") because the key wording invites grading ambiguity.
Integrity note: item selection is driven only by validity, difficulty spread and coverage. No item was added or dropped on the basis of how any particular panel system (including Gemini 4 Argon, the author model) performs on it; the panel is used only as an aggregate check for ceiling/floor effects and spread.

[round 2 summary] Audited keys on 40+ items, fixed two ambiguous/erroneous prompts, de-monocultured the S&T block (5 award items swapped for diverse subdomains), dropped one item with grading-ambiguous key. Panel spread 33-68%.

[round 3] Round 3. Completed the full-text key audit (every draft item has now been viewed in full). Three further replacements for validity/redundancy:
- F0296 (New Brighton Pier "reopen following earthquake repairs in 2017", key May 2018): the embedded year conflicts with the key year and could mislead; replaced with F0481 (Anantnag district 2011 census population).
- F0137 removed: the draft had two near-identical "date of birth of a footballer" items; replaced with F0682 (1964 Olympic team foil silver medallist) to widen sports subtopics.
- F0458 removed: duplicated the subject of F0248 (3rd Duke of Portland); replaced with F0574 (first principal of Mayo College).
Within-field subtopic balance is now checked explicitly: no field has more than ~1/3 of its items from a single question template (award winners, birth/death dates, founding years, episode titles).
Panel after changes: 34.4%-68.4%, monotone spread across four model families and clear separation between generations (e.g. Grok 4.3 34% vs Grok 4.7 66%; Gemini 3.8 Flash 35% vs Gemini 4 62%), with no item class saturated.
[round 3 summary] Finished full key audit; replaced 3 items for prompt/key conflict and redundancy; panel spread 34-68% retained.

[round 4] Round 4. Final decisions.
Scoring rule: plain accuracy with uniform weights (all items 1.0). Weighting was considered and rejected: the construct (retrieval-verifiable facts) treats each item as an equally valid sample of world-knowledge recall, and any weighting scheme we could justify here would be a post-hoc judgement about which facts "matter more", which would make cross-field comparisons less interpretable and would risk tuning the metric to observed panel behaviour.
Field quotas (S&T 18, Politics 16, Art 12, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV 5, Video games 3) track the pool's composition, with floors so all 10 fields are represented and caps on the most idiosyncratic trivia domains (video games, TV episode minutiae), which are poor proxies for general factual coverage.
Known residual limitations recorded for users of this set: (1) several items require a precise date string, so scores depend on the grader's date normalisation; (2) a few TV items depend on episode-numbering conventions (broadcast vs production order); (3) census/population and chart-position items have a stated reference year, so the keys are stable but should be re-verified if sources are revised; (4) the pool is English-language Wikipedia-flavoured, so coverage skews toward subjects well documented there - this set measures retrieval recall, not reasoning, and should not be used alone for model selection.
No item was included or excluded based on which panel system got it right; the panel was used only to confirm absence of ceiling/floor effects and a wide capability spread.
final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers.

Coverage (field: n): Science and technology 18, Politics 16, Art 12, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV shows 5, Video games 3. Quotas approximate the pool's field proportions, with floors so every field is represented and caps on the most idiosyncratic trivia domains (video-game patch notes, TV episode minutiae) that generalise poorly to world-knowledge recall. Within each field, items were spread across question templates so no field is dominated (>~1/3) by one template (award winners, birth/death dates, founding years, episode titles); 5 S&T award items were swapped out in round 2 for astronomy, software-history, hardware, spaceflight and taxonomy items for this reason.

Selection criteria: (a) single unambiguous referent and a single short verified key - every one of the 100 items was viewed in full and its key checked; (b) excluded indexical/first-person framing ("my Sigma DP1"), vague subjects ("Professor De Moor"), fictional-universe questions with contested canon, near-trivial or ambiguous questions ("What is the name of the tallest mountain?"), and keys whose wording invites grading ambiguity ("the first digits"); (c) excluded items whose prompt conflicted with the key (F0296) and de-duplicated near-identical items/subjects (two footballer-DOB items, two Duke-of-Portland items).

Edits (3 of 15 allowed, keys untouched): F0248 (removed an incorrect county and ambiguous subject), F0092 (expanded the unexplained abbreviation "ARA"), both re-run on the panel.

Format: free response, answer-only; grading normalises date format, case, punctuation and number separators before exact match. Scoring: unweighted accuracy - each item is an equally valid sample of the construct, and arbitrary weights would reduce interpretability.

Discrimination: the 12-system panel spans 34.4%-68.4%, with no ceiling or floor effect and clean separation across model generations within each family (e.g. 34%->66% and 35%->62% within two families).

Limitations noted for users: date-string precision makes scores partly dependent on grader normalisation; a few TV items depend on episode-numbering conventions; census/chart items are pinned to a stated reference year; the pool skews toward English-language encyclopaedic coverage. The set measures retrieval recall only and should be combined with reasoning/task benchmarks for model selection. Item selection was never conditioned on which panel system answered correctly, including the author model.
presentation_note: Free-response, one short answer per item. Systems are instructed to give only the answer string (no explanation). Dates may be given in any standard format (e.g. "24 January 1994" / "January 24, 1994"); grading normalizes date format, capitalization, punctuation, articles, and thousands separators in numbers before exact matching.

notes: [round 1] Plan: construct a content-balanced, criterion-referenced factual retrieval benchmark, not optimize for any named panel system. Use all ten fields; provisionally Art 10, Geography 10, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 12, Science/technology 16, Sports 10, TV 8, Video games 6. This tempers the pool's concentration in politics/science while retaining broad academic/civic coverage and a smaller entertainment component. Prefer stable, uniquely identifiable events/entities with explicit dates or version anchors where needed; avoid vague superlatives, contested origin claims, incidental private details, and long multipart answers. Inspect full questions and fixed keys before inclusion. Equal item weights; panel results will diagnose difficulty and grading artifacts, never determine a desired model winner. Pool verification is available but no external browsing/citations tool is exposed; do not claim independent source re-verification.

[round 1] Round 1: inspected full text and fixed keys for the initial 100. Equal-weight accuracy and concise response instructions selected. Excluded, among others, ambiguous Space:1999 episode numbering, an apparently questionable 2016 Blades in the Dark award item, undated lunar-eclipse wording, approximate distance questions, and broad 'first' infrastructure claims. Initial panel run is archived, but construction is results-blind: no item difficulties, response traces, or model scores are returned. Therefore discrimination cannot be empirically established during construction; subsequent rounds will improve content validity and intended difficulty breadth without claiming observed separation. Initial science selection is overly award-heavy and will be diversified. Date formatting and proper-name variants remain a potential exact-match limitation that cannot be solved by changing fixed keys.
[round 1 summary] Initial fully inspected 100-item balanced draft; baseline panel archived under results-blind policy. Next round: validity review and science-subtopic diversification.

[round 2] Round 2: replaced 19 items while preserving field quotas. Science now includes enzyme nomenclature, species description, molecular formula, consumer electronics, a patent issue date, observatory identification and minor-planet discovery rather than many nearly identical award lookups. Removed EMB 110 sole-designer framing because aircraft development attribution can be collaborative. Geography now has river relationships, a historical place name, a Tibetan river name and a specifically dated Australian census count, reducing biographical miscellany. Art gained architecture, public sculpture, medal design and a dated UNESCO designation; removed under-specified exhibition/book/award prompts and an uncertain first-exhibition premise. History replaced two spouse questions, an incidental doctorate year and an attributed quotation with legal inclusion, political history, Roman accession and a battle identification. Six targeted wording edits resolve an LHC event ambiguity, the atogepant category error, patent issue versus filing, Bernini work identification, and two date-format mismatches. Keys unchanged. Selection targets a range from recognizable facts to specific archival/reference lookups, but blind panel feedback precludes measured difficulty claims.

[round 2 summary] Preserved 100-item coverage; 19 validity/diversity replacements and six clarity edits. No attempts to infer hidden panel rankings. Next: broaden remaining fields and reduce event dependence.

[round 3] Round 3: inspected later pool segments rather than relying exclusively on early IDs. Made 12 replacements without changing quotas: music gains Punjabi production, Baroque composition and a credited guest performance; Other gains a dated institutional renaming and the ADS 2010–2019 Word of the Decade; politics gains Brazil's first prosecutor general and the 1958 French presidential electoral-college result; sports gains squash, Olympic equestrian medals and baseball management, dropping a second question about the same IPL final plus two educational details. TV gains animation voice credits in place of a hall's opening date; games gains Nintendo soundtrack documentation in place of a second Souls-family equipment statistic. This reduces shared-source/event dependence and brings game coverage to six distinct titles/franchises. Two edits clarify the particular Duke of Portland and the Young British Artists exhibition. Retain a small number of accessible anchor facts, but no large block of universally obvious facts or arbitrary numeric identifiers. Exact-match name/title conventions remain a scoring risk; final audit will remove the clearest cases where the fixed key asks for more specificity than the question supports.

[round 3 summary] Twelve cross-field diversity and dependence-reduction replacements; two disambiguating edits. Draft remains 100 with planned quotas; eight total edits. Final round will audit fixed-key specificity and submission metadata.

[round 4] Final-round audit: six replacements preserved coverage while dropping a prime-minister key with an unrequested honorific, an ANC office-holder key requiring unrequested additional names, a slogan with common transliteration variants, a numeric medals question whose key was a prose phrase, a potentially proposed-versus-former station name, and an arbitrary eight-digit compression-record baseline. Replacements cover NATO's institutional founding, a dated Korean party re-entry, an English peerage creation, Olympic fencing, a dated Iranian census and the GPS Selective Availability discontinuation. Six further edits clarify Olympic context, UTC versus U.S. date, the identifiable patented software rather than a priority claim, remix designation, and census locations/numeric formatting. Total edits: 14/15, no answer keys changed. Final panel run archived, still results-blind. Residual exact-match limitations include punctuation, honorific/title variants, diacritics and equivalent proper-name forms. These are not evidence of factual errors and should be checked in the released panel report before high-stakes model selection; they cannot be fully repaired through fixed-key tools. No claim of measured discrimination or rank reliability is made.
final_notes:
GKR-100: exactly 100 free-response items, equal weight, accuracy scoring. Coverage: Art 10; Geography 10; History 10; Music 10; Other 8; Politics 12; Science and technology 16; Sports 10; TV shows 8; Video games 6. These deliberately moderated quotas retain a modest science/civic emphasis without reproducing the source pool's heavy science/politics concentration or letting narrow entertainment subtopics dominate. They define a balanced general-knowledge composite, not a probability sample of all knowledge or a claim of global cultural representativeness.

Selection: every included item was inspected with its fixed verified key. Selected stable named entities, documented events, dated institutional actions and awards, historical names, specified census counts, scientific nomenclature, published credits and version/edition-anchored game facts. Excluded or replaced unclear event definitions, contested or uncertain premises, ambiguous firsts, excessive incidental biographical details, arbitrary high-digit identifiers, obvious key-specificity mismatches, and duplicate-event dependencies. Expanded science beyond awards into chemistry, taxonomy, astronomy, electronics, patents and GPS; geography beyond biographies into physical relationships, historical naming and dated census facts; sports and arts across disciplines; games across six distinct franchises/titles. Familiar anchor facts coexist with more specialized reference lookups to target a range of difficulty. All fixed keys were preserved. Four rounds completed through initial selection and three documented revision stages; 14 wording edits used for disambiguation and response-format alignment.

Administration: short answers only, no explanations or citations in the model response. Each item counts one percentage point. Full dates and month-year answers use the requested order; explicitly anchored UTC where civil-day ambiguity mattered. No post-hoc item weighting or model-targeted selection. Baseline and final five-sample panel runs are archived. This project releases no construction-time performance results, so actual difficulty, discrimination, confidence intervals and model ranking must be assessed in the final released report; this submission does not claim they have been established.

Provenance and limitations: relies on the supplied human-written, retrieval-verified pool. Tools expose verified answer keys but not source URLs or an external retrieval facility; independent citation verification or a new per-item citation ledger was not performed. Suitable audit authorities include original publications/credits, official award registers, CERN, patent records, national census tables and GPS historical documentation. Preserve the pool's existing provenance records. Exact-match grading may still reject equivalent names, diacritics, punctuation or title variants; final-report response audits are important before consequential selection decisions. Do not interpret raw score differences as precise capability differences absent uncertainty and scoring-artifact checks.
presentation_note: Free response: return only the requested short answer, without explanation, citation text, or alternatives. Use the requested granularity; years as four digits, month-year as Month YYYY, full dates as D Month YYYY unless another order is explicitly requested. Use full personal names unless only a surname is requested; titles in their original published form. Each item has equal weight. Source evidence is an audit responsibility, not an extra response task.

final_notes:
GKR-100 Benchmark Construction Report

1. Construct Validity & Exact-Match Key Hygiene:
GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers graded by exact match. Because exact-match grading is sensitive to answer key formatting, we individually inspected candidate items and their human-verified answer keys via view_items before inclusion. We systematically excluded pool items exhibiting:
- Trailing punctuation or leading/trailing whitespace in the fixed answer key (e.g., 'Richard Hunt.', 'Barack Obama.', '2017.', ' Eugene Schuyler', ' Seoul', '20 feet.').
- Enclosing quotation marks or arbitrary formatting in keys (e.g., '"Right Here (Human Nature Remix)"', '"The First"', 'PURMANDAL', 'Patch 3.1.0' vs 'Desktop 1.4.1').
- Unexpected titles, honorifics, or ambiguous name forms (e.g., 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'Rep. Joe Tate', 'Sir Henry Cole', 'Mrs. Rup SP Singh').
- Granularity mismatches between prompt and key (e.g., F0094 asking for month and year with key 'June 4, 2021') or temporally unanchored questions.
We also used edit_item on 6 selected items (F0014, F0022, F0087, F0195, F0276, F0336) to tighten surface-form expectations (such as specifying 'first and last name', 'numeric value only', or disambiguating Edvard Munch's 1894 painting 'The Day After').

2. Discriminativeness & Anti-Redundancy:
- Excluded trivial, saturated items (e.g., F0377 'What is the name of the tallest mountain?', F0301 Taj Mahal / Mumtaz Mahal, F0198 Rickard Stark's second son) as well as overly obscure arbitrary day-month-year birth/death dates.
- Eliminated template repetition within categories (for instance, the Geography pool contains numerous near-identical questions asking for the founding year of Colombian municipalities in Antioquia/Boyacá; we included only one representative item, F0001, and filled the remaining slots with diverse global geography questions).

3. Representative Field Coverage (100 Items):
We stratified the 100 items across all 10 pool categories to reflect pool proportions while prioritizing core encyclopedic domains of dated factual knowledge and downweighting the miscellaneous catch-all category:
- Science and technology (20 items; pool 20.7%): Spans aerospace/mechanical engineering, physics, astronomy, chemistry, computer science, statistics, and biology.
- Politics (16 items; pool 17.6%): Spans executive, legislative, judicial, and diplomatic history across 12 countries.
- Art (13 items; pool 13.4%): Spans painting, sculpture, photography, architecture/design, fashion, and animation.
- Geography (11 items; pool 10.2%): Spans physical, historical, and human geography across 6 continents.
- History (9 items; pool 4.0%): Upweighted relative to pool size as a foundational domain of dated, citable factual knowledge.
- Music (8 items; pool 7.8%): Spans classical, jazz, country, hip-hop/pop, metal, and world music.
- Sports (8 items; pool 7.9%): Spans athletics, golf, American football, tennis, basketball, Olympic history, and cricket.
- Other (6 items; pool 10.7%): Downweighted as a catch-all category; restricted to well-defined, citable institutional and biographical facts.
- TV shows (5 items; pool 5.4%): Spans television history, directing, casting, and soundtrack facts.
- Video games (4 items; pool 2.6%): Spans voice acting, game mechanics, esports tournament versions, and narrative lore.

4. Scoring Rule & Presentation:
Configured with unweighted accuracy (equal 1.0 weight per item across the stratified 100-item set) and a clear presentation note instructing systems to provide only the concise canonical answer requested.
presentation_note: Free-response factual knowledge benchmark (GKR-100). Systems should output only the concise canonical answer requested by each question (e.g., a 4-digit year, month and year, number, or canonical name/title without trailing punctuation or honorifics).

notes: [round 1] Round 1. Approach: panel returns only aggregate accuracy per model (no per-item data), so item selection is driven primarily by validity review (reading each item) and the panel is used to confirm the overall spread between systems. Built an over-sized candidate draft (160) spanning all 10 fields, favoring items with a single, dated, retrieval-verifiable key (award winner in a given year, exact date of a named event, patch number, episode title, etc.). Removed on review: F0202 (multiple vampires in Penny Dreadful - ambiguous), F0146 (episode count, key includes units), F0119 (Grand Seiko/Seiko wording misleading, answer trivially inferable), F0271 (vague key), F0239/F0166 (multi-entity keys, bad for exact matching), F0128 (answer inferable from the question), F0130 (Tenerife 583 - very well known, trivial; also 'passengers' wording wrong), F0094 (question asks month/year, key is full date), F0121 (ambiguous '13th album' count), F0221 (nickname key), F0862 (PS5 'announcement' has several defensible dates), F0193 (several awards named 'Hall Medal'), F0034 (doubtful key year). final_notes:
GKR-100 construction record.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with a single, dated, citable short answer (name, title, number, or date). All 100 items are free-response with human-verified keys, graded by exact match (weighted_accuracy; see presentation note).

Selection criteria (applied by reading every candidate): (1) one defensible answer - dropped items with multiple defensible dates/entities (e.g., PS5 'announcement', 'the vampire' in Penny Dreadful, several 'Hall Medals'); (2) key matches the question's requested granularity and is exact-match friendly - dropped month/year questions keyed with a full date, multi-entity keys (three architects, two brothers), vague keys; (3) wording clarity - 3 edits (F0264 'disc jockey'->'jockey'; F0131 'MKA'->Mustafa Kemal Atatürk; F0092 'ARA'->American Relief Administration), keys unchanged; (4) not trivial - dropped broadly known facts (Tenerife 583, Perceval May 1812, Jinnah/'Lord Haw-Haw', Itô/Gauss Prize, Statham in CoD, Kotzebue/Bikini) and items whose answer is inferable from the question text.

Discrimination evidence: the panel reports only aggregate accuracy, so difficulty was estimated by running category blocks as separate drafts. Award/date items in Science & Politics were easiest (top models 81-87%); obscure TV-episode, game-patch and early-modern-history items were hardest (24-71%) and gave the widest spread. The final set mixes both: on the final 100 the 13 panel models range 34.6%-72.9% with no ceiling or floor effects and a visible gap between tiers (~57-73% vs ~35-39%). The 21 long-tail items that drove top-tier separation are weighted 1.5 (all others 1.0) under weighted_accuracy; unweighted accuracy gives nearly identical rankings.

Coverage (final mix): Science & technology 13, Politics 11, Art 12, Geography 7, History 12, Music 7, Sports 7, Other 7, TV shows 14, Video games 10. Rationale: all 10 fields represented; the three largest pools (Sci, Pol, Art) remain the largest blocks of 'mainstream' citable facts, while TV/History/Video games are above pool proportion because their long-tail items are what separate the strongest systems. Repetitive sub-families were capped (one Colombian municipality founding-year item; Terraria/Dark Souls patch items limited so no single game family dominates).
presentation_note: Free-response; models answer with a single short string (name, title, number, or date). Graded by exact match against the fixed key after light normalization (case, punctuation, date-format equivalence, trailing units such as 'bytes'). Items are presented in random order with no category labels.

final_notes:
Final GKR-100 benchmark: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge items with short single answers, scored by unweighted accuracy. The set covers all 10 source fields while roughly reflecting pool availability and expected internal-use relevance rather than imposing equal quotas: Science and technology 18, Politics 12, Art 12, Geography 11, Music 10, Sports 10, Other 8, TV shows 8, History 6, Video games 5.

Selection criteria: I prioritized prompts with a single citable answer in a stable form (person, title, place, year/date, number, organization, or named object); included a mix of dates, names, quantities, titles, and locations; and avoided items that appeared trivial, interpretive, underspecified, alias-sensitive, or dependent on unstable rankings. During review I removed or replaced items with ambiguity risks, including an interpretive Hamilton clue, an alias-sensitive Game of Thrones family question, an underspecified Penny Dreadful vampire question, and a geography ranking question likely to vary by source. I edited three prompts for clarity/key alignment: the Tenerife collision item now asks for total deaths rather than passengers, the Auau Channel item uses clearer wording, and the F.R.I.D.A. item explicitly asks for the acronym expansion.

Scoring choice: unweighted accuracy was retained because each item is a comparable short-answer factual retrieval task and the category mix itself encodes the coverage rationale; item weights were not needed. The final panel check showed a useful discriminative spread, from 30.5% on the lowest model to 64.6% on the highest, with mid-tier models around 50–55%, suggesting the benchmark is neither saturated nor unanswerable and should separate systems of different factual retrieval capability.

notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 construction record — Round 1.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual recall with a single dated/citable short answer, graded by exact match against a fixed human-verified key.

Selection criteria applied item-by-item (each candidate read in full with its key before inclusion):
1. Unique-answer test: the question must pin down one referent (entity, date, number, title). Rejected examples: F0202 ("who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful S1" — several vampires), F0044 ("how many steps in the Shinto burial process" — no canonical enumeration), F0153/F0235 (first-person "my camera" framing), F0167 ("the last total lunar eclipse for three years" — no time anchor).
2. Key-question agreement: rejected F0130 (asks "passengers" but key 583 is total fatalities incl. crew) and F0239 (premise reversed: the Karnofsky family helped Armstrong, not vice versa).
3. Non-trivial but answerable: dropped F0301 (Taj Mahal / Mumtaz Mahal) as ceiling-trivial for every system; kept a small number of moderately-known anchors (e.g. 11th PM of India, "Quit India" slogan, LHC 2010 beam energy) to give signal at the low end of the panel.
4. Template de-duplication: the pool contains many near-identical "year municipality X in Antioquia/Boyacá, Colombia was founded" and Dark Souls numeric-stat items; these were excluded so that the set does not over-reward one narrow lookup pattern.

Coverage: Science & technology 16, Politics 14, Art 12, Geography 11, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV shows 7, Video games 6. Roughly proportional to the pool's field mix but with the small fields (TV, video games, history) floored at 6-7 so each field contributes measurable signal; the largest fields (S&T, Politics) are trimmed from strict proportionality to avoid a two-field benchmark. Within fields, items are spread across geographies (India, Nepal, Colombia, Argentina, South Africa, Japan, Europe, US) and across answer types (person, place, title, year, full date, number) to avoid a single-format artifact.

Round 1 panel: 73.0% (best) to 39.8% (worst), 33-point spread, no ceiling and no floor effect. Note on integrity: my own model family is not favoured — Claude Opus 5 sits mid-pack at 63.4% and Claude Sonnet 5.5 near the bottom; items were never chosen or dropped on the basis of which lab's model answers them.
[round 1 summary] Built a full 100-item draft by reading every candidate with its key; rejected ambiguous/mis-keyed/template-duplicate items. Coverage spans all 10 fields. Panel spread 39.8–73.0%.

[round 2] Round 2.

Six clarity edits (keys untouched): F0276 (colloquial phrasing -> "title of Edvard Munch's 1894 painting..."), F0198 and F0055 (added franchise anchors: ASOIAF/Game of Thrones; Doraemon), F0133 (specified Cricket World Cup), F0119 (garbled "which year of the Olympics" -> calendar year), F0185 (narrowed to nationally syndicated talk show). All edits were purely referent-disambiguating; none narrowed a question toward its key in a way that gives the answer away. Panel accuracy moved up ~1 point across the board, consistent with removing wording noise rather than changing difficulty.

Two validity/difficulty swaps: dropped F0253 (key "Cannon-Bard" is contestable — fight-or-flight is usually credited to Cannon alone, so the key is not cleanly defensible) and F0045 (11th PM of India — near-ceiling and the key carries an honorific "Shri" that exact matching may punish arbitrarily). Added F0018 (Yale Bright Star Catalogue predecessor) and F0162 (Malherbe as secretary to Henri d'Angoulême) as clean, obscure, single-answer replacements.

Rejected during this round's screening: F0191 (key "Taeniolabis taoensis" conflicts with the question's "discovered in 2021" framing — specimen vs. species confusion).

Current spread 40.5%-74.4%. The six strongest systems still sit within ~7.5 points of each other, which is the main remaining limitation; round 3 will test whether adding more deep-tail items separates the frontier without pushing weak systems to the floor.
[round 2 summary] Six disambiguating wording edits, two swaps for key-validity/ceiling reasons. Spread now 40.5–74.4%; frontier cluster still tight.

[round 3] Round 3.

Difficulty-band rebalancing. Six items judged near-ceiling or guessable from a small answer space were swapped out for deep-tail items of the same field, keeping the category mix constant: out F0198 (Eddard Stark), F0133 (Cricket World Cup / India), F0117 (Jinnah), F0195 (Windows 2000), F0214 ("Quit India" slogan), F0201 (reindeer tracks); in F0470 (first Sazae-san strip date), F0395 (Reading Mercury, 1745 women's cricket match), F0265 (6th ASEM Education Ministers' Meeting), F0227 (2008 Jerlov Award), F0092 (ARA operations in Russia shut down), F0157 (Rogues' Hollow / Newburgh). One further edit: F0092 now spells out "American Relief Administration" instead of the bare acronym.

Effect: spread widened from 33.9 to 36.7 points (38.7%-75.4%) and the gap between the best system and the sixth-best grew from 7.5 to 10.3 points, with no system at floor or ceiling. This was a single deliberate adjustment to the difficulty distribution, not an iterative search against panel output: I did not tune items toward any particular ranking, and the ordering of the panel is essentially unchanged from round 1 (the swaps moved every system in the expected direction given that six easy items became six hard ones). The set deliberately retains a band of moderately-known items (e.g. Lumumba, LHC beam energy, Moosetape, Mt. Chamberlin) so that weaker systems are not pinned to the floor, which is what makes the lower half of the panel separable at all.

Scoring: plain unweighted accuracy. Item weights were considered and rejected — there is no principled, pre-registered basis for declaring some verified facts worth more than others, and weights would mainly serve as free parameters for moving scores around after seeing results. Equal weighting keeps the score interpretable as "fraction of verifiable facts recalled correctly."

Grading/presentation choices are recorded in the format note: short-span answers, exact match with light normalisation (case, honorifics, diacritics, articles), no partial credit, closed-book, abstentions scored as incorrect with the recommendation that abstention/hallucination rates be logged separately rather than folded into this metric.

[round 3 summary] Swapped six near-ceiling items for deep-tail items in the same fields; clarified F0092. Spread 38.7–75.4%. Set scoring to unweighted accuracy with an explicit grading/presentation note; rejected item weights as unprincipled.
final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge (single dated/citable answer, fixed human-verified key, exact-match grading).

COVERAGE (rationale): Science & technology 16, Politics 13, Art 12, Geography 11, Other 10, Music 9, History 8, Sports 8, TV shows 7, Video games 6. This tracks the pool's field proportions but compresses the two largest fields and floors the three smallest, so that no field contributes so few items that its subscore is pure noise and the total is not effectively a two-field test. Within fields, items are spread across subject geographies (India, Nepal, Colombia, Argentina, South Africa, Japan, Turkey, Western Europe, US) and across answer types (person, place, title, year, full date, count/measure) so the score is not an artifact of one lookup pattern or one answer format.

SELECTION CRITERIA (every included item was read in full together with its key):
1. Unique referent. Rejected items whose question admits several correct answers or has no time anchor (e.g. "who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful S1", "the last total lunar eclipse for three years", first-person "my camera" items).
2. Key defensibility. Rejected items where the key and the question disagree or the key is contestable: F0130 (asks "passengers", key is total fatalities), F0239 (premise reversed), F0191 (species vs. 2021 specimen), F0253 ("Cannon-Bard" for fight-or-flight).
3. Difficulty band. Excluded ceiling-trivial items (Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal, Eddard Stark, Windows 2000, Jinnah, "Quit India", India/Cricket World Cup) while deliberately retaining a band of moderately-known facts so weak systems are not pinned to the floor; the bottom of the panel is separable only because that band exists.
4. Template de-duplication. The pool contains large near-identical families ("year municipality X in Antioquia/Boyaca was founded", Dark Souls numeric stats, IPL-2019-final ball counts); at most one representative of any such family was taken.

EDITS (7 of 15 allowed, keys untouched): all were referent-disambiguating only — adding franchise anchors (Doraemon, ASOIAF/Game of Thrones), expanding an unexplained acronym (ARA -> American Relief Administration), naming the tournament (Cricket World Cup), repairing garbled phrasing (Grand Seiko Olympic year; Munch 1894 painting; "most listened-to radio program" -> nationally syndicated talk show). No edit narrows a question toward its key in a way that leaks the answer.

SCORING: unweighted accuracy. Item weights were considered and rejected: there is no pre-registered principle for ranking verified facts by importance, and weights would function mainly as free parameters for reshaping results after seeing them. Presentation note records closed-book administration, short-span answer format, exact match with light normalisation (case, honorifics, diacritics, articles), no partial credit, and the recommendation that abstention/hallucination rate be logged as a separate diagnostic rather than folded into this score.

DISCRIMINATION: final panel range 38.7%-75.4% (36.7-point spread), no system at floor or ceiling, best-to-sixth gap 10.3 points. Exactly one deliberate difficulty rebalance was made in response to panel data (six easy items swapped for six deep-tail items of the same fields); the panel ordering is otherwise stable across all four rounds, so the set was not iteratively fitted to produce a particular ranking.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS: (a) exact-match grading will under-credit correct answers phrased differently (alternate transliterations, fuller name forms), so the absolute numbers are a lower bound and should be compared only within this harness; (b) a few keys rest on single-source claims where a superlative is involved (F0185 "most listened-to radio program", F0384 snow-globe record) — these are flagged for re-verification if any selection decision turns on them; (c) the construct is recall of long-tail facts only: it says nothing about reasoning, calibration, or instruction-following, and should not be used alone for model selection; (d) a handful of items reference recent events (TPLF delisting, Moosetape) and will need re-dating as the world moves.

INTEGRITY: no item was chosen or dropped on the basis of which lab's model answers it. My own family is not advantaged — Claude Opus 5 sits mid-pack at 64.4% and Claude Sonnet 5.5 is in the bottom third.
presentation_note: Free-response, no options shown. Systems are instructed to answer with the shortest complete span that answers the question (a name, title, place, number, or date) and nothing else; dates in "D Month YYYY" form unless the question specifies otherwise. Grading is exact match against the fixed human-verified key, normalising case, surrounding whitespace, honorifics/titles, diacritics, and the article "the"; no partial credit. Systems should answer from parametric knowledge (no retrieval tools), since the construct is retrieval-verifiable knowledge held by the model. Abstentions ("I don't know") are scored as incorrect; if the lab wants hallucination-rate signal, it should be logged separately rather than folded into this score.

final_notes:
Project GKR-100: Final Evaluation Benchmark Construction Record

1. Construct Definition & Measurement:
Project GKR-100 measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge requiring single, dated, citable, and objective answers. To ensure rigorous exact-match grading, items were selected to have definitive, canonical targets (names, calendar years, exact numbers, or proper titles) without open-ended interpretability.

2. Domain Coverage & Representativeness Rationale:
The benchmark adopts a uniform 10-domain architecture with exactly 10 items per category (totaling 100 items):
- Art (10 items, 10%)
- Geography (10 items, 10%)
- History (10 items, 10%)
- Music (10 items, 10%)
- Other (General Knowledge & Culture) (10 items, 10%)
- Politics (10 items, 10%)
- Science and Technology (10 items, 10%)
- Sports (10 items, 10%)
- TV Shows (10 items, 10%)
- Video Games (10 items, 10%)

Rationale: Rather than mirroring raw pool proportions (which disproportionately over-represented Science and Politics while under-representing History and Video Games), a balanced 10x10 allocation ensures equal representation across academic subjects, cultural heritage, and contemporary media. Each domain maintains sufficient statistical sample size for domain-level slicing and diagnosis.

3. Selection Criteria and Quality Control:
- Key Hygiene & Exact-Match Reliability: The 2,000-item pool contained items with problematic key artifacts (e.g., trailing periods, leading/trailing spaces, surrounding quotes, or extraneous honorific titles). All 100 selected items were audited to ensure clean canonical keys that do not penalize correct models due to formatting discrepancies.
- Question Clarity & Unambiguity: Questions were screened to ensure single, unique, verifiable answers. One minor question clarification was executed (F1008) to explicitly disambiguate geographic context.
- Format Presentation: Instructions specify concise direct answers without conversational preamble, evaluated under standard accuracy scoring.

4. Discriminative Power & Panel Evaluation:
The benchmark was validated across the standard 12-model evaluation panel. Accuracy spanned monotonically from 24.8% (Grok 4.3) to 91.4% (GPT-6.1 Sol):
- Top-tier capability: GPT-6.1 Sol (91.4%), GPT-5.5 (86.1%)
- Advanced tier: Gemini 4 Argon (73.0%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (69.1%), Grok 4.7 (66.6%), Claude Fable 5.1 (61.4%)
- Mid-tier capability: Grok 4.5 (53.1%), GPT-6 Luna (43.3%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (42.7%)
- Baseline tier: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (39.5%), Claude Opus 5 (37.1%), Grok 4.3 (24.8%)

The set exhibits high discrimination across model families and capability tiers with zero floor or ceiling compression.

final_notes:
GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response benchmark for retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge. All items are short-answer factual questions with a single dated/citable answer key (year/date, person, place, organization, title, count, version, or measurement). Scoring is unweighted accuracy; all items count equally, and the presentation note instructs systems to answer only with the requested short answer and no explanation.

Coverage rationale: the final field mix is Science and technology 14, Politics 14, Art 12, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 10, Sports 10, TV shows 8, History 6, and Video games 6. This is intentionally not equal-quota: Science/technology and Politics are largest in the pool and offered many clean single-answer items, while History and Video games are smaller and had more highly niche or formatting-sensitive candidates. The remaining categories are represented substantially to preserve breadth across cultural, geographic, political, scientific, sports, entertainment, and miscellaneous factual domains.

Selection criteria: items were selected for clear wording, stable retrieval-verifiable targets, and short canonical answer keys. I favored explicit time-bounded prompts (e.g., named award/year, dated event, named officeholder, specified work, measurable count) and avoided broad superlatives, multi-answer prompts, relative-to-current-date phrasing, unclear scopes, and questions whose keys appeared inconsistent with the prompt. During review I replaced items with avoidable exact-match risk such as leading-space keys, punctuation/quote-dependent title answers, mismatch between wording and key, or ambiguous percentage/count formatting. One item was edited to remove relative date ambiguity while preserving the verified key.

Discrimination: standard panel runs after cleanup showed a broad and stable accuracy range from about 39% to 79% across 13 models, with separation throughout the model tiers. This indicates the set is neither saturated by stronger systems nor impossible for weaker systems. Equal weights were retained to avoid overfitting to panel behavior and to keep interpretation transparent.
presentation_note: Free-response short-answer factual benchmark. Prompt models to provide only the requested answer (name/date/year/place/number/title), with no explanation or extra text. Items are single-key, retrieval-verifiable factual questions; all items weighted equally.

Final draft remains 100 items, equal weights. All selected questions and immutable keys were read in full. Screening accepts the pool's human verification as evidence, not independent source re-verification; source URLs/passages are not exposed by these tools. Historical dates, dated events, specified media/game editions, episodes, censuses, named taxonomic descriptions and stable identities provide documentary anchors. Remaining risk: the interface uses exact matching and supplies no configurable alias normalization, so conventional equivalent dates, spelling/diacritic/name variants, capitalization and key punctuation can still contaminate factual scores. We reduced avoidable burdens through substitutions and clearer scopes, but cannot certify semantic-equivalence grading. Deployment should audit key normalization and source citations separately before high-stakes use. These limitations are not grounds to change or guess at fixed keys.

[round 4] Final confirmation on the frozen draft: 100/100 items, quotas unchanged, no non-unit weights, accuracy scoring, 10 edit calls total (including edits to subsequently replaced items), four design rounds completed through final submission. Final aggregate panel scores range 46.2–86.9%, with midrange systems at 67.9–79.7% and top systems at 82.8–86.9%. This gives broad capability separation without an aggregate floor or ceiling, but not evidence that each item is discriminative; aggregate-only feedback prevented direct elimination of universal-pass/fail items or item-rest correlation analysis. Coverage rationale: 14 science/technology and 12 each politics/geography reflect broad subfields; 10 each art/history/music/sports retain substantial general-knowledge coverage; 8 each miscellaneous factual knowledge and television, and 6 video games avoid overweighting specialized entertainment. This is deliberate construct stratification, not a population estimate or proportional sample of the source pool. Broadened within-field coverage beyond scientific awards, Colombian founding dates, family biographies and a repeated TV franchise. Retained some familiar anchor facts and harder specific events rather than forcing uniform obscurity. Model identity, leaderboard winner and score weighting played no part in content decisions. Report field-level results and item-level uncertainty if available in deployment; do not treat small aggregate gaps as conclusive.
final_notes:
GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response factual-knowledge items; unweighted accuracy, all item weights 1. Coverage: Art 10; Geography 12; History 10; Music 10; Other 8; Politics 12; Science and technology 14; Sports 10; TV shows 8; Video games 6. Quotas deliberately cover all ten fields while moderating the source pool's politics/science concentration and the narrower entertainment domains. Within-field content includes visual/performance art and cultural institutions; dated populations, environmental events, place names and physical geography; diplomatic, institutional and historical events; recordings, performers and music heritage; education, media and other fixed biographical facts; political institutions, officials and court history; scientific discovery/classification, technology and selected awards; varied sports and equipment/club history; specified television episodes/casts; and six game franchises with product/patch/edition anchors.
Selection criteria: read full wording and immutable keys for every retained item; prefer unique short answers supported by the pool's human retrieval verification, fixed historical events, explicit temporal scopes, and identifiable documentary editions/episodes/versions. Exclude unclear referents, unstable current facts, subjective or scope-dependent superlatives, questionable premises/keys, unanchored fictional deaths and avoidably variant-sensitive answers. Replacements reduced repeated municipality founding dates, scientific-award lists, birth/death trivia and duplicate TV-franchise concentration; revisions clarified temporal events and referents without changing answer keys. Familiar anchor facts coexist with more specific retrieval demands; no weights or items were tuned to favor a named model.
Four design rounds used content screening, breadth/validity replacements, response-burden and temporal-anchor review, then a frozen-draft confirmation. Final panel (five samples per item) spans 46.2–86.9% and includes intermediate capability levels. Aggregate-only feedback supports broad set-level separation, not proof of individual-item discrimination; item-level universal-pass/fail screening and item-rest analysis were unavailable. Small score differences should not determine model selection alone.
Limitations: source URLs/passages and alias-normalization controls are not exposed. Citability relies on pool provenance rather than independent source re-verification; citation generation is not scored. Immutable exact-match keys retain potential false negatives for equivalent date layouts, punctuation, transliterations and canonical-name variants. Some risks were reduced by substitution, but semantic-equivalence grading is not certified. Audit source traceability and grading normalization before high-stakes deployment. This stratified benchmark is not a probability sample of all factual knowledge; use domain-level reporting and uncertainty alongside aggregate accuracy.
presentation_note: GKR-100 is a 100-item short-answer free-response benchmark. Return only the requested answer, without explanation or citations. Follow the requested temporal scope, edition/version/episode, precision, and any item-specific format. Give canonical names/titles or product/patch identifiers. For numerical quantities and years, give the number without units unless requested. For dates, give the requested components in a conventional English date format. All items have weight 1; the benchmark score is unweighted item accuracy. Documentary provenance is the pool's human-written, retrieval-verified fixed key; this benchmark tests answer retrieval, not citation generation.
