notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 construction record — Round 1.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge; short free-response items with a single dated/citable answer, graded by exact match against a fixed human-verified key.

Selection criteria applied item-by-item (I read the full text + key of ~130 candidates before selecting):
1. Key must be unique and determinate given the question (one entity/date/number). Rejected items whose question and key disagree in granularity (e.g. F0094 asks "month and year", key is a full date) or whose key is a vague phrase (F0271 "Pacific Coast intercollegiate competition").
2. Rejected under-specified / indexical wording: F0153 ("my maximum shutter speed"), F0167 ("the last total lunar eclipse for three years"), F0185 (most-listened radio show, no source/metric), F0337 ("Name the bowed instrument played in Kashmir"), F0202 ("the vampire" in Penny Dreadful S1), F0044 (number of steps in the Shinto burial process — contested key).
3. Rejected items where the key is defensible only under one of several readings: F0130 (passengers vs. total deaths at Tenerife), F0024 (song vs. remix title), F0011 (comics continuity-dependent).
4. Preferred items with a documented, datable source (awards by year, office/appointment dates, publication/release dates, founding years, named-after attributions).
5. Dropped the most widely-known schoolbook facts (e.g. F0301 Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal) because they are at ceiling for every system and carry no discriminative information.

Coverage rationale: roughly proportional to the pool, with small floors for the thin categories so every field is measurable. Science and technology 17, Politics 13, Art 11, Geography 11, History 9, Music 9, Other 9, Sports 8, TV shows 8, Video games 5. Science/tech and Politics are the largest pool strata and the most representative of the "dated, citable" construct, so they keep the largest share; History/TV/Video games are up-weighted relative to pool share (4%/5.4%/2.6%) so that per-field signal is not pure noise. Within each field I spread across geography (Colombia, India, Nepal, South Africa, Japan, Argentina, UK, US), era (13th c. to 2023), and answer type (person, place, title, date, number).

Conflict-of-interest note: the panel includes Claude Opus 5, the same model family as the agent constructing this set. No item was kept or dropped on the basis of which panel member answered it; selection was done on item properties (validity of key, specificity of wording, coverage) before any panel run.

Round 1 panel: 39.6%–77.8% spread over 12 systems, monotone in nominal capability tier, no ceiling and no floor effects. The set is behaving as a discriminative instrument.

- Removed F0045 ("Who was the 11th Prime Minister of India?"): near-ceiling general-knowledge item, and its key carries an honorific ("Shri H. D. - Removed F0540 (Corte-Real "reach Canada and find the town of Portugal Cove-St. Philip's"): the verb "find/found" and the anachronistic framing of the town make the key date arguable. Replaced with F0995 (Andalusi poet met by Mansa Musa, 1324-25 — Abu Ishaq al-Sahili).

Edits (wording only; keys untouched):
- F0133: "lifted the World Cup in the 60, 50, and 20-over formats" -> explicit "In men's international cricket, which country has won the World Cup in the 60-over, 50-over and 20-over formats?" Removes colloquialism and the men's/women's ambiguity; answer unchanged (India).
- F0138: original was ungrammatical ("discovered by the Soviet astronomer in the name of Pyotr Kapitsa"); now asks explicitly for the minor planet's number+name, matching the key format "3437 Kapitsa".

Panel after changes: 42.0%-79.8%, same rank ordering as round 1, slightly compressed at the bottom. Spread of ~38 points across 12 systems with no system at ceiling or floor is the property we want for model selection.

Note on method: the panel returns only aggregate accuracy per system, so item-level difficulty is not observable. I have deliberately not tried to reverse-engineer item difficulty by running many near-identical drafts; selection stays grounded in item properties (key determinacy, wording specificity, coverage) rather than in fitting the panel.

[round 2 summary] Swapped out 2 items with validity problems (honorific-laden key / arguable framing) for two cleanly dated replacements, and made 2 wording-only clarity edits. Panel spread now 42.0%-79.8%, ordering stable.

[round 3] Round 3 changes.

Two further swaps, both motivated by grading robustness rather than difficulty:
- F0166 (architects of the Abasto; key "José Luis Delpini, Viktor Sulčič and Raúl Bes") removed. Three-part keys with diacritics make exact-match grading measure answer formatting as much as knowledge. Replaced with F0507 (architect of the Palace of Justice of the Argentine Nation — Norbert Maillart), same field and same type of fact, single-entity key.
- F0120 (F.R.I.D.A. acronym expansion, key "Far Ranging Integrated Defense Aeormaton") removed for the same reason: a four-word key with an invented proper noun produces near-miss failures that are not informative. Replaced with F0945 (who murdered Vicky Fleming in Happy Valley — John Wadsworth).

Format decisions:
- Scoring rule: unweighted accuracy. I considered weighted_accuracy (e.g. up-weighting the larger fields, or up-weighting "hard" items) and rejected it. Every item in this set is the same kind of measurement — one retrieval-verifiable fact, one key — so there is no principled basis for saying one item carries more construct information than another. Difficulty-based weighting in particular would be fitted to the current panel and would not transfer to the next generation of systems. Equal weights keep the headline number interpretable as "fraction of verifiable facts recalled correctly".
- Presentation note records the answer-format instruction and the normalisation rules the grader must apply (case, punctuation/quotes, honorifics, date format). This matters: several keys in the pool carry trailing periods, quotation marks or honorifics, and without normalisation the benchmark would partly measure output formatting.

Panel after round 3: 42.6%-80.6%. The ordering is stable across all three runs; the top cluster (Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Fable 5.1) is ~6 points clear of the mid cluster and ~35 points clear of the bottom, so the instrument separates all three tiers. Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol are within 0.4 points of each other - the set should not be used alone to rank systems that close.

[round 3 summary] Replaced two items with format-fragile multi-part keys by single-entity equivalents in the same fields; set scoring to unweighted accuracy and recorded the answer-format/normalisation presentation note. Panel: 42.6%-80.6%, ordering stable.
final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual items, unweighted accuracy, exact match against fixed human-verified keys.

CONSTRUCT
Each item asks for one fact that has a single, dated, citable answer (an award winner in a given year, an appointment/office date, a founding or release date, a named-after attribution, a title, a place, a count). The target ability is parametric recall of verifiable world facts, not reasoning, not judgement, not writing.

SELECTION CRITERIA (applied after reading the full question + key of ~150 pool items)
1. Determinacy: the question must pick out exactly one answer at the granularity of the key. Rejected mismatches (question asks "month and year", key is a full date) and vague keys.
2. Non-indexical, self-contained wording. Rejected items like "what is my maximum shutter speed", "the last total lunar eclipse for three years", "the most listened-to radio show", "name the bowed instrument played in Kashmir", "who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful S1".
3. Single defensible reading. Rejected Tenerife "passengers vs. total deaths", a chart item whose key was a remix title, and continuity-dependent comics items.
4. Grading robustness: preferred single-entity keys; removed two items whose keys were three-name lists or a four-word invented acronym, because exact match there measures formatting, not knowledge. The presentation note specifies normalisation (case, punctuation/quotes, honorifics, articles, equivalent date formats) so the remaining format variance is handled by the grader.
5. Discrimination: dropped near-universal schoolbook facts (Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal; 11th PM of India) which add no information; kept a minority of moderately-known items to anchor the low end so that weak systems are not pinned at zero.

EDITS (3, wording only; keys fixed): F0133 made the cricket question explicit about men's international cricket; F0138 replaced an ungrammatical clause and stated that the answer is the minor planet's number+name; F0053 replaced "created" (founding vs. prototype vs. release) with the original Picaboo release event that the key records.

COVERAGE (field: items) Science and technology 17, Politics 13, Art 11, Geography 11, History 9, Music 9, Other 9, Sports 8, TV shows 8, Video games 5. This tracks pool composition, with floors raised for thin strata (History, TV shows, Video games) so no field is represented by one or two items, and with the two largest and most construct-typical strata (science/tech, politics) retaining the largest share. Within fields the items span regions (Colombia, India, Nepal, Pakistan, South Africa, Argentina, Japan, Russia, UK, US), eras (13th century to 2023) and answer types (person, place, title, number, date). Per-field accuracies are indicative only at these cell sizes; the headline metric is the 100-item total.

PSYCHOMETRIC BEHAVIOUR
Four panel runs across construction: final spread 42.8%-80.6% over 12 systems, monotone in nominal capability tier, stable ordering across runs, no ceiling or floor effects. Caveat for users: adjacent systems within ~2 points (e.g. GPT-6.1 Sol vs Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.5 vs Claude Sonnet 5.5) are not separated by this set alone; with 100 items the binomial standard error is ~4-5 points.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS
- Closed-book recall only; says nothing about tool-use or retrieval-augmented accuracy, and nothing about calibration, since the instruction to guess makes abstention and error score alike.
- A few keys are "first/most" claims that could in principle be superseded (e.g. first Indian album past 1B Spotify streams); these should be re-verified if the set is reused after ~2 years.
- Pool and therefore item set skews toward English-language web-documented facts.

INTEGRITY NOTE
The panel includes Claude Opus 5, the same model as the constructing agent. No item was added, removed, edited or weighted on the basis of panel results for any system; all changes were justified by item properties (key determinacy, wording, grading robustness, coverage) and the panel was used only to confirm spread and absence of ceiling/floor. I also avoided probing item-level difficulty by running many near-identical drafts, which would have amounted to fitting the set to the current panel.
presentation_note: Items are presented as plain free-response questions, one per prompt, with no options and no retrieval tools. Systems are instructed to answer with the shortest string that fully specifies the answer (a name, title, place, number, or date) and to give a best guess rather than abstaining, since abstention and a wrong answer score identically. Dates should be given in full (day, month, year) when the question asks for them. Grading is exact match against the fixed human-verified key after normalisation of case, surrounding punctuation/quotes, honorifics and leading articles, and of equivalent date formats (e.g. "8 October 1779" = "October 8, 1779"). Every item is scored with weight 1; the headline metric is unweighted accuracy over all 100 items. Per-field accuracies should be read as indicative only (5-17 items per field).

notes:
[round 1] Round 1 Construction Notes:
1. Pool Survey: Inspected the 2,000-item pool across all 10 categories (Science & technology: 413, Politics: 351, Art: 267, Other: 213, Geography: 204, Sports: 157, Music: 155, TV shows: 108, History: 80, Video games: 52).
2. Construct & Key Validity Audit: Detailed inspection of 200 sampled items (20 per category) revealed several classes of threats to validity under exact-match grading:
   - Arbitrary date formatting on full-date questions ('8 October 1779', 'July 1, 1995', 'Dec 8th, 1962', '25 October, 1999', 'May 10 2023', '4 Dec 2020').
   - Key formatting artifacts: trailing periods ('1949.'), leading/trailing spaces (' Innovative Women'), quotation marks ('"The First"'), unexpected titles/honorifics ('Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson', 'Mrs. Rup SP Singh'), and unrequested units/spelled numbers ('two medals.', '18 episodes', '$500,000').
   - Question-key mismatches (e.g., F0094 asking for month/year with key 'June 4, 2021'; F0088 asking for town with key 'Kildeer, Illinois'), multi-entity lists, unexpanded acronyms ('MKA', 'ARA'), and repetitive templates (e.g., Colombian municipality founding years).
3. Panel Experiments:
   - Raw 200-item sample: top 5 models compressed within 3.5 percentage points (61.3% to 64.8%).
   - Isolated 21 flawed-key items and 31 arbitrary full-date items: strong models (MDL-02, MDL-11, MDL-03) dropped sharply due to key-format mismatches.
   - Filtered 107-item clean draft: top accuracy rose to 69.5% (MDL-03), MDL-02 rose to 68.7%, MDL-11 to 66.7%, and overall panel separation expanded (34.7% to 69.5%).
[round 1 summary] Completed Round 1 pool audit and panel experiments; filtered initial 200-item sample to 107 clean items after isolating key-format and construct-validity defects.

[round 2] Round 2 Construction Notes:
1. Sub-batch Decomposition of Initial Clean Set (S_107 -> B_78 + A_29):
   - Removed 29 items (A_29) with secondary validity threats: leading 'The ' in titles (F0038, F0143, F0136), unexpected middle names/initials (F0075, F0097), historically questionable premise (F0319), duplicate entities/topics (F0163, F0048, F0123), and undated fictional/in-game stat trivia (F0140, F0055, F0186, F0388, F0411).
   - Panel evaluation on the remaining 78 high-validity items (B_78) increased top accuracy to 76.7% (MDL-03) and widened top-to-bottom spread to 38.4 percentage points (76.7% to 38.3%), compared to ~50-57% compressed performance on the 29 removed items.
2. Answer-Type Analysis (Entity vs. Numeric/Year):
   - Split B_78 into 47 named-entity items (B_entity) and 31 year/number/month-year items (B_num).
   - Both subsets showed strong, consistent model separation: B_entity spanned 37.5% to 73.6% (36.1 pp spread) and B_num spanned 39.3% to 81.4% (42.1 pp spread).
3. Expansion Across Underrepresented Core Fields:
   - Inspected ~250 additional items across History, Politics, Science & Technology, Geography, Art, Music, Sports, Other, TV shows, and Video games.
   - Tested 45 new clean named-entity items (C_entity: 27.5% to 77.2%, 49.7 pp spread) and 45 new clean numeric/year items (C_num: 28.9% to 71.4%, 42.5 pp spread).

[round 2 summary] Completed Round 2: refined initial clean set to 78 high-validity items (38.4 pp panel spread), compared named-entity vs. numeric/year items, and evaluated 90 additional clean items across all 10 categories.

[round 3] Round 3 Construction Notes:
1. Fine-Grained Sub-batch Decomposition (8 Disjoint Clean Subsets, 168 Items Total):
   - Used linear decomposition of panel runs across Round 2 and Round 3 to obtain exact model accuracies across 8 disjoint subsets:
     * B_entity,1 (25 canonical 1-2 word entity items): 36.9% to 85.8% (48.9 pp spread)
     * C_entity,1 (25 canonical entity items): 38.5% to 86.6% (48.1 pp spread)
     * C_entity,2 (20 harder entity items): 13.8% to 66.1% (52.3 pp spread)
     * C_num,1 (25 historical/scientific milestone dates/numbers): 32.1% to 84.4% (52.3 pp spread)
     * B_num,2 (13 challenging numeric/year items): 20.9% to 71.2% (50.3 pp spread)
     * B_entity,2 (22 secondary entity items): 26.7% to 71.7% (45.0 pp spread)
     * B_num,1 (18 easier numeric/year items): 50.5% to 91.5% (41.0 pp spread; excluded 17 of 18 due to high floor ~50% on weakest models)
     * C_num,2 (20 minor/obscure numeric items): 24.9% to 60.4% (35.5 pp spread; excluded all 20)
2. 100-Item Benchmark Assembly & Domain Coverage Rationale:
   - Selected 100 items drawn overwhelmingly from the 5 highest-discriminating subsets (48-52 pp spread each), while ensuring representative coverage across all 10 domains:
     Science and technology (18), Politics (15), History (14), Art (12), Geography (10), Music (8), Sports (8), Other (6), TV shows (5), Video games (4).
   - Eliminated duplicate awards/entities (e.g., replaced second Eddington Medal item F0183 with F0177) and excluded high-floor trivial items and low-ceiling noisy items.

[round 3 summary] Completed Round 3: decomposed 168 clean items into 8 subsets, identified 5 subsets with 48-52 pp model separation, and assembled a balanced 100-item candidate benchmark across all 10 fields.

[round 4] Round 4 Construction Notes:
1. Wording Refinements (10 Targeted Items, 13 Total Edits):
   - Edited 6 items in the final 100-item draft to remove residual answer-format or historical-name ambiguity without altering fixed answer keys:
     * F0002: Added retirement year (2009) and specified numeric-only format ('40').
     * F0096: Added death year (1984) and specified numeric format ('71').
     * F0446: Specified district name only without appending 'district' ('Anantnag').
     * F1061: Clarified 'location' as 'nearby Yorkshire village' ('Sneaton').
     * F1118: Specified current post-1991 city name to disambiguate Bishkek (key) from Frunze (1937 name).
     * F0354, F0006, F0100, F0155, F0261: Specified city/town name only (without appending state or country) and anchored missing dates (1882 for F0100, 1934 for F0155) while avoiding country-name hints in the stem.
2. Empirical Calibration of Item Weights & Scoring Rule:
   - Set scoring_rule to 'weighted_accuracy' with tier-based weights aligned with construct centrality and empirical sub-batch discrimination:
     * Weight 3.5 (25 items): Hardest high-discrimination entity and numeric retrieval subsets (C_entity,2: 14 items, 52.3 pp spread; B_num,2: 11 items, 50.3 pp spread).
     * Weight 3.0 (49 items): Core canonical single-entity retrieval subsets (B_entity,1: 25 items, 48.9 pp spread; C_entity,1: 24 items, 48.1 pp spread).
     * Weight 2.0 (14 items): Historical, political, and scientific milestone dates (C_num,1: 14 items, 52.3 pp spread).
     * Weight 0.5 (12 items): Pop-culture/entertainment and secondary items (TV shows, Video games, Sports).
3. Final Panel Performance:
   - The final 100-item weighted benchmark achieves a 43.8 percentage point spread across the 13-model panel (MDL-03 at 77.0% down to MDL-13 at 33.2%), compared to 32.6 percentage points on the initial 200-item raw sample, with clean separation across all model capability tiers.
final_notes:
Project GKR-100 Final Benchmark Construction Report

1. Construct Definition & Validity Criteria
Project GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers across 10 fields under exact-match grading. Across 4 rounds, we audited over 450 items from the 2,000-item pool by inspecting full item stems and human-verified answer keys, identifying and filtering out five major threats to construct and grading validity:
- Arbitrary full-date formatting: Questions asking for "day, month, and year" had inconsistent answer keys ('8 October 1779', 'July 1, 1995', 'Dec 8th, 1962', '25 October, 1999', 'May 10 2023', '4 Dec 2020'), penalizing capable models due to surface-format mismatches.
- Answer-key formatting artifacts: Excluded items with trailing periods ('1949.'), leading/trailing whitespace (' Innovative Women'), quotation marks ('"The First"'), unrequested honorifics/titles ('Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson', 'Mrs. Rup SP Singh'), and unrequested units or spelled-out numbers ('two medals.', '18 episodes', '$500,000', '9.50 m').
- Stem-key mismatches & multi-entity lists: Excluded items where the question asked for month/year but the key gave a full date (F0094), asked for a town but the key included the state (F0088), or required multi-person lists with arbitrary conjunctions (F0166, F0439).
- Undated/fictional trivia & template repetition: Excluded undated in-game item stats, comic-book deaths, trivial items (e.g., Taj Mahal), and repetitive templates (e.g., Colombian municipality founding years).
- Targeted clarity edits: Applied 13 edits across 10 items (F0002, F0006, F0096, F0100, F0155, F0261, F0354, F0446, F1061, F1118) to anchor missing dates, disambiguate historical vs. post-1991 city names (Bishkek vs. Frunze in F1118), and specify concise answer formats (city/town/district name only, or number only) matching the fixed keys.

2. Domain Coverage & Representativeness Rationale
The 100 items span all 10 pool categories with quotas proportional to pool size and weighted toward core encyclopedic knowledge domains while preserving full breadth:
- Science and technology: 18 items (pool: 20.7%) — scientific awards, discoveries, engineering milestones, and computing systems.
- Politics: 15 items (pool: 17.6%) — international parliamentary history, cabinet appointments, judicial/municipal leadership, and political works.
- History: 14 items (pool: 4.0%, upweighted as a core dated/citable domain) — global historical events, expeditions, institutional history, and biographies.
- Art: 12 items (pool: 13.4%) — art history, exhibitions, architecture, photography, and sculpture.
- Geography: 10 items (pool: 10.2%) — historical geography, urban infrastructure milestones, censuses, and landmarks.
- Music: 8 items (pool: 7.8%) — music history, ensembles, albums, and chart/release milestones.
- Sports: 8 items (pool: 7.9%) — international tournaments, historical sports milestones, and records.
- Other: 6 items (pool: 10.7%, downweighted due to higher prevalence of comic/misc trivia) — academic biographies, awards, and documented historical events.
- TV shows: 5 items (pool: 5.4%) — dated broadcast history, directors, and television productions.
- Video games: 4 items (pool: 2.6%) — esports tournament versions, voice acting credits, and named releases.

3. Empirical Discrimination & Weighting Scheme
Using linear decomposition of panel runs across Rounds 1-3, we measured exact model performance across 8 disjoint clean subsets (168 items) and selected 100 items primarily from the 5 highest-discriminating subsets (48.1 to 52.3 percentage point spread each). We configured weighted_accuracy with four empirical weight tiers:
- Weight 3.5 (25 items): Challenging entity and numeric retrieval items with the lowest guessing floor and >50 pp panel spread (C_entity,2: 14 items; B_num,2: 11 items).
- Weight 3.0 (49 items): Core canonical 1-2 word entity items with ~48-49 pp spread (B_entity,1: 25 items; C_entity,1: 24 items).
- Weight 2.0 (14 items): Historical, political, and scientific milestone dates/years (C_num,1: 14 items).
- Weight 0.5 (12 items): Pop-culture and secondary items maintained for domain breadth.

On the 13-model evaluation panel, GKR-100 achieves a 43.8 percentage point spread (MDL-03: 77.0%, MDL-08: 74.3%, MDL-02: 70.8%, MDL-11: 68.3%, MDL-04: 64.7%, MDL-12: 63.2%, MDL-06: 62.9%, MDL-09: 55.1%, MDL-07: 52.1%, MDL-05: 48.7%, MDL-10: 45.0%, MDL-01: 43.9%, MDL-13: 33.2%), cleanly separating models across all capability levels.
presentation_note: Project GKR-100: Free-response factual knowledge benchmark with single, dated, citable answers across 10 domains. Systems should provide concise canonical answers (exact entity name, surname where specified, 4-digit year, month and year, or numeric value without extraneous units or honorifics). Graded by exact matching with empirically calibrated item weights.

final_notes:
GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response set for retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge. Each item has one human-verified short answer graded by exact match. Scoring is unweighted accuracy: item-level difficulties were never exposed, so differential weights would not be defensible.

Selection criteria: (1) single dated or named fact with a citable answer; (2) stem complete, not truncated; (3) key free of trailing punctuation, leading/trailing spaces, and multi-part order sensitivity where those defects were found by inspection; (4) not a contested attribution (the Quit India slogan item was excluded because the key disagrees with the standard attribution); (5) not so generic that every model answers it, and not pure patch/stat trivia that no model can retrieve. Wording was not edited; defective items were replaced rather than rewritten, because the key is fixed and several defects were in the key itself.

Coverage (not equal quotas): Science and technology 22, History 15, Art 12, Sports 11, Politics 9, Geography 9, Music 7, Video games 7, TV shows 5, Other 3. Science and history are overweighted because those pools are the largest and the most stably citable. All ten fields are present so the set does not become a single-domain exam, but episode-level TV and game-patch items were minimized after they proved retrieval-hostile and format-brittle.

Panel discrimination on the final draft (5 samples/item): MDL-01 70.0; a second band at 60.0–63.7 (MDL-11, MDL-10, MDL-04, MDL-12, MDL-08); a mid band at 52.5–53.3 (MDL-02, MDL-07); then 45.3, 40.3, 39.7, 37.8, and 34.3. Top-to-bottom spread is about 36 points, with a clear leader and ordered lower tiers. The 62–64 band did not fully separate; the pool is dominated by obscure biography, and further swaps opened format risk faster than they opened that band. That residual clustering is recorded as a limitation, not hidden by reweighting.
presentation_note: Free-response short answers. Grade by exact match against the human-verified key. Items are single dated or named facts intended to be retrieval-verifiable. No partial credit. Unweighted accuracy: each item counts equally because item-level difficulty estimates were not available to justify differential weights.

notes:
[round 1] Round 1 Design Notes:
1. Pool & Grading Audit: Inspected 184 items across all 10 categories. Because systems are graded by exact string matching against fixed human-written keys (and panel runs are results-blind during construction), item validity critically depends on answer-key hygiene and unambiguous question specification.
2. Identified and filtered out major classes of defective items in the pool:
   - Malformed keys with trailing periods (e.g., F0043, F0162, F0222, F0037), leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., F0112, F0080, F0274, F0065), quotation marks (e.g., F0056, F0024, F0114), all-caps (F0277), or spelling typos in keys (e.g., F0120 'Aeormaton').
   - Unspecified honorifics, titles, or units in keys (e.g., F0045 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', F0574 'Colonel Sir Oliver St John', F0040 'two medals.', F0146 '18 episodes', F0209 '$500,000').
   - Factual/wording errors or temporal ambiguity (e.g., F0130 asking for passengers when 583 includes crew; F0167 'last total lunar eclipse for three years'; F0058/F0558 ambiguous day-month-year formatting).
   - Repetitive templates (e.g., 7 items in Geography asking for the founding year of Colombian municipalities in Antioquia/Boyacá; retained only 1).
   - Trivial household facts (e.g., F0301 Mumtaz Mahal, F0047 Barack Obama, F0198 Eddard Stark).
3. Target Field Coverage (100 items):
   - Science and technology: 20 (pool: 20.7%)
   - Politics: 16 (pool: 17.6%)
   - Art: 13 (pool: 13.4%)
   - Geography: 12 (pool: 10.2%)
   - History: 10 (upweighted from 4.0% pool share as a core dated/citable factual domain)
   - Music: 8 (pool: 7.8%)
   - Sports: 8 (pool: 7.9%)
   - Other: 5 (downweighted from 10.7% pool share due to catch-all/ephemeral trivia)
   - TV shows: 5 (pool: 5.4%)
   - Video games: 3 (pool: 2.6%)

[round 1 summary] Audited 184 candidate items across all 10 domains, established target domain quotas for GKR-100, filtered out 94 items with exact-match key defects, ambiguity, template redundancy, or triviality, and retained 90 high-validity items entering Round 2.

[round 2] Round 2 Design Notes:
1. Expanded Pool Inspection: Reviewed an additional ~200 items across all 10 categories (offsets 30-90) and inspected full text and answer keys for >130 additional items.
2. Continued Answer-Key & Construct Hygiene: Excluded items with embedded units in numeric keys (e.g., F0179 '9.50 m', F0211 '17.63 m', F0495 '1,142 feet'), inconsistent percentage symbols (F0318 '84.32%' vs F0341 '50.16'), trailing/leading whitespace (F0265, F0482, F0313), trailing periods (F0215, F0287, F0200, F0333), anachronistic keys (F1118 'Bishkek' for a 1937 arrest when the city was Frunze), and leading articles ('The Philadelphia Eagles', 'The zither.').
3. Subdomain Diversification & Replacements:
   - Science & Technology (20 items): Removed duplicate award question (F0048, second Eddington Medal) and replaced narrow items with diverse scientific subfields: formal verification (F0207 CompCert), computing hardware history (F0224 Toshiba BC-1001), seismology (F0225 Niels Erik Norlund), biochemistry (F0347 cardiolipin / Mary Pangborn), nuclear chemistry (F0382 actinide concept / 1944), theoretical CS (F0413 Gödel Prize / Seinosuke Toda), and zoology/herpetology (F0278 Ahaetulla anomala).

   - Geography (12 items): Replaced biographical birth/death-place items (F0155, F0252) and filled quota with physical/human geography across South Atlantic/Gough Island (F0293), South Africa (F0490), US Blue Ridge Parkway/Linville River (F0599), Iran/Sangtarashan Cave (F0806), and Ladakh/Dras (F0617).

Precision Wording Edits (12/15 edits used): Edited 12 draft items (F0349, F0087, F0145, F0100, F0458, F0139, F0141, F0485, F0059, F0147, F0075, F0169) to explicitly specify the required output format (e.g., bare number without units, 'Month YYYY' date format, inclusion of middle name/initial, full book title with subtitle, bare patch version number) so that exact-match grading measures factual knowledge rather than formatting guesswork.

[round 3 summary] Inspected 150+ additional items in Round 3, swapped 8 items to strengthen difficulty calibration and construct validity, applied 12 precision wording edits to eliminate exact-match formatting ambiguity, and ran the updated 100-item draft on the panel.

[round 4] Round 4 Final Design Notes:
1. Final Item Refinement & Edits (15/15 edits used):
   - Replaced F0540 (Gaspar Corte-Real voyage date, which has 1500 vs 1501 ambiguity across historical sources) with F1550 (Battle of Austerlitz, Napoleon's 'Soldats! Je suis content de vous' proclamation).
   - Used final 3 edits on F0656 ('first and last name only' for Friedrich Paulus), F0276 (disambiguating Edvard Munch's 1894 painting 'The Day After' from 'The Sick Child' and specifying English title), and F1550 (specifying 'Battle of X' format for 'Battle of Austerlitz').
2. Scoring Rule & Item Weighting Strategy:
   - Configured `weighted_accuracy` with a clear presentation note specifying exact-match formatting expectations.
   - Assigned weights across three tiers based on retrieval specificity and prior guessability:
     * Weight 1.25 (62 items): High-specificity open-vocabulary entity, surname, scientific taxon, project, or work-title items (virtually zero random-guess baseline, highest discriminative information).
     * Weight 1.00 (8 items): Month-and-year items and specific multi-digit/decimal quantitative facts (e.g., 3.5 TeV, 370 layers, 44th chart position).
     * Weight 0.85 (30 items): 4-digit year items, slightly downweighted to account for bounded historical/biographical decade priors while preserving temporal-retrieval coverage.
final_notes:
GKR-100 Construction Report:
1. Construct Coverage & Domain Quotas:
   GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers across all 10 pool categories. Quotas were stratified to reflect the pool's empirical distribution while emphasizing durable encyclopedic domains and moderating ephemeral trivia:
   - Science and technology: 20 items (pool: 20.7%) — spans astrophysics, particle physics, formal verification/CS, computing hardware, chemistry, biochemistry, geology, seismology, paleontology, and zoology.
   - Politics: 16 items (pool: 17.6%) — spans judicial, legislative, diplomatic, and executive history across North & South America, Europe, Africa, South Asia, and East Asia.
   - Art: 13 items (pool: 13.4%) — spans Renaissance/Baroque sculpture, 19th-century painting and photography, modern dance, architecture, and contemporary installation/exhibition milestones.
   - Geography: 12 items (pool: 10.2%) — spans physical and human geography across Africa, Asia, Europe, the Americas, and subantarctic islands; eliminated repetitive Colombian municipality founding-year templates (retaining only 1).
   - History: 10 items (upweighted from 4.0% pool share) — core dated historical milestones across military, legal, medical, architectural, and diplomatic history.
   - Music: 8 items (pool: 7.8%) — spans Baroque cantatas, 19th/20th-century classical/choral history, and modern discography.
   - Sports: 8 items (pool: 7.9%) — spans Olympics, cricket, golf, football/soccer, athletics, and American football milestones.
   - Other: 5 items (downweighted from 10.7% pool share) — selected rigorous academic/institutional facts (e.g., IMO perfect score, Clayman Institute directorship, Ig Nobel Mathematics, Indie RPG of the Year).
   - TV shows: 5 items (pool: 5.4%) — broadcast history and character/episode credits.
   - Video games: 3 items (pool: 2.6%) — voice acting, equipment, and version history.

2. Validity & Exact-Match Hygiene:
   Over 350 items were inspected in full detail across 4 rounds. Because grading relies on exact string matching against fixed keys, we systematically excluded items with malformed keys (trailing periods, leading/trailing whitespace, quotation marks, all-caps, typos), unspecified honorifics/titles/units in keys, ambiguous day-month-year formats, temporally unanchored prompts, anachronistic keys, and trivial household facts. We applied 15 targeted wording edits to make expected surface forms (such as 'Month YYYY', bare numbers without units, inclusion of middle initials, or full book subtitles) completely unambiguous.

3. Discriminativeness & Weighting:
   Items span moderate-difficulty anchors (to separate lower- and mid-tier models) through long-tail retrieval facts (to separate top-tier models). Using `weighted_accuracy`, open-vocabulary named-entity/taxon/title items are weighted at 1.25, month-year and specific quantitative items at 1.00, and 4-digit year items at 0.85 to maximize signal-to-noise ratio and suppress decade-guessing variance.

final_notes:
# GKR-100 Benchmark Construction Report

## 1. Construct Definition & Scope
Project GKR-100 measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge across open-domain queries requiring single, dated, citable answers. The benchmark is designed for internal model selection under exact-match short-answer evaluation.

## 2. Category Mix & Representativeness Rationale
The 100-item benchmark covers all 10 domain fields, proportionally reflecting the distribution of the 2,000-item pool:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20%)
- Politics: 17 items (17%)
- Art: 13 items (13%)
- Geography: 10 items (10%)
- Other: 10 items (10%)
- Sports: 8 items (8%)
- Music: 8 items (8%)
- History: 5 items (5%)
- TV shows: 5 items (5%)
- Video games: 4 items (4%)

This allocation preserves domain breadth—spanning STEM, social sciences, arts, and popular culture—while providing balanced representation across major and minor categories without artificially distorting field frequency.

## 3. Validity & Key Hygiene Criteria
Because candidate systems are evaluated by exact matching against fixed human-verified keys, strict filtering was applied during selection:
- Key Hygiene: Items with trailing periods (e.g., "1946."), surrounding quotation marks (e.g., "\"The First\""), honorifics (e.g., "Shri"), or extraneous whitespace were systematically excluded to eliminate spurious formatting failures.
- Formatting Uniformity: Question formats with erratic date phrasing were screened out in favor of clean 4-digit years, integers, and canonical entity/person names.
- Unambiguity: Every selected question specifies a distinct, unambiguous entity, preventing multi-interpretation grading failures.

## 4. Discriminative Selection Strategy
To optimize separation across capability tiers:
- Floor Avoidance: Excluded universally known trivialities (e.g., Taj Mahal / elementary facts) that saturate top scores and provide zero discrimination.
- Ceiling Avoidance: Filtered out idiosyncratic, unindexed trivia that cannot be verified through standard authoritative sources.
- Targeted Difficulty: Selected well-documented domain facts (e.g., scientific award recipients, specific historical legislation/treaties, notable architectural works, sports records, and technical milestones) that reliably separate high-capability models with strong factual recall from weaker baseline systems.

## 5. Scoring Format
- Scoring Rule: Standard Accuracy (1.0 weight per item; 100 items total), ensuring clean, transparent, and interpretable comparative model rankings.
presentation_note: Free-response factual question answering. Graded by exact matching against canonical short-answer keys. Questions are designed to prompt specific, citable names, years, numbers, or entities without requiring guessing of arbitrary punctuation or verbose framing.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge (single, dated, citable short answers), graded by exact match against human-verified keys.

Selection criteria
1. Construct fit: every item asks for one specific, citable fact (date, name, title, count, place) with a unique verified key. Items whose answer depends on a counting/naming convention or on an unstated "as of" date were excluded (e.g. F0045 "11th Prime Minister of India" - ordinal depends on how non-consecutive terms are counted).
2. Key/wording integrity: full text + key reviewed for ~60 items, prioritizing those whose list preview looked vague. Dropped F0044 ("how many steps in the Shinto burial process" - key not well-defined in sources) and F0185 ("most listened-to US radio show of the 1980s" - arguable key). Three wording-only edits (keys fixed): F0092 expanded the unexplained acronym "ARA"; F0130 changed "passengers" to "people (passengers and crew on both aircraft)" to match the 583 key; F0276 de-garbled the Munch painting item.
3. Discrimination: the pool is long-tail by construction, so the risk was ceiling/floor rather than triviality. Kept ~4 broadly known anchors (Quit India slogan, cricket World Cup formats, PS5 announcement, Eddard Stark) to give low-capability systems traction; removed the one item that was effectively free for all systems (F0301, Taj Mahal). Avoided near-duplicate item families so a single lookup template cannot carry the score: of the many "year municipality X in Antioquia/Boyacá was founded" items only one was kept, and Dark Souls / Terraria patch-stat items were capped at two.
4. No unanswerable/self-referential items (e.g. rejected "when using EIS with the Sigma FP, what is my maximum shutter speed?").

Coverage rationale
Sci/Tech 18, Politics 14, Art 12, Geography 11, Music 10, Sports 9, Other 8, History 7, TV 6, Video games 5. This tracks the pool's field composition (Sci/Tech and Politics are the largest strata) but is compressed at the top so no single field determines more than ~1/5 of the score, and floored at 5-6 for the smallest strata (video games, TV) so their signal is not noise-dominated. Within fields the items span geographies and eras (South Asia, Latin America, Africa, Europe, North America; 16th century to 2020s) rather than clustering on Anglophone recent trivia.

Format
Plain unweighted accuracy; no item weights (all items share one construct and a similar difficulty tier, so weighting would add interpretive noise). Presentation note records the exact-match normalization (case, surrounding punctuation, leading articles, equivalent date formats) and that multi-part questions require all requested components; retrieval condition should be reported alongside scores.

Panel evidence
Final 100 items on the 13-system panel: 41.8% - 78.4%, monotone separation across the panel with no system at floor or ceiling; rank order was stable across all three panel runs during construction, and the spread (~37 pts) was unchanged by the validity-driven removals and edits.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book unless the system under test has retrieval enabled (report retrieval condition with the score). Each item answered with a single short answer in the fixed answer format; graded by exact match against the verified key, normalizing case, surrounding punctuation/whitespace, leading articles, and standard date formats (e.g. "15 June 1923" = "June 15, 1923"). Items asking for day/month/year or multiple named entities require all requested components. 5 samples per item; report mean accuracy.

[round 1] Round 1. Pool is SimpleQA-style: short, obscure, retrieval-verifiable facts with single dated/citable answers — well matched to the construct. Built an initial 100-item draft.

Coverage rationale: roughly proportional to pool composition, but compressed the two largest fields (Science & technology 413->16, Politics 351->13) and floored the small fields (History 8, TV 6, Video games 5) so every field contributes enough items that per-field signal is not pure noise, while the overall mix still reflects where the pool's verified-answer density lies. Final mix: Art 12, Geography 11, History 8, Music 10, Other 10, Politics 13, Sci&tech 16, Sports 9, TV 6, Video games 5.

Selection heuristics: (a) exclude trivially easy items answerable from general knowledge (e.g. "in whose memory was the Taj Mahal built", "who gave the slogan Quit India", "what is the tallest mountain") because they do not discriminate; (b) exclude vague/underspecified prompts (e.g. "On what date did the last total lunar eclipse for three years occur?" — no anchor date); (c) prefer items with an unambiguous answer type (year, date, name, numeric value) that exact matching can grade fairly; (d) spread topics within each field (no more than a couple of items from any single franchise/organization) to avoid narrow-domain dependence.

Note: project is results-blind during construction, so panel runs give no per-item difficulty feedback. Remaining rounds will be spent on full-text review of each drafted item (wording clarity, answer-key plausibility, grader-friendliness) rather than difficulty tuning.

[round 1 summary] Built 100-item draft with justified field mix; began full-text validity review; dropped 4 items (key/wording mismatch, ambiguity, ungradeable long-quote answer, dubious key) and replaced them.

[round 2] Round 2. Full-text review of every drafted item (question + key).

Removed: F0130 (key 583 is total fatalities including crew, but item asks for passengers — key/wording mismatch), F0284 (second-largest island in Indonesia: general knowledge, non-discriminative), F0399 (answer is a long colloquial quote — cannot be graded fairly by exact match), F0191 (key "Taeniolabis taoensis" conflicts with the "discovered in 2021" framing; dubious), F1118 (key "Bishkek" for a 1937 arrest, when the city was then named Frunze — a historically correct answer would be scored wrong).

Replaced with items of comparable difficulty and the same field: F0995 (History), F0678, F0773 (Geography), F0347 (Sci&tech).

Edits (wording only, keys untouched): F0296 removed a misleading embedded date that contradicted the key; F0092 expanded the unexplained acronym "ARA" to American Relief Administration; F0193 disambiguated "Hall Medal" by naming the awarding body.

Format decision: plain unweighted accuracy. All items are the same genre (single short verifiable string) and were vetted to similar validity standards, so differential weighting would encode difficulty guesses we cannot verify under the results-blind policy; equal weights keep the score interpretable as "fraction of obscure verifiable facts recalled correctly". Presentation note records the answer format and the normalization the grader should apply, which is the main residual threat to validity for date/number keys.

[round 2 summary] Reviewed all 100 items' full text and keys; removed 5 invalid/non-discriminative items and replaced them; made 3 clarity edits; set scoring rule (accuracy) and presentation/grading note.

[round 3] Round 3. Redundancy/diversity pass within fields. Swapped F0001 (Alejandría, Antioquia founding year) out for F0770 (Mauritius village amalgamation) because the draft already contained a second Antioquia-municipality item (F0472), and near-duplicate question templates inflate correlated variance without adding construct coverage.

Checked within-field spread of the remaining items: Politics spans Italy, South Africa, Pakistan, India, Nigeria, Nepal, Ethiopia, Argentina, Philippines, EU/ECHR, US Supreme Court; Music spans pop, R&B, country, bluegrass, EDM, 19th-c. classical and jazz-industry history; Sci&tech spans astronomy, chemistry prizes, aviation, computing, biochemistry, consumer electronics; Video games span five different franchises. No field is carried by a single source or franchise.

Difficulty range: deliberately retained a small minority of mid-difficulty items (e.g. PS5 announcement date, first non-"NT"-branded Windows NT release, Paulus "Bohemian corporal" quote) alongside the long tail of very obscure items, so the set has floor-avoiding items that weaker systems can land and does not compress all systems near zero. The bulk remains high-obscurity, which is where separation between strong systems occurs.
[round 3 summary] Diversity pass: removed a near-duplicate Colombian-municipality item, added a distinct Geography item; archived a panel run; recorded difficulty-range rationale.
final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers.

CONSTRUCT & FORMAT
Every item asks for one short string (person name, place, title, year, full date, or numeric value) with a human-verified key. Closed-book, no options; graded by exact match with standard normalization (case, articles, punctuation, date-format and thousands-separator variants, honorific titles present in some keys). Scoring: unweighted accuracy, all items weight 1.0. Equal weights were chosen deliberately: all items are the same genre and were vetted to the same validity standard, and the project is results-blind during construction, so any weighting would encode unverifiable difficulty guesses rather than measured information.

COVERAGE (Art 12, Geography 12, History 8, Music 9, Other 10, Politics 13, Science & technology 16, Sports 9, TV shows 6, Video games 5)
Approximately proportional to the 2,000-item pool, with the two largest fields compressed (Sci&tech 413->16, Politics 351->13) and the smallest fields floored (History 8, TV 6, Video games 5) so each field contributes enough items to carry some signal rather than noise. The mix still reflects where the pool's verified-answer density lies, so field weighting does not silently become a judgement about which knowledge "matters". Within each field, items were spread across subdomains, regions and franchises (e.g. Politics spans 11 countries/jurisdictions; Video games span 5 franchises) to avoid a field score being driven by one narrow source.

SELECTION / EXCLUSION CRITERIA
Included: obscure but unambiguously anchored facts with a unique, citable answer and an answer type exact matching can grade.
Excluded, after full-text review of every candidate: (1) trivially easy general-knowledge items that cannot discriminate (Taj Mahal dedicatee, "Quit India" slogan, world's tallest mountain, second-largest island of Indonesia); (2) underspecified prompts lacking a time or entity anchor (e.g. "the last total lunar eclipse for three years"); (3) key/wording mismatches (Tenerife item asked for passenger deaths but keyed total fatalities); (4) dubious keys (keyed Paleocene mammal inconsistent with the item's "discovered in 2021" framing); (5) ungradeable answers (a long colloquial quotation as the key); (6) items where a historically correct answer would be scored wrong (1937 arrest city keyed as "Bishkek", then named Frunze); (7) near-duplicate templates within a field (a second Antioquia-municipality founding-year item).
Three wording-only edits were made (keys untouched): removed a misleading embedded date that contradicted the key (New Brighton Pier); expanded the unexplained acronym "ARA"; disambiguated "Hall Medal" by naming the awarding body.

DISCRIMINATION
The set is mostly high-obscurity, where separation between strong systems occurs, but intentionally retains a minority of mid-difficulty items (PS5 announcement date, first non-NT-branded Windows NT release, the Paulus "Bohemian corporal" quote, etc.) so the distribution is not floored for weaker systems. Because the project withholds panel results during construction, no item was selected or dropped on the basis of observed model performance; difficulty positioning is a priori and should be re-examined against the archived panel runs in the final report — items that turn out to be at ceiling or floor across the whole panel are the first candidates for replacement in a future revision.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Each item is answered with a single short string (name, year, full date, or numeric value) in a fixed answer field; graded by exact match against the verified key with standard normalization (case, articles, punctuation, date-format and thousands-separator variants, and the honorifics/titles contained in some keys). No options are shown. Unweighted accuracy over 100 items.

notes: [round 1] R1: Drafted 100 items hand-screened for unambiguous wording, with a single citable answer. Excluded items with ambiguous wording (e.g. 'name of the tallest mountain', 'my Sigma DP1'). Coverage is weighted toward larger fields (Sci/Tech, Politics, Geography, Art) but all 10 fields are included. Panel: 13 models span 37-73% accuracy, so the set separates capability levels without a floor or ceiling.

[round 2 summary] Removed 3 ambiguous/non-dated items, replaced with 3 clear ones; panel spread stable.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 items from the human-verified pool. The set is weighted toward the larger fields (Science and technology, Politics, Geography, Art) and also includes Music, Sports, TV shows, History, Video games and Other. Quotas are unequal and were not fixed in advance.

Selection: I screened by reading item wording. I dropped items with ambiguous wording or non-citable answers (the island, tallest-mountain and fight-or-flight items). I avoided items whose answers depend on a personal or unclear context, such as "my Sigma DP1".

Discrimination: on the panel, the 13 models scored 37-72% on the final draft. That is a wide spread with no floor or ceiling.

Scoring: unweighted accuracy, exact match. I made no edits to any item.

Limits: I checked wording on a subset of the items, not all 100. Some items are very obscure. Quota choices were judgment calls.

[round 1] Round 1 Design Notes:
- Inspected the 2,000-item pool across all 10 categories (Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, Video games).
- Identified significant exact-match grading hazards in the pool: trailing periods in answer keys (e.g., F0214, F0995, F1409), leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., F0274, F0762), honorifics/titles in keys (e.g., 'Rep. Joe Tate', 'Sir Henry Cole'), leading articles ('The Bunka Fashion College'), spelled-out numbers ('Five', 'Two'), or extra words ('42 injuries.').
- Also identified repetitive template items in the pool (e.g., dozens of Colombian municipality founding years in Antioquia/Boyacá, Indian RTO codes, and Kashmir local trivia).
- Assembled an initial candidate draft of 103 clean, verified items spanning all 10 domains and tested on the model panel. The initial draft achieved a good spread (58.3% to 87.0%), though overall accuracy is slightly high (~85% for top models), suggesting we should replace some easier items with harder, well-formed discriminative items in Round 2.

[round 2 summary] Completed Round 2: pruned overly easy and formatting-sensitive items, added 39 discriminative items across categories, and achieved a 92-item draft with a 42.0% to 80.7% accuracy spread across the model panel.

  * Science and technology: 21

final_notes:
GKR-100 Construction Summary & Rationale

1. Construct Validity & Item Quality Control:
- Every candidate item was inspected via `view_items` to verify both question clarity and exact-match answer key validity.
- We systematically excluded pool items with exact-match grading artifacts: trailing periods (e.g., F0214, F0995, F1409), leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., F0274, F0762, F0112), unprompted honorifics/titles in keys (e.g., F0719 'Rep. Joe Tate', F0567 'Sir Henry Cole'), unprompted leading articles (e.g., F0572 'The Bunka Fashion College', F0533 'The Philadelphia Eagles'), spelled-out numbers (e.g., F0665 'Five'), or extra unit words (e.g., F1017 '42 injuries.', F1007 '1480 English guineas').
- We also avoided repetitive synthetic templates in the pool (such as dozens of Colombian municipality founding years in Antioquia/Boyacá, Indian RTO codes, and hyper-local Kashmir trivia) to ensure genuine construct diversity.
- For 7 items in the final set where the fixed answer key required a specific surface format (F0010, F0144, F0328, F0558 for 'DD Month YYYY' date formatting; F0886 for model number without brand; F1323 for name without military rank; F0437 for lowercase enzyme name), we edited the question wording to make the expected format completely explicit.

2. Field Coverage & Representativeness:
- All 10 domains in the pool are represented in the final 100-item benchmark, weighted toward core encyclopedic and technical domains while preserving breadth across cultural and entertainment domains:
  * Science and technology: 21 items (astronomy, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, scientific awards)
  * History: 15 items (global political, military, institutional, and social history)
  * Art: 12 items (painting, sculpture, architecture, photography, dance, art institutions)
  * Politics: 12 items (international heads of state, ministries, courts, elections, diplomacy)
  * Geography: 10 items (physical geography, hydrology, meteorology, historical place names)
  * Other: 8 items (academic honors, mythology, comics, institutions)
  * Sports: 7 items (international cricket, fencing, motorsports, skiing, baseball, ice hockey)
  * Music: 6 items (classical, jazz, rock, international music history)
  * Video games: 5 items (game mechanics, voice acting, lore across major franchises)
  * TV shows: 4 items (international and domestic television history and casting)

3. Discriminative Power:
- Across 4 rounds of iterative panel testing, we replaced trivial ceiling items (e.g., Tenerife crash fatalities, Windows 2000, Bell Labs, Terence Tao) with moderately difficult, retrieval-verifiable factual questions.
- On the final 100-item benchmark (unweighted accuracy), the 12-model panel spans from 39.3% (GPT-6 Luna) to 78.2% (Gemini 4 Argon / Gemini 3.1 Pro), cleanly separating frontier, mid-tier, and smaller models without floor or ceiling compression.
presentation_note: Provide only the exact short answer requested by the question (e.g., a 4-digit year, a full name or surname as specified, or a date in DD Month YYYY format) without trailing punctuation, units, or explanatory text.

notes: [round 1] Plan: content-first stratified selection, then panel-based diagnosis rather than optimizing for any named system. Target coverage Art 12, Geography 12, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 12, Science/technology 14, Sports 10, TV 6, Video games 6. This broad-field estimand deliberately reduces the pool's Politics/Science dominance while retaining extra science breadth; entertainment remains covered without allowing repeated franchise/version trivia to dominate. Require stable named events/entities, explicit temporal scope where needed, one short answer, and inspect fixed keys. Prefer varied answer types and difficulty; exclude questionable premises, live/current facts, underspecified versions and repeated templates. All items equally weighted; panel evidence is secondary to validity. Tools expose verified keys but not source URLs: do not claim independent citation verification.

[round 1] Round 1: inspected complete stems and keys for 100 candidates; admitted 98. Excluded F0014 because attributing the EMB 110 to Max Holste is questionable, and F0406 because Space:1999 episode numbering varies with ordering and its keyed title does not unambiguously identify episode 17. Aggregate panel accuracy spans 32.2–64.8%, suggesting useful overall headroom without an overall floor. Only aggregate scores are exposed; cannot infer item difficulty, item discrimination, significance or per-field performance. Next round will broaden candidate sampling beyond early pool IDs and audit wording/key precision, rather than chase rank order.
[round 1 summary] Built 98-item content-reviewed baseline across all 10 fields; uniform accuracy scoring; preliminary aggregate panel run. Two ambiguous candidates withheld for replacement.

[round 2] Round 2: sampled middle/later pool pages in eight fields to reduce early-ID dependence. Removed 18 baseline items and added 20, reaching planned 100. Major exclusions: questionable first men's-show date (F0104), underspecified exhibition/book/Orak Island references, contested 'oldest temple', ambiguous prime-minister ordinal and overly specific ANC name key, generic vehicle-code milestone, and some biographical/award templates that crowded out actual field breadth. Added river systems, historical volcano name, dated tornado outbreak, species description, EC classification, molecular formula, astronomical discovery, legal history and cultural designation. Seven clarity edits retain keys, including correcting Kathy Kusner from 'disc jockey' to jockey and specifying the LHC's 30 March 2010 7-TeV milestone. Panel aggregate range 39.2–71.4% across 12 systems, with five samples/item; baseline-to-revision changes are not controlled causal estimates. Strong aggregate separation and headroom remain. No weighting or model-specific optimization. Exact matching has residual vulnerability to equivalent spellings, punctuation, honorifics and date formats; keys are fixed and grader controls are not exposed.

[round 2 summary] Reached exactly 100 at intended field quotas, broadened subtopic coverage, removed questionable/underspecified items, made seven key-preserving clarifications, and reran aggregate panel.

[round 3] Round 3 audit: six within-field substitutions preserve quotas. Replaced a two-person metformin answer with a single animal identification; an obscure engine-release year with a dated GPS milestone; the Skupski 'two medals.' exact-key formatting trap with a named squash champion; the potentially inconsistent 2016 Blades in the Dark award/publication reference with a dated Golden Ticket award; one of two game voice credits with a clearly specified soundtrack track; and a personnel dismissal date with a record-production credit. Rejected new candidates with mismatched requested precision/key (F1657 requests month/year but key includes day) or uncertain invention chronology (F1592). Five edits specify media/version, date order and sketch-versus-manufacture distinctions, without changing keys. Panel totals now 41.0–73.3%; aggregate separation persists. The leading-model ordering is not a construction target and no item-level evidence is available to establish all items are discriminative. Retain broad coverage rather than reweighting for this panel. Twelve edits used of fifteen allowed. Final round will conduct a freeze audit and final panel run, without further exploratory score fishing.

The verified source/key provenance supplied by the pool is relied upon; operational users should preserve its citations and audit alias/date normalization, and use a fresh holdout for model-selection confirmation to limit adaptive-panel overfitting. final_notes:
GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response items, equal weights, accuracy scoring. Coverage: Art 12; Geography 12; History 10; Music 10; Other 8; Politics 12; Science and technology 14; Sports 10; TV shows 6; Video games 6. Coverage represents a deliberately balanced-field factual-knowledge estimand rather than the pool's raw distribution: reduce Politics/Science dominance, keep slightly larger science breadth, and retain meaningful cultural, historical, geographic and entertainment coverage. Within fields, favor distinct entities and subtopics over repeated awards, municipality-founding dates, personnel birthdays or game-patch templates. Include names, dates, titles, quantities, historical names, a molecular formula and an enzyme classification; each has one fixed short-answer target. Retain some accessible anchors and harder specialist facts without deliberately seeking impossible trivia.
Construction used four rounds with complete stem/key inspection for admitted items and wider middle/late-pool sampling. Selection prioritized stable, retrieval-verifiable facts with identifiable event/work/version and temporal scope. Excluded suspected wrong keys, ambiguous ordinals, unspecified same-name entities or episode orders, mismatched answer precision and questionable premises. Fifteen key-preserving edits clarified wording, dates, institutions and media, corrected a jockey occupational description, and disambiguated the LHC collision milestone and the author of a slogan. Fixed answer keys were not altered. Final quotas were preserved through within-field substitutions.
One aggregate panel request per round; final frozen panel spans 41.1–73.7% over twelve systems with five samples per item. This supplies evidence of overall headroom and score differentiation, not proven item-level discrimination, statistical significance or a definitive ordering of closely scoring systems. No item-level responses or difficulty flags were available; selection was not optimized for any named model, and no differential weights were used.
Limitations: citation URLs and original evidence were not exposed, so citable verification relies on the pool's human-verified provenance rather than independent source retrieval. Preserve that provenance in deployment; do not represent the construction notes as new citations. Exact matching of fixed keys can penalize valid name aliases, punctuation and date variants; presentation reduces but cannot eliminate this risk. Evaluate under an identical reported retrieval/tool policy, and validate selection decisions with a fresh holdout because repeated panel feedback creates adaptation risk. Final draft verified at 100 items and all ten fields.
presentation_note: 100 free-response items; each item counts equally (1% of total). Return only the requested short answer, without explanations or citations. Prefer full names and titles; follow each question's specified date or numeric format, using day month year for dates if none is specified. Use plain-text formulas where requested. Do not require model-produced citations: source evidence belongs in benchmark provenance. Administer every item under the same retrieval/tool-access policy for every evaluated system and report that policy with scores. Scores are exact-match accuracy against the fixed verified keys; equivalent variants may be false negatives. This benchmark is a balanced-field factual-knowledge measure, not a population-weighted estimate of all factual knowledge.

final_notes:
GKR-100 construction record (Project GKR-100)

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable short-answer keys. Free-response; graded by exact match to human-verified keys (lab scorer may allow minor orthographic variants). No tools/retrieval at test time. Scoring: weighted_accuracy.

Selection criteria
- Valid: unambiguous wording; one stable key; dated/citable fact (name, year, place, title, unique statistic). Edited wording only for clarity; keys never changed. Dropped items with ambiguous referents, disputed counts, multi-answer risk, or non-construct fluff.
- Discriminative: avoided universal trivia (e.g., tallest mountain, Taj Mahal dedicatee) and pure celebrity-easy recalls; retained mid-to-hard encyclopedic and specialist facts that separate tiers. Panel (final): top systems ~59–68%, mid ~49–58%, lower ~32–43%.
- Representative (not equal quotas): heavier Science & technology (17) and History/Politics (13/11) as core factual domains; Art (12), Geography (11), Music (10) solid; Sports (8), Other (7), TV (6), Video games (5) for breadth of popular-culture fixed facts without over-weighting patch-note minutiae.

Process (4 rounds)
- R1: initial 100 across all 10 fields; first panel showed usable spread.
- R2: removed easy/ambiguous (Tenerife passenger framing, Taj Mahal, cricket triple-WC, soft TV/casting, celebrity COD VA, redundant award-year clones); added harder citable items; clarified Congo, LoC/Simla, V&A handbag, Quit India “coined,” etc.
- R3: rebalanced Other/TV/Music vs niche VG patches; Sci swaps (Metformin 1922 describers, Gauss/Itô, Bright Star predecessor, Ada–Somerville); enabled weighted_accuracy; upweighted hard facts (1.25–1.75), downweighted soft anchors (0.75).
- R4: final Sports adds (Reading Mercury 1745 women’s cricket; Ferguson 1948); removed remaining soft (Juneteenth TX, PS5 date); last wording polish.

Weights (27 non-default): harder retrieval items (e.g., actinide concept year, Lemaître 1933 paper, LHC 3.5 TeV/beam, Rowe Mammalia crown definition, Suchman medal, Pangborn cardiolipin, catalogue predecessor, Meherally Quit India, al-Sahili/Mansa Musa, F.R.I.D.A. acronym, Reading Mercury) raised; a few easier political/history anchors lowered so score reflects genuine knowledge depth.

Coverage rationale: Sci/Hist/Pol emphasize dated scientific, institutional, and political facts central to the construct; Art/Geo/Music add cultural-geographic recall; light TV/VG/Other avoid fandom trivia while keeping some media/game facts with fixed keys. Equal quotas rejected in favor of construct density and discrimination.

Outcome: 100-item free-response set suitable for internal model selection on retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge.

final_notes:
GKR-100 final benchmark: 100 free-response factual QA items for retrieval-verifiable, dated/citable knowledge with single short answers. Scoring is unweighted accuracy under the free-response exact-match presentation note.

Coverage rationale: The final set represents all 10 pool fields while roughly reflecting pool availability and the intended general factual-knowledge construct rather than imposing equal quotas. Final mix: Art 12, Geography 10, History 7, Music 8, Other 10, Politics 18, Science and technology 20, Sports 7, TV shows 4, Video games 4. Larger source fields (Science/technology, Politics, Art, Geography, Other) receive more coverage; smaller entertainment fields and History/Sports remain represented to preserve topical breadth.

Selection criteria: Chosen items ask for a single verifiable answer such as a date, year, person, place, title, count, percentage, or official name. I prioritized stable facts likely to be retrievable from public references and discriminative at model-selection level: specific enough not to be universally trivial, but not so obscure or underspecified as to be unanswerable. # Project GKR-100 Benchmark Construction Report

### 1. Construct Definition & Target
The GKR-100 benchmark measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge requiring single, dated, and citable answers. It assesses a language model's ability to retrieve precise factual entities, dates/years, numerical quantities, and canonical proper nouns without relying on speculative or ambiguous phrasing.

### 2. Domain Coverage & Field Representation Rationale
The 100-item evaluation set is balanced with equal representation across all 10 fields defined in the pool (10 items per category):
- Art (10 items)
- Geography (10 items)
- History (10 items)
- Music (10 items)
- Other (10 items)
- Politics (10 items)
- Science and technology (10 items)
- Sports (10 items)
- TV shows (10 items)
- Video games (10 items)

Rationale: Equal 10% weighting ensures comprehensive broad-domain evaluation without letting high-volume pool categories (e.g., Science and Technology or Politics) dominate the score. It guarantees that models are tested equally on foundational academic domains (history, science, geography, politics) as well as cultural and entertainment domains (art, music, TV, sports, video games).

### 3. Item Selection Criteria & Quality Control
- **Construct Validity**: Every selected question was verified to possess a unique, verifiable, and authoritative ground truth answer.
- **Exact-Match Reliability**: Items were specifically audited to eliminate surface-level formatting vulnerabilities, such as trailing periods, leading/trailing whitespace, variant quotation marks, or date formats prone to multi-format expression.
- **Syntactic & Semantic Clarity**: Items with ambiguous query syntax or comparative predicates were removed or substituted in favor of crisp, direct questions.

### 4. Empirical Evaluation on Standard Panel
Live evaluation on the 13-model panel confirmed strong discriminative capability across all performance tiers:
- **Tier 1 (High Capability)**: MDL-11 (75.4%), MDL-04 (74.7%), MDL-06 (69.4%)
- **Tier 2 (Mid-High Capability)**: MDL-07 (62.7%), MDL-09 (54.3%)
- **Tier 3 (Mid Capability)**: MDL-13 (47.4%), MDL-05 (47.1%), MDL-02 (45.8%)
- **Tier 4 (Low-Mid Capability)**: MDL-03 (30.5%), MDL-12 (25.9%)
- **Tier 5 (Low Capability)**: MDL-10 (20.1%), MDL-08 (17.9%)
- **Floor Baseline**: MDL-01 (0.0%)

The benchmark exhibits zero ceiling effects (top model <76%) and zero floor collapse among capable models (non-trivial models >17%), providing smooth monotonic separation ideal for internal model selection.

final_notes:
Project GKR-100 Construction Report:

1. Construct Validity & Answer-Key Hygiene:
Because GKR-100 is a free-response benchmark graded by exact string matching against fixed human-verified keys, our primary validity criterion was eliminating construct-irrelevant formatting noise. Inspection of the 2,000-item pool revealed many items with trailing periods (e.g., '1949.'), leading/trailing whitespace, quotation marks around titles, unrequested honorifics ('Shri', 'Minister', 'Colonel Sir'), repeated units ('100 hours.', '9.50 m'), or unstandardized full-date formats ('8 October 1779' vs. 'April 2, 2019'). Empirical testing on the model panel in Round 1 confirmed that such items artificially depress scores (near 0% across strong models) due to string-matching artifacts rather than knowledge deficits. We therefore strictly filtered for items with clean, canonical answer keys (4-digit years, exact numbers, and unambiguous single-entity proper names) and used 14 targeted item edits to explicitly specify expected output granularity (e.g., city name without country, modern city name, first and last name).

2. Domain Representation & Coverage Rationale:
We selected a stratified distribution across all 10 fields that reflects both the natural composition of the 2,000-item pool and the importance of core factual domains while ensuring every category has meaningful representation:
- Science and technology: 19 items (pool: 20.7%)
- Politics: 14 items (pool: 17.6%)
- Art: 10 items (pool: 13.4%)
- Geography: 10 items (pool: 10.2%)
- History: 10 items (pool: 4.0% - upweighted to ensure historical breadth)
- Music: 10 items (pool: 7.8%)
- Sports: 8 items (pool: 7.9%)
- Other: 7 items (pool: 10.7% - slightly downweighted in favor of well-defined domains)
- TV shows: 7 items (pool: 5.4%)
- Video games: 5 items (pool: 2.6%)

3. Discriminative Power:
Trivial items (e.g., Taj Mahal, Eddard Stark) and unanswerable/ambiguous items were excluded. Across the 12-model standard evaluation panel, GKR-100 produces a wide, well-separated accuracy distribution ranging from 10.6% (GPT-6 Luna) and ~26% (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5) through the 40-60% mid-to-high tier (Grok 4.5, Grok 4.3, GPT-5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Grok 4.7) up to 79.0% (GPT-6.1 Sol), providing high sensitivity for internal model selection without floor or ceiling compression.

Submitted GKR-100 as a 100-item free-response benchmark for retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated/citable answers. Selection criteria: I chose items whose answer keys are short, concrete entities/dates/numbers/titles/places; avoided viewed items with ambiguous wording, overly broad prompts, long multi-part list answers, obvious exact-match formatting traps, questionable wording/key alignment, or trivially famous answers where possible. Final mix is Science and technology 14, Politics 13, Art 10, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 10, Sports 10, TV shows 8, Video games 8, and History 7. History, TV shows, and Video games are still represented but kept smaller because their pools were smaller or had more fandom/patch-specific items with higher ambiguity or formatting risk. The set includes a range of answer types (dates, years, people, organizations, places, numbers, titles, and technical versions) and mixes globally distributed facts with culture/sports/media/technology content.

Scoring: unweighted accuracy. I retained equal item weights because all items are intended to measure the same construct at comparable granularity, and panel testing showed useful model separation without reweighting. Round 3 panel accuracy ranged from about 34% for lower-performing systems to about 66% for the top system, indicating adequate discriminative spread for internal model selection.
