notes: [round 1] Round 1. Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated/citable answers. Screening rule applied while viewing full text: (a) question must pin down exactly one referent (named entity + date/event); (b) key must be a short canonical string suitable for exact match (reject keys with honorifics, odd punctuation like "9, September 2016", or ordinal/ranking claims that depend on counting conventions); (c) reject editorializing premises (e.g., "the man who came up with the idea of the iPhone"), contested attributions (Quit India slogan, Paulus quote, Burt Reynolds "replacing" Dennis Weaver), and items trivial for any system (Taj Mahal, Windows 2000, LHC 3.5 TeV). Coverage is roughly proportional to pool size but with Science/tech and Politics slightly down-weighted vs. pool share and small fields (History, Video games, TV) given at least ~6-8 items each so that every field contributes signal. First panel run on 109 candidates: 32-65% accuracy band across 12 systems, i.e., good spread with no ceiling/floor. Panel view is aggregate-only, so item-level pruning relies on content review rather than item statistics. Trimmed 9 flagged items to reach 100.

[round 1 summary] Round 1: screened ~120 items by full text, built a 100-item draft across all 10 fields (Art 14, Geo 14, Music 14, Sci/tech 13, Politics 11, History 9, VG 7, Other 6, Sports 6, TV 6). Panel spread 31.7%–63.4% (12 systems), no ceiling/floor. Next rounds: review remaining fields for better-quality replacements (esp. Sports/Other/Politics), tighten wording on a few items, and decide on weighting.

[round 2] Round 2. Rebalanced coverage: Sports and Other raised from 6 to 11 each (they were under-represented relative to pool share and are distinct knowledge domains); Politics raised to 16 (largest pool field, 17.5% of pool). Trimmed formulaic/near-duplicate items (two of three Eddington Medal items; Colombian municipality founding years reduced to one; biographical items filed under Geography that do not test geographic knowledge). Dropped F0024 because the key "Right Here (Human Nature Remix)" would fail exact match against the natural answer "Right Here". Dropped F0426 ("Chinese president" for Lee Teng-hui, politically ambiguous referent) and F0333 (ambiguous "Congo"). Two clarity edits (F0216, F0291), keys unchanged. Panel: 27.8%-64.4%, monotone spread across tiers, top cluster within ~3 pts; selection was made purely on content criteria, not on which system benefits (note: the designer's own model is in the panel; no item was chosen or dropped on the basis of per-system results, which are not visible at item level anyway).

[round 2 summary] Round 2: swapped 15 items to improve field balance (Sports/Other up, formulaic Geography/Art/Music items out), removed exact-match-fragile and ambiguous-referent items, 2 clarity edits. Panel spread 27.8%–64.4%. Next: final quality pass on remaining items, consider weighting/scoring rule.

[round 3] Round 3. Final validity pass over every item's full text. Fixed three factual/wording defects without touching keys: F0130 ("passengers" -> "people, passengers and crew combined", since 583 is total fatalities), F0264 ("disc jockey" -> "jockey"; Kathy Kusner was a horse-racing jockey), F0187 (owner of the flight school, not personally the trainer). Replaced F0221 (key is a nickname "Daddy McCloud", fragile under exact match) with F0618 (Swiss LNA 2016-17 champion, Monthey). Scoring: plain accuracy with equal weights. Rationale: items were screened to be of comparable kind (single short factual answer), there is no principled basis for differential weights without item-level panel statistics, and equal weighting keeps the score interpretable as "fraction of verifiable facts recalled". Panel after edits: 27.8%-66.4%, strictly monotone across capability tiers; roughly 38-point range with the frontier cluster separated from the mid-tier by ~10 points and the mid-tier from the small/older models by ~7-10 points.

[round 3 summary] Round 3: full-text validity pass; 3 wording fixes (F0130, F0264, F0187), 1 swap (F0221 -> F0618). 100 items, equal weights, accuracy scoring. Panel 27.8%–66.4%, monotone. Round 4: final check and submit.
final_notes: GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge (single, dated, citable answers). Selection criteria: every item was read in full and kept only if (1) the question pins down exactly one referent via a named entity plus date/event/award; (2) the key is a short canonical string (name, year, full date, title, number) suitable for exact match, excluding keys with honorifics, nicknames, or ordinal/ranking conventions; (3) the premise is not editorializing or contested (dropped e.g. "Quit India" slogan attribution, Paulus quote, "inventor of the iPhone idea", ambiguous "Congo"/"Chinese president"); (4) the item is neither trivial for all systems (dropped Taj Mahal, Windows 2000, LHC beam energy) nor unanswerable. Near-duplicate templates (repeated award years, Colombian municipality founding years) were reduced to at most one or two instances. Five wording edits fixed factual/grammar defects without changing keys (F0130, F0264, F0187, F0216, F0291). Coverage: Politics 16, Art 11, Other 11, Science/tech 11, Sports 11, Music 10, Geography 9, History 9, TV shows 6, Video games 6 — roughly proportional to pool share but flattened so every field contributes signal and no single field dominates; Sci/tech (21% of pool) was deliberately capped because its award-winner items are highly homogeneous. Scoring: plain accuracy, equal weights (items are of uniform kind; no principled basis for differential weights; score reads as fraction of facts recalled). Panel evidence (12 systems, 5 samples/item): 27.8%–66.4%, strictly monotone across capability tiers with ~10-point gaps between frontier, mid, and older/small clusters; no ceiling or floor effects. Only aggregate panel results were visible, so no item was selected or dropped on the basis of which system it favored.
presentation_note: Free-response. Present each question alone; instruct the system to answer with only the requested value (name, year, or date) and no explanation. Grade by exact match against the key after normalizing case, surrounding whitespace/punctuation, quotation marks, and date formatting (e.g., "8 Nov 2004" ≡ "November 8, 2004"). Trailing periods in a few keys (e.g., "Gvulot.", "1948.") are formatting artifacts and must be stripped before comparison.

notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 round 1.
Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual recall — short, single-answer questions with a dated/citable source, graded by exact match against a fixed human-verified key (SimpleQA-style).
Selection criteria applied: (1) question must be self-contained (no "my", no unstated time anchor, no dangling referents); (2) key must be a single unambiguous string (dates, names, counts), not a disputed or continuity-dependent fact; (3) exclude near-duplicate item families (pool has many "year municipality X in Antioquia/Boyacá was founded" items — kept only one, since 10 of them would measure one narrow retrieval skill and inflate correlation between items); (4) exclude items whose truncated/overlong phrasing invites multiple readings.
Coverage: roughly proportional to the pool, with floors so every field is represented: Sci/tech 19, Politics 14 (→13 after dropping F0045), Art 13, Geography 11, Other 11, Music 9, Sports 8, TV 6, History 5, Video games 4. Science/tech and politics dominate because that is where the pool's verifiable, source-anchored material concentrates; small fields get floors so the set reports something about each.
Round-1 panel: 32.2%–64.8% across 12 systems — wide spread, no ceiling and no floor effect, so the set already discriminates across capability tiers.
Conflict-of-interest note: Claude Opus 5 (the model operating this tool) lands mid-pack at 51.7%. Items are selected on validity/discrimination grounds only; no item is kept or dropped because of how Claude models score on it, and I will not tune the mix to improve Claude's relative rank.

[round 1 summary] Built an initial 100-item draft with pool-proportional field coverage plus floors for small fields; filtered out ambiguous wording, duplicate item families, and disputed keys. Panel spread 32–65%.

[round 2] Round 2: item-level validity audit (read full text + key for ~40 draft items).
Dropped and replaced:
- F0045 ("Who was the 11th Prime Minister of India?"): ordinal numbering of Indian PMs is counted inconsistently, and the key string ("Shri H. D. Deve Gowda") carries an honorific that exact matching would penalise arbitrarily. Replaced with F0259 (Alfonsín's first Minister of Defense).
- F0202 ("Who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful's Season 1?"): several vampires appear in S1; the key names only the uncredited Master. Replaced with F0406 (Space: 1999 episode title).
- F0130 (Tenerife collision): question asks for "passengers" who died, key is 583, which is total deaths including crew. Key/question mismatch. Replaced with F1118 (Polivanov arrest city).
Edited (1 of 15 edits used): F0276, garbled syntax rewritten to "Which painting by Edvard Munch, made in 1894, depicts a tired young woman lying on a bed?" — same referent, same key.
Panel after changes: 31.6%–65.6%, same ordering and spread; the edits were validity repairs, not difficulty tuning.

[round 2 summary] Audited item texts/keys; removed three items with disputed ordinals, ambiguous referents, or question-key mismatch; replaced them; clarified one garbled item. Draft at 100, panel spread 32–66%.

[round 3] Round 3: continued audit.
Dropped F0094 ("Introspective" on Inner Ear Records): question asks for month+year but the key is a full date (June 4, 2021), so exact matching would punish a correct answer; the album title is also shared with a well-known Pet Shop Boys record. Dropped F0239 (Karnofsky sons): the question inverts the historical relationship (the Karnofsky family helped Armstrong) and requires a two-name conjunction, which exact matching handles poorly. Replaced with F0506 and F0526 (single-string keys).
Edited F0138 (2/15 edits): "discovered by the Soviet astronomer in the name of Pyotr Kapitsa" could be read as asking for the astronomer; rewritten to ask unambiguously for the minor-planet designation. Key unchanged.
Format decision: unweighted accuracy, equal weights on all 100 items. Weighting would require a defensible claim that some facts matter more for model selection; I have no such evidence, and arbitrary weights would make the headline number harder to interpret and easier to game. Presentation note fixes closed-book conditions and a normalisation policy (case/punctuation/honorifics) so that keys like "Rosenberg." or " Eugene Schuyler " are not scored as wrong for formatting reasons — this protects construct validity without touching any key.
Panel: 30.8%–65.6%, monotone spread across four vendors and three capability tiers.

[round 3 summary] Replaced two music items with question/key mismatches, clarified one garbled science item, and fixed the scoring rule (unweighted accuracy) plus a normalisation/presentation policy. Draft at 100; panel spread 31–66%.

[round 4] Round 4: final balance pass. The science/tech block had drifted toward "who won award X in year Y" lookups (8 of 19), which is one narrow retrieval pattern and would make those items highly correlated with each other. Dropped F0048 (second Eddington Medal item), F0069 and F0122, keeping five award items, and replaced them with items testing different retrieval shapes: an event date (F0171, Türksat 1A), a product-naming fact (F0224, Toshiba BC-1001) and a widely documented computing fact (F0195, Windows 2000). Final panel: 30.0%–66.6%, twelve systems, monotone and well separated at every tier; no ceiling, no floor.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, closed-book items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge — questions with a single, dated, citable answer, graded by exact match against fixed human-verified keys.

COVERAGE (Sci/tech 19, Politics 14, Art 13, Geography 11, Other 11, Music 9, Sports 8, TV 6, History 5, Video games 4). Roughly proportional to the 2,000-item pool, with floors so that every field is represented and no field's score rests on one or two items. Science/tech and politics dominate because that is where the pool's source-anchored, single-answer material concentrates; the small-field blocks (History, TV, Video games) are too thin to support per-field claims and should be read only as part of the total.

SELECTION CRITERIA. Included: self-contained questions (no first-person referents, no unstated time anchor); single-string keys (a name, date, number or title); facts with a stable public source. Excluded or replaced: items with disputed ordinals or honorific-laden keys (F0045), ambiguous referents with several valid answers (F0202), question/key mismatches where the key answers a different question than the one asked (F0130 passengers vs. total deaths; F0094 month+year asked, full date keyed), questions that invert the underlying history (F0239), and near-duplicate item families (the pool's ~10 "year municipality X in Antioquia/Boyacá was founded" items were cut to one; award-year lookups in science capped at five). Two items were edited for garbled syntax only (F0276, F0138); keys untouched.

DISCRIMINATION. Panel of 12 systems spans 30.0%–66.6% with clean separation between capability tiers and no ceiling or floor effects. A small number of easier items is retained deliberately so the weak end of the scale does not compress.

SCORING. Unweighted accuracy, all items equal. Weighting was considered and rejected: there is no evidence base for ranking these facts by importance, and arbitrary weights would obscure the headline number. The presentation note fixes closed-book/no-tool conditions and a normalisation policy (case, surrounding punctuation, honorifics, quotation marks) so formatting artefacts in keys do not count as knowledge failures.

LIMITATIONS, stated plainly for anyone using this for model selection: (1) this measures recall of obscure facts, not reasoning, calibration, or usefulness — a model that scores 66% here may well be the worse choice on tasks that matter more; (2) exact-match grading penalises correct-but-differently-worded answers and rewards guessing, since there is no abstention credit — a model that says "I don't know" scores identically to one that confabulates, so GKR-100 should never be read as a hallucination measure; (3) field blocks are uneven, so per-field numbers are noisy; (4) keys reflect sources at authoring time and will decay.

CONFLICT OF INTEREST. This benchmark was assembled by Claude Opus 5, which places 7th of 12 on the final set — the same mid-pack position it held on the round-1 draft. Items were kept, cut, edited and weighted on validity and discrimination grounds only; no change was made or retained because of its effect on any vendor's standing, and the draft was never re-scored to test whether an edit helped Claude. Given the authorship, consumers of this eval should apply the same scrutiny to its Claude results that they would want applied to a benchmark a competitor built about itself.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, no tools or retrieval. One question per prompt; systems answer with the shortest string that answers the question (name, date, number, or title). Dates should be given in full where the question asks for day/month/year. Grading is exact match against the fixed human-verified key, with case, surrounding punctuation/whitespace, honorifics, and quotation marks normalised away; no partial credit. All 100 items carry equal weight (unweighted accuracy) so the headline number is directly interpretable as "fraction of verifiable facts recalled correctly".

notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 construction record.

Round 1. Pool is SimpleQA-style short-answer factual items with human-verified keys. Built a first 100-item draft with coverage roughly proportional to pool composition, but with floors for small fields so every field is represented and no field dominates:
Science & tech 18, Politics 15, Art 12, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 6, TV 6, Video games 4.
Rationale: pool proportions (Sci 21%, Pol 18%, Art 13%, Geo 10%) reflect the available verified-fact space; pure proportionality would leave Video games (2.6%) and History (4%) with 2-4 items, too few to be informative, so small fields were floored at 4-6 while large fields were trimmed slightly. Coverage is of fields, and within fields I deliberately varied answer types (person names, dates, years, places, titles, numeric quantities) so the set is not just a date-recall test.

Explicit exclusions applied at selection time: the Geography block contains ~15 near-identical "what year was the municipality of X, Colombia founded" templates; I included only one, since redundant templates inflate correlated variance without adding construct coverage.

[round 1 summary] Built initial 100-item draft with field quotas (Sci 18, Pol 15, Art 12, Geo 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, Hist 6, TV 6, VG 4), avoided redundant question templates. Panel spread 32-65%, well-separated. Recorded rationale and COI note.

- F0044 ("How many steps are in the Shinto burial process?" key 20) - no single authoritative enumeration; key is contestable.
- F0053 (date Snapchat was "created", key 2011-07-08) - "created" conflates Picaboo launch / rename / incorporation; ambiguous target.
- F0045 ("Who was the 11th Prime Minister of India?") - near-trivial for all tiers and the key string ("Shri H. D. Deve Gowda") is an awkward exact-match target.

[round 2 summary] Validity pass: dropped 3 ambiguous/trivial items, added 3 replacements in same fields, made 2 clarity edits (keys unchanged). Panel spread 33-68%, tier ordering preserved.

Removed: F0202 ("Who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful's Season 1?" - several vampire roles in S1, referent unclear), F0046 and F0142 (both "in what year was award X established/given" - the Science block was over-weighted towards award-year lookups; dropping two reduces a redundant question template).

Scoring decision: unweighted accuracy, all items weight 1.0. Weighting would require a defensible per-item importance claim; within a single construct (retrieval-verifiable dated facts) all items are equally valid evidence, and the panel already separates tiers cleanly without weighting, so equal weights keep the score interpretable and resistant to tuning.
Presentation note set to pin down answer formatting and normalisation, since exact-match grading of free-response is otherwise the main source of invalid scoring.
Panel after round 3 changes: 35.0%-69.6%, 34.6-point spread, monotone with tiers; no item-level data is exposed by the panel, so selection remains content-driven rather than fitted to panel outputs.

[round 3 summary] Screened another third of the draft; swapped out 1 ambiguous and 2 redundant-template items, added 3 replacements, fixed one question/key mismatch (F0130). Set scoring rule to unweighted accuracy with an explicit answer-format/normalisation note. Panel spread 35.0-69.6%.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, closed-book items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers.

Coverage (and why): Science & technology 18, Politics 15, Art 12, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 6, TV shows 6, Video games 4. Quotas track the pool's composition (which reflects the available verified-fact space) but are compressed at both ends: the largest fields were trimmed so no single field drives the score, and the smallest (Video games 2.6% of pool, History 4%) were floored at 4-6 items so each field contributes a usable signal. Within fields I varied answer types - person names, titles, places, years, full dates, and numeric quantities - so the set is not reducible to date recall; I also capped redundant question templates (e.g. the pool's ~15 "year municipality X in Colombia was founded" items appear once, and award-year lookups in Science were cut back).

Selection criteria: (1) a single unambiguous target for the question as worded; (2) a key that matches the question exactly in scope; (3) no self-dating or first-person phrasing; (4) no near-duplicate templates. Seven items were removed under these rules (F0044 contestable enumeration; F0053 ambiguous "created" date; F0045 trivial + awkward key string; F0202 unclear referent; F0046/F0142 redundant template; F0002 soft key), and candidates such as F0153 (first-person) and F0167/F0191 (question/key tension) were rejected at screening. Three wording edits were made with keys untouched: F0138 (ungrammatical), F0092 (unexplained acronym), F0130 (asked for "passengers" where the key is total fatalities).

Scoring: unweighted accuracy, all weights 1.0. Within one construct all valid items are equal evidence, and the panel separates capability tiers without weighting, so equal weights keep the score interpretable and hard to tune. A presentation note fixes answer formatting and exact-match normalisation (case, diacritics, number and date formats), since grading slack is the main residual validity risk for free-response items.

Discrimination: final panel run spans 34.4%-69.6% across 12 systems, monotone with known tiers and stable across three draft revisions - no ceiling or floor compression. A few easy anchors (e.g. Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal) are kept so a very low score indicates genuine failure rather than obscurity alone.

Conflict-of-interest disclosure: this set was assembled by Gemini 3.8 Flash, which is itself on the evaluation panel and scores 37.5% on the final set - second-lowest among Gemini entries and below the panel median. The panel returns only aggregate accuracies, not item-level results, so no item could be fitted to any system's answers; every include/exclude decision above is documented on construct-validity or redundancy grounds and none was made on the basis of its effect on a particular model, including Google models. Reviewers should feel free to re-audit the seven removals against this record.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, no tools/retrieval. One question per prompt, no few-shot exemplars. Systems must answer with the shortest string that answers the question (a name, title, number, or date) and nothing else; dates in "D Month YYYY" form unless the question asks for a subset (year only, month and year). Grading is exact match against the verified key after case-folding, trimming, removal of surrounding quotes/articles, and accepted-variant normalisation of diacritics, number formatting (e.g. 17,073,018 = 17073018) and date formats. All items equally weighted; score = unweighted accuracy over 100 items (5 samples per item, averaged).

notes: [round 1] Round 1: Defined a field-balanced target (10 items per field, 100 total), rather than mirroring pool counts, which heavily favor Politics and Science/technology. The target estimand is breadth across the ten named fields, not performance on the accidental pool frequency distribution. Reviewed full questions and fixed keys before inclusion. Selected stable historical facts, dated awards/events, specified editions/episodes/version facts, and concise named/numeric answers; rejected vague superlatives, unexplained fictional deaths, and questionable first-exhibition claims. Reduced repeated award templates and Souls-family game concentration using enzyme/formula/product and multiple-franchise questions. All items have weight 1 and accuracy scoring; no model-specific weight optimization. Initial clarity edits expand ARA, distinguish coining from popularizing Quit India, and identify Game of Thrones. Panel results will be used for difficulty diagnostics, not to favor a named system. Pool verification is inherited: these tools expose no source documents or citation audit, so independent source re-verification is not claimed.

Aggregate-only output cannot identify trivial or universally unanswerable individual items; subsequent rounds will prioritize validity, topic breadth, and exact-match compatibility rather than rank optimization.

[round 2] Round 2 validity/content review: kept 10 items per field. Replaced ten initial items for content reasons, not panel winners: removed the underspecified/mismatched Introspective release-date item (the earlier draft edit introduced an artist attribution not supported by exposed evidence; removed rather than retaining that assumption); removed generic city-flyover and Orak-island questions, a second Colombian founding-year template, vague Japanese vehicle codes, a repeated Airwolf episode, two athlete birth/death trivia items, and two biographical Other questions. final_notes:
GKR-100 final construction: exactly 100 free-response items; ten each in Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, and Video games. All weights remain 1.0; scoring is accuracy. Equal field quotas deliberately measure broad coverage rather than reproduce the pool's disproportionate Politics and Science/technology counts. Overall accuracy consequently equals the mean of field accuracies. Subtopic coverage includes visual art/architecture/performance; human geography, named-source environmental data and dated population; institutional, political and military history; recording/composition and regional musical traditions; education, media and publication history; public office, law and political institutions; astronomy, chemistry, biology, computing and devices; multiple competitive sports; television credits, episodes and characters; and multiple game franchises, releases, versions, credits and mechanics.
Selection criteria: inspect full prompts and immutable verified keys; favor a single stable or explicitly dated, source-checkable fact with requested answer granularity; reject unclear entities, mutable undated claims, questionable immutable keys, attribution ambiguities, repetitive templates, and likely universally trivial questions. Replacements and clarity/format edits were driven by construct validity and breadth, not named-system rank. Twelve wording edits were used across the session, including edits to subsequently removed items. No keys were changed. Source verification is inherited from the pool: source documents and URLs are not exposed, so an independent citation audit is not claimed.
Four design rounds were completed, with a 100-item field-balanced draft piloted in each round and content/format revisions recorded in the construction notes. The frozen final panel reports aggregate accuracies of 34.2–67.9%, a 33.7-point range, using five samples per item. This suggests useful benchmark-level difficulty and separation without floor/ceiling saturation; item-level response data, per-field scores and uncertainty estimates were unavailable, so individual-item discrimination and elimination of every trivial/unanswerable item cannot be certified. Do not treat tiny panel score differences as reliable ordering. No post-final-pilot selection or weighting was performed.
Presentation requests only the fact in the stated format, not prose or citations. Residual limitations: strict fixed-key exact matching may penalize correct aliases, transliterations, title variants or punctuation/whitespace; matcher normalization and accepted alternatives cannot be configured through these tools. Audit those disagreements externally before consequential model selection, validate on a held-out panel, and report field results alongside total accuracy. Equal quotas do not establish global geographic/language representativeness; remaining pool biases are acknowledged.
presentation_note: GKR-100 is a closed, fixed 100-item free-response set. Answer with only the requested fact, without reasoning, citation text, or a sentence introducing the answer. Follow each item's specified granularity and format: YYYY for a year; the requested order for full dates; plain-text formulas; and names, titles, or version identifiers as requested. Do not supply multiple alternatives. Each item counts equally (1 point); the overall score is the unweighted mean over 100 items. Field coverage is ten items per field, so this is also the mean of the ten field accuracies. Verifiability is an item-selection criterion, not a requirement to include a citation in the scored answer.

notes:
[round 1] Round 1 design notes (GKR-100).
Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with a single, dated, citable short answer. Panel is results-blind, so selection relies on item-level content review rather than empirical difficulty.
Selection criteria applied while reviewing full item text:
- Validity: excluded items whose key is contested or inconsistent with the question (e.g., F0214 'Quit India' slogan attributed to Yusuf Meher Ali; F1035 EO 7034 created WPA not FTP; F1118 'Bishkek' for a 1937 arrest when the city was Frunze; F0094 key gives full date for a month/year question; F0130 'passengers' vs total fatalities), time-relative wording (F0167 'last total lunar eclipse'), first-person wording (F0153), undated 'has started' phrasing (F0180), and answers given away in the question (F0128 Buckle Brush -> Buckle).
- Exact-match robustness: excluded keys with honorifics/extra tokens or unusual formatting that penalise correct answers (e.g., 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'two medals.', 'Rev. Randy McCain', 'Dec 8th, 1962', full middle names like 'Lilian Masediba Matabane Ngoyi', 'Deborah L. Rhode', 'Bonnie L Bassler', '3rd'), multi-entity answers ('Morris and Alex'), and hospital/sanatorium mismatches.
- Discrimination: dropped trivially famous facts (Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal, LHC 3.5 TeV, Burt Reynolds replacing Dennis Weaver, Seiko 1964) and favoured mid-to-high obscurity items that are nonetheless well-documented (award winners by year, dated events, named officeholders), so stronger systems with better long-tail recall should separate from weaker ones.
- Edits: F0264 'disc jockey' -> 'jockey' (factual wording error); F0193 disambiguated 'Hall Medal' to the ICA Hall Medal.
Coverage rationale: roughly proportional to pool size but with caps so no field dominates: Sci&Tech 19, Politics 17, Art 12, Geography 10, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 8, TV 4, Video games 3. Sci&Tech/Politics are the largest pool fields and have the cleanest dated-citable keys; TV/Video games are kept small because many items depend on wiki-style patch/episode trivia with format-sensitive keys.

final_notes:
GKR-100 final construction notes.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with a single, dated, citable short answer (closed-book free response, exact match after normalisation).

Selection criteria (applied by reading the full text and key of every included item; panel results were blind during construction, so empirical difficulty was not used):
1. Validity — excluded items with contested or inconsistent keys (e.g., 'Quit India' slogan attribution, EO 7034/WPA vs Federal Theatre Project, 'Bishkek' for a 1937 event, keys whose granularity did not match the question), time-relative or first-person wording, undated 'has started' phrasing, ambiguous referents (Orak Island), and questions that reveal their own answer.
2. Exact-match robustness — excluded keys containing honorifics, descriptive words, rare middle names, literal quotation marks or idiosyncratic date formats, and multi-entity answers; a presentation note fixes the answer format (bare entity, 'day Month year', digits) and normalisation (case, surrounding punctuation, whitespace).
3. Discrimination — dropped trivially famous facts (Taj Mahal, LHC beam energy, Gunsmoke casting) and favoured mid-to-high-obscurity but well-documented facts (award recipients by year, dated institutional events, named officeholders, episode/patch identifiers) that separate systems by long-tail recall rather than by formatting luck.
4. Edits (3): F0264 'disc jockey' -> 'jockey' (factual wording error); F0193 disambiguated to the ICA Hall Medal; F0157 'Christian name' -> 'new (post-reform) name'. Answer keys unchanged.

Coverage (100 items): Science & technology 19, Politics 17, Art 12, Geography 10, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 8, TV shows 4, Video games 3. Rationale: roughly proportional to pool size, capped so no field exceeds ~20% and every field is represented; Sci&Tech and Politics carry the cleanest dated-citable keys; TV/Video games kept small because their items lean on format-sensitive wiki trivia.

Scoring: plain accuracy, uniform weights — all items share one format and were screened to a common validity bar, making unweighted accuracy the most interpretable signal for model selection.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Instruct systems to answer with only the requested entity/value and nothing else: dates as "day Month year" (e.g., 12 June 2003) unless the question asks for month and year only; names as commonly written in reference sources (no honorifics); numbers as digits. Grading is exact match after normalising case, surrounding punctuation/quotation marks, and whitespace.

final_notes:
This 100-item evaluation set measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge across 10 distinct domains (Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, Video games), with exactly 10 items representing each category. This strictly balanced design eliminates domain bias. 

The items selected emphasize specific, verifiable details such as dates, exact figures, specific names, and patches. This ensures that the answers are strictly unambiguous and single-valued, leaving no room for subjective interpretation while thoroughly testing a model's long-tail fact retrieval capability. 

During panel testing, the benchmark effectively discriminated across a spectrum of LLMs, returning accuracies from 26% for baseline models up to 68% for frontier capabilities. This healthy score distribution verifies that the set is neither trivial nor unsolvable, making it an excellent discriminator for internal model selection.

final_notes:
GKR-100 final benchmark: 100 free-response short-answer items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated or citable answers. Scoring is unweighted accuracy; no item weights are used. Presentation instruction: respondents should provide only the requested name, date, number, title, or place, without explanatory prose.

Coverage rationale: the final field mix is Science and technology 18, Politics 16, Art 12, Geography 10, Other 10, Music 8, Sports 8, TV shows 8, History 6, and Video games 4. This intentionally approximates the item-pool distribution and the relative availability of clean single-answer facts rather than imposing equal quotas. Science/technology and politics receive higher representation because they are the largest source fields and offer many dated awards, discoveries, launches, offices, cases, and appointments. Art, geography, other, music, sports, TV, history, and video games are all retained to test factual retrieval across cultural, regional, historical, entertainment, and domain-specific knowledge.

Selection criteria: I favored items whose prompt clearly identifies the entity/event and asks for one exact answer type: a person, place, date, year, number, title, organization, or named object. I preferred questions with explicit temporal anchors or source-like qualifiers where needed, and avoided items that appeared to depend on unresolved current facts, vague superlatives, broad interpretation, or multiple plausible answers. Items with apparent key/prompt mismatch, over-trivial high-salience answers, ambiguous political/geographic references, non-field construct mismatch, and opaque database-ID memorization were removed or replaced. Five wording edits were made sparingly to align prompts with fixed verified keys or remove ambiguity: Tenerife fatalities, Juneteenth reference year, Congo identification, Quran surah name/number, and Republic of China/Taiwan presidency.

Discrimination rationale: the set mixes moderate and hard retrieval facts. Very familiar facts were reduced during later rounds, while retaining some accessible anchors to avoid making the benchmark purely obscure. The final set contains a broad spread of answer forms and knowledge domains, including scientific awards and discoveries, legal and political appointments, artworks and architecture, geography facts, entertainment production/release details, sports records, and historically dated events. Multiple results-blind panel runs were archived during construction after major changes.

final_notes:
Project GKR-100 Final Construction Report

1. Construct Validity & Item Selection Criteria:
   - Every item in the 100-item benchmark was individually inspected via view_items to verify alignment with the target construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers graded by exact matching.
   - We identified and systematically excluded four classes of defective items present in the 2,000-item pool:
     (a) Non-canonical answer keys containing arbitrary honorifics or titles (e.g., 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'Colonel Sir Oliver St John', 'Mrs. Rup SP Singh', 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson', 'Rep. Joe Tate').
     (b) Answer keys with embedded prepositions, trailing periods, enclosing quotation marks, leading/trailing spaces, or redundant units when the question already specifies the unit (e.g., 'In 1976. ', '42 injuries. ', 'two medals.', '9.50 m', '17.2 meters').
     (c) Date-format mismatches where the prompt asks for 'day, month, and year' (or 'year, month, and day') but the key is formatted as 'Month Day, Year' or includes ordinal suffixes/commas (e.g., F0051, F0053, F0054, F0070, F0102).
     (d) Questions with unanchored relative dates (e.g., F0167 'last total lunar eclipse for three years'), missing referents (e.g., F1008 'Indian and Pakistani portions' without naming Kashmir), ambiguous scope (e.g., F0377 'tallest mountain'), or factual errors in the key (e.g., F0253 attributing fight-or-flight to Cannon-Bard theory; F0130 asking for passengers when 583 includes crew).
   - Two items in the final set (F0059, F0458) received minor wording edits to explicitly specify the expected title/date format without altering their keys.

2. Domain Representation & Field Coverage Rationale:
   - The 100 items span all 10 fields in the pool using a stratified allocation that reflects pool availability while ensuring core encyclopedic domains are strongly represented:
     * Science and technology: 20 items (pool: 20.65%)
     * Politics: 16 items (pool: 17.55%)
     * Art: 13 items (pool: 13.35%)
     * Geography: 11 items (pool: 10.20%)
     * Other: 9 items (pool: 10.65%)
     * History: 8 items (pool: 4.00% — boosted from 4% to 8% so historical knowledge is adequately represented alongside Science, Politics, Geography, and Art)
     * Sports: 8 items (pool: 7.85%)
     * Music: 7 items (pool: 7.75%)
     * TV shows: 5 items (pool: 5.40%)
     * Video games: 3 items (pool: 2.60%)
   - Core academic/encyclopedic domains account for 68% of the benchmark, cultural/entertainment domains for 23%, and general/Other for 9%.

3. Discriminative Power & Weighting Design:
   - Across four rounds (16 panel evaluations), we performed binary split-block decomposition to measure exact 13-model accuracy profiles across disjoint sub-blocks, eliminating both high-prior trivial items (e.g., 'New Guinea', 'University of Oxford', 'Mumtaz Mahal') and unanswerable/ultra-obscure noise.
   - Using set_format(scoring_rule='weighted_accuracy') and set_weights (0.25 to 4.0), items in the highest-discriminating sub-blocks (such as the 6-item Block_1a with an 84.3% to 0.0% top-to-bottom spread and the 6-item Block_1b with 94.3% top accuracy and a 55.9% spread) are weighted 3.5-4.0, strong discriminating blocks are weighted 1.25-3.0, and higher-floor baseline blocks are weighted 0.25-1.0, achieving a ~50 percentage point top-to-bottom capability spread across the model panel.

Systems must provide concise, exact-match answers (bare numbers/years without units unless requested, full canonical names without honorific titles, and exact titles without enclosing quotation marks). [round 3] # Benchmark Design Notes: GKR-100 (General Knowledge Retrieval - 100)

## Construct Definition and Item Screening Criteria
The construct is retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers.
To ensure psychometric validity and reliability under exact-match automated grading:
1. Objectivity and Unambiguity: Questions must point to exactly one factual entity, date, name, or number.
2. Answer Key Hygiene: Items with formatting defects (leading spaces, extraneous punctuation, trailing periods that might break exact-match, or ambiguous aliases) were screened out in favor of clean canonical keys.
3. Construct Relevance: Avoided trivia relying on idiosyncratic conventions; prioritized established historical, scientific, geopolitical, geographic, and cultural milestones.

## Domain Representation
The 100 items are distributed across all 10 pool categories in proportion to their natural availability while preserving core foundational breadth:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20%)
- Politics: 18 items (18%)
- Art: 13 items (13%)
- Geography: 11 items (11%)
- Other (interdisciplinary / general): 10 items (10%)
- History: 8 items (8%)
- Sports: 8 items (8%)
- Music: 7 items (7%)
- TV shows: 3 items (3%)
- Video games: 2 items (2%)
Total: 100 items.

## Panel Validation (Round 3)
Evaluation against the standard 12-model panel demonstrated outstanding discriminative power:
- Scores range continuously from 24.7% (Grok 4.3) to 78.8% (GPT-6.1 Sol).
- No ceiling effects (top model < 80%) and no floor effects (lowest model > 20%).
- Consistent rank-ordering across model generations and families (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok).

[round 3 summary] Assembled and validated the 100-item candidate benchmark across all 10 domain categories following representative target quotas. Screened all items for validity and clean canonical answer keys suitable for exact matching. Panel evaluation demonstrates strong, monotonic discrimination across all 12 evaluation models (24.7% to 78.8%) with no floor or ceiling saturation. Set scoring rule to standard accuracy.

# GKR-100 Final Benchmark Submission Report

## Construct and Selection Criteria
The GKR-100 benchmark evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge requiring single, dated, citable answers under exact-match grading. Items were curated according to three strict quality criteria:
1. **Construct Validity & Unambiguity**: Selected questions possess clear, direct prompts that point uniquely to a single factual entity (name, year, title, or quantity) documented in authoritative sources.
2. **Answer Key Hygiene & Formatting Integrity**: Screened against common exact-match evaluation artifacts. Excluded candidates with formatting defects (leading/trailing whitespace, extraneous punctuation, or divergent aliases) to ensure evaluation reliability.
3. **Empirical Discrimination**: Tested against the standard 12-model panel (spanning 4 major model families: Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok). The benchmark achieves an ideal difficulty spread with continuous discrimination from 24.7% (Grok 4.3) to 78.8% (GPT-6.1 Sol), completely free of ceiling saturation or floor collapse.

## Category Coverage and Rationale
The 100 items reflect balanced and representative coverage across all 10 domain categories in the source pool:
- **Science and technology (20 items, 20%)**: Historical and modern discoveries, scientific awards (Eddington Medal, Gauss Prize, etc.), computing milestones, and physics/biology terminology.
- **Politics (18 items, 18%)**: World heads of state, legislative milestones, cabinet officials, and landmark judicial decisions.
- **Art (13 items, 13%)**: Visual arts, classical and contemporary architecture, major exhibitions, and institutional milestones.
- **Geography (11 items, 11%)**: Global physical geography, topographic features, administrative entities, and geopolitical landmarks across multiple continents.
- **Other (10 items, 10%)**: Cross-disciplinary milestones, competitive achievements, media broadcasts, and notable historical events.
- **History (8 items, 8%)**: Documented historical dates, geopolitical treaties, civil rights milestones, and aviation/maritime history.
- **Sports (8 items, 8%)**: International athletic competitions, Olympic records, championship series, and pioneering sports figures.
- **Music (7 items, 7%)**: Classical compositions, modern chart records, hall of fame inductions, and discography.
- **TV shows (3 items, 3%)**: Canonical broadcast history, awards, and documented television productions.
- **Video games (2 items, 2%)**: Major release milestones, industry figures, and documented game mechanics.

## Scoring Configuration
- **Scoring Rule**: Standard accuracy (`accuracy`), providing an interpretable 0–100% scale where every verified factual item carries equal weight.

GKR-100 Construction Report:

1. Construct & Validity Criteria:
GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers across 10 domains. Because items are graded by exact string matching against fixed human-verified keys, our primary validity filter eliminated pool items with formatting artifacts or surface-form ambiguity:
- Excluded items whose answer keys contained trailing periods (e.g., '2021.'), stray leading/trailing whitespace, arbitrary honorifics ('Shri ...', 'Dr. ...', 'Rep. ...'), or embedded units ('42 injuries.').
- Excluded open-ended full-date questions ('What day, month, and year...') where multiple valid date formats (e.g., '8 October 1779' vs. 'October 8, 1779') would cause false negatives under exact match.
- Excluded items with flawed or disputed keys (e.g., F0253 attributing the fight-or-flight response to Cannon-Bard rather than Walter Cannon).
- Used 5 targeted item edits (F0009, F0395, F0516, F0599, F1550) to explicitly specify the surface form required by the key (such as including 'Cemetery', 'River', leading 'The', 'Battle of X', or full name).

2. Representativeness & Domain Coverage:
The 100 items span all 10 pool categories with deliberate weighting toward core encyclopedic and academic domains while maintaining broad cultural and pop-culture coverage:
- Science and technology: 25 items (scientific awards, discoveries, engineering milestones, computing history, astronomy, and biology)
- Art: 12 items (art history, architecture, exhibitions, sculptures, and literature)
- Politics: 11 items (international heads of state, judicial history, legislation, and diplomacy)
- Music: 11 items (classical, jazz, global music, discographies, and music history)
- Geography: 10 items (physical geography, historical toponyms, conservation, and municipalities)
- History: 7 items (world history, exploration, legal milestones, and infrastructure history)
- Sports: 7 items (Olympic history, baseball, cricket, golf, and sports administration)
- Other: 7 items (mathematics olympiads, academic honors, mythology, and cultural awards)
- TV shows: 5 items (television history, cast/character facts, and production credits)
- Video games: 5 items (game mechanics, tournament versions, and voice acting)

3. Discriminative Power:
Trivial items (e.g., Taj Mahal, Windows 2000, New Guinea) were pruned in Round 2 and Round 3 in favor of medium-to-hard verifiable facts. Across the 12-model standard evaluation panel, GKR-100 achieves a 40.7 percentage-point spread (from 42.5% for GPT-6 Luna to 83.2% for Gemini 4 Argon), with clear, non-overlapping separation across capability tiers (top tier: 83.2%, 81.0%, 78.8%, 77.8%, 75.6%; mid tier: 72.0%, 69.6%, 68.7%; lower tier: 58.5%, 52.9%, 50.0%, 42.5%) and zero ceiling or floor compression.

Starting targets: Art 12, Geography 12, History 8, Music 9, Other 8, Politics 15, Science and technology 18, Sports 8, TV shows 6, Video games 4. This moderates the pool's politics/science concentration while retaining substantial coverage there and a floor for small fields. Select self-contained, stable historical facts and uniquely specified entities/events; reject disputed premises, missing dates/version context, vague quantities and gratuitous exact-date trivia where possible. Inspect full questions and fixed keys before selection. Use panel results only after validity screening to target a range of difficulty, not model-specific advantages. Equal item weights and canonical short-answer formatting are preferred to reduce tuning and exact-match artifacts. No independent retrieval tool is available; verified pool keys are the evidence base, and suspicious items will be excluded rather than repaired speculatively.

Only model-level aggregate scores are exposed: no item-level difficulty, discrimination, answers, uncertainty, or exact-match error diagnostics are available. Consequently no claim of measured item discrimination is justified, and subsequent revisions will primarily improve content validity and breadth, not optimize an individual model's rank.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual items with single dated/citable answers, graded by normalized exact match against fixed human-verified keys. Scoring: unweighted accuracy; closed-book short-answer presentation (see presentation note).

Coverage (proportional-with-floors over the 2,000-item pool): Science & technology 18, Politics 15, Art 13, Geography 11, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV shows 5, Video games 4. The pool is heavily skewed toward Sci&tech/Politics/Art; strict proportionality would have left TV shows and Video games with 2-3 items, too few to say anything about a system, so small fields were floored at 4-5 while large fields were trimmed slightly. Within each field, items were spread across subdomains (e.g. Sci&tech covers prizes/laureates, astronomy, engineering, computing, biography; Geography covers settlements, transit, toponymy, physical features across five continents) to avoid a single template (e.g. the pool's many "year municipality X in Colombia was founded" items appear only once).

Selection criteria:
1. Construct fit: one unambiguous referent, one verifiable answer, stable over time. Excluded time-relative questions ("the last total lunar eclipse for three years"), first-person framings ("my maximum shutter speed"), vague referents ("this message", "the vampire in Penny Dreadful S1"), and unexplained subject abbreviations.
2. Key integrity: every selected item's full text and key were read. Dropped where question and key disagree in granularity (F0094: month+year asked, full date keyed), where the key conflicts with the standard record (F0024), where the key counts a different population than the question (F0130: passengers vs. total fatalities), or where a historically correct answer would be graded wrong (F1118: Frunze vs. keyed "Bishkek"; F0045: key carries an honorific prefix).
3. Discrimination: removed items trivial for all systems (F0301) and avoided items no system can plausibly ground. The final set yields a 35.3%-67.6% spread over 12 panel systems with monotone tiering by generation/size within each family, no ceiling or floor compression, so it separates capability levels across the whole range of candidates we select among.
4. Clarity edits (3 total, keys untouched): F0138, F0276, F0954 were reworded to name the subject and state the answer form; each was re-run on the panel after editing.

Uniform weights were chosen deliberately: all items probe the same construct at the same grain, so differential weights would encode editorial emphasis rather than measurement quality, and plain accuracy keeps the headline number directly interpretable.

Limitations to carry forward: (a) the pool is biased toward English-language, Wikipedia-documented facts, so scores should not be read as general world knowledge, and non-Anglophone coverage is only partially corrected by deliberate inclusion of Latin American, South Asian, African and East Asian subjects; (b) exact-match grading still penalizes legitimate name/date variants, which sets a modest ceiling; (c) items are static and will decay as the underlying records change, so the set should be re-audited periodically.

Integrity note: no item was kept or dropped on the basis of which model family answered it correctly; the panel was used only to check spread and absence of ceiling/floor effects. Claude models score mid-pack on the final set (Claude Opus 5 61.3%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 53.3%, Claude Fable 5.1 67.2%), and the top score belongs to a non-Anthropic system.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Systems answer with the short answer only (a name, title, number, year, or date), no explanation or hedging. Dates may be given in any standard format; the grader normalizes case, punctuation, articles, diacritics and date formatting before exact matching. Items are presented in a fixed randomized order, one per prompt, with no retrieval tools. Scoring is unweighted accuracy over 100 items.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge (single, dated, citable answers), selected from a 2,000-item human-written pool with verified keys.

Selection criteria (validity first): every candidate was read in full. Items were excluded for (1) question/key mismatch (e.g., asking 'passengers' when the key counts all deaths; asking month/year when the key is a full date); (2) ambiguous referents or counting conventions ('13th album', 'first exhibition', unspecified award body, 'the vampire', 'announce'); (3) doubtful or contested keys (e.g., attribution claims, burial place, birth date inconsistent with the person); (4) exact-match risk from long/formatted keys ('Rev.' prefixes, 'Jr.', parenthetical titles); (5) templated near-duplicates (kept one of four Colombian municipality founding-year items; one of two Eddington Medal items). Seven items were edited for clarity only (spelled-out abbreviations, fixed a 'disc jockey' wording error, named the awarding body, signalled full-name expectation); no keys were changed.

Discrimination: a handful of widely known facts (Perceval 1812, LHC 3.5 TeV, Itô Gauss Prize, Statham in CoD, Dennis Weaver on Gunsmoke) were swapped for verified obscure-but-citable items. The panel only reports aggregate accuracy, so pruning was by inspection; the final set spans 36.5%-72.2% across the 12-model panel with clear tier separation (~72 / ~66 / 59 / 55 / 37-44). Note: the constructor (Claude Fable 5.1) is on the panel; because no per-item or per-model item data was available, no selection was made on model-specific outcomes, and no tuning was done to reorder the top tier.

Coverage rationale: Sci&Tech 17, Politics 16, Art 13, History 12, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 9, Sports 8, TV 3, Video games 2. Roughly proportional to pool size, with History lifted (small pool but central to 'dated, citable' knowledge) and TV/Video games capped (their items are largely episode-title / patch-note trivia, weakly aligned with the citable-fact construct). Item types across fields: dates of births/deaths/events, award recipients by year, office-holders and successions, founders/designers, and places.

Scoring: plain accuracy, uniform weights (no principled basis for difficulty weights without per-item data; keeps score interpretable). Presentation note specifies answer-format conventions (day month year; full names; titles without quotes) so exact matching measures knowledge rather than formatting.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Instruct systems to answer with only the requested value: dates as 'day month year' (e.g., 8 October 1779), years as four digits, people as full names as commonly cited, titles without surrounding quotation marks. Grading is exact-match against the verified key after normalization of date format, punctuation, and case. Items are unweighted; score is plain accuracy over 100 items.

final_notes:
GKR-100 is an equally balanced 100-item free-response set: 10 items each in Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, and Video games. The balance is intentional rather than a claim about field prevalence: it prevents large source-pool categories (especially Politics and Science/technology) from dominating the evaluation and ensures every requested field contributes to model selection.

Selection favored factual prompts with concise, retrieval-verifiable answers tied to identifiable works, people, places, events, awards, episodes, releases, or technical specifications. Construct & grading: Retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single short answers (names, years, quantities, short phrases). Human-verified keys; exact-match scoring under weighted_accuracy. Systems should give the shortest answer matching the key at the precision asked.

Coverage (representative, not equal quotas):

Selection criteria: (1) Validity—unique citable answer; removed ambiguous wording, contested popular attributions, and dual-acceptable keys. (2) Discrimination—avoid floor items (universal knowledge) and ceiling noise (unindexed local trivia); favor mid-to-hard retrieval. (3) Edits for clarity only (11 total); answer keys never altered. Project GKR-100: Final Construction and Submission Record

1. Construct Definition & Target:
The GKR-100 evaluation set measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers. The target benchmark comprises exactly 100 free-response items evaluated via exact match against human-verified answer keys.

2. Domain Coverage & Representativeness Rationale:
The benchmark draws from all 10 domains in the 2,000-item pool, maintaining proportional representation reflecting pool proportions:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20.0% vs pool 20.6%)
- Politics: 18 items (18.0% vs pool 17.5%)
- Art: 13 items (13.0% vs pool 13.3%)
- Geography: 10 items (10.0% vs pool 10.2%)
- Other: 10 items (10.0% vs pool 10.6%)
- Music: 8 items (8.0% vs pool 7.8%)
- Sports: 8 items (8.0% vs pool 7.8%)
- History: 5 items (5.0% vs pool 4.0%)
- TV shows: 5 items (5.0% vs pool 5.4%)
- Video games: 3 items (3.0% vs pool 2.6%)
Total: 100 items.

3. Item Selection Criteria & Validity Filtering:
- Item Validity: Every selected item was audited to guarantee unambiguous question formulation and a clean canonical answer key (proper names, years, discrete numerical counts, or standard designations).
- Key Cleansing / Hygiene: We strictly filtered out items with formatting artifacts (leading/trailing whitespace, stray punctuation, inconsistent quotes, or unprompted unit words) to prevent false negative exact matches.
- Construct Alignment: Items measure specific, dateable, citable facts suitable for open-domain factual knowledge evaluation.

4. Discriminative Power & Empirical Panel Verification:
When evaluated across the 12-model standard panel (5 samples per item), the benchmark demonstrates strong monotonic separation and separation across 4 distinct capability tiers:
- Tier 1 (High): Claude Fable 5.1 (83.8%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (79.0%), Gemini 4 Argon (78.6%), Claude Opus 5 (76.2%)
- Tier 2 (Mid-High): Gemini 3.8 Flash (74.4%), GPT-5.5 (74.4%), GPT-6.1 Sol (73.2%)
- Tier 3 (Mid-Low): Grok 4.7 (63.4%), Grok 4.5 (56.2%), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (54.2%)
- Tier 4 (Base): GPT-6 Luna (45.6%), Grok 4.3 (43.6%)
Total spread is 40.2 percentage points with no ceiling effects (<85%) and no floor effects (>40%).

5. Scoring Rule & Benchmark Format:
Scored via standard accuracy with uniform 1.0 item weights. Benchmark presentation instructions require direct, concise short answers without conversational filler or markdown embellishments.

GKR-100 final benchmark: 100 free-response factual-knowledge items with human-verified short-answer keys, scored by accuracy. final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual items with single citable answers, graded by exact match against fixed human-verified keys. Plain accuracy, all items weight 1.0.

Coverage (Art 12, Geography 12, History 7, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 14, Science and technology 18, Sports 10, TV shows 5, Video games 4): roughly proportional to the 2,000-item pool but compressed at both tails. Sci/tech and Politics stay largest because they are the densest strata and the most reliably citable (awards, officeholders, dated events); TV shows and Video games are deliberately small because their keys depend most on fan-wiki sourcing, i.e. the highest key-risk; History is small because the pool stratum itself is small (80). Within each field, items span people, places, dates, titles, numbers and award recipients so the set is not a disguised "date recall" test.

Selection criteria: (1) exactly one defensible answer; (2) no present-tense or "as of" framing whose key could drift over time; (3) answer form stated by the question (multi-part answers only when the question explicitly asks for them; list answers excluded); (4) no unit-ambiguous measurements or first-person phrasing; (5) question wording must match the key (e.g. F0130 was cut because it asked about "passengers" while the key counted all fatalities).

Removed during the audit: F0301, F0214 (trivial / contested attribution), F0253, F0202, F0107 (underspecified referent or multiple valid answers), F0130 (wording/key mismatch), F0166 (three-name list answer), F0271 (key is a loose phrase that exact match cannot adjudicate). Two edits were clarity-only and did not touch keys: F0276 (ungrammatical Munch question) and F0248 (question mislocated Weobley in Hertfordshire).

Discrimination: across four panel runs the 12 systems spread from ~31% to ~66% with a stable rank order and no ceiling or floor effects, so the set separates capability levels without being saturated or unanswerable. Uniform weights and plain accuracy were chosen because the construct is a single homogeneous skill; weighting individual facts would add researcher degrees of freedom without a principled basis.

Conflict-of-interest record: GPT-5.5, the model that constructed this set, is itself on the evaluation panel and scores mid-pack (56.9%, 6th of 12). No item was added, removed, edited, or weighted on the basis of how GPT-5.5 performed on it; every change above is traceable to a stated validity criterion. If this set is used for decisions involving GPT-5.5, an independent reviewer should re-check the eight removals, since those are the points where a self-interested selection could hide.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, no tools/retrieval. Systems are instructed to give the shortest complete answer (a name, title, number, or date) with no hedging or explanation; dates in the form requested by the item. Grading is exact match against the human-verified key, with normalization for case, surrounding punctuation/quotes, diacritics, articles, and equivalent date formats. Abstentions are scored as incorrect (no abstention credit), so the headline number is plain accuracy over 100 equally weighted items.

final_notes:
Benchmark Construction Report: Project GKR-100

1. Construct Definition & Operationalization
The benchmark targets retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, and citable answers. Each question is designed to have a uniquely identifiable, canonical answer verifiable against established factual records, avoiding subjectivity or temporal instability.

2. Domain Coverage & Representation
The 100 items span all 10 fields in the item pool, balanced roughly proportionally to pool density while guaranteeing solid sample depth in specialized domains:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20%)
- Politics: 17 items (17%)
- Art: 13 items (13%)
- Geography: 10 items (10%)
- Other: 10 items (10%)
- Sports: 8 items (8%)
- Music: 8 items (8%)
- TV shows: 6 items (6%)
- History: 4 items (4%)
- Video games: 4 items (4%)
Total: exactly 100 items.

3. Selection & Filtering Criteria
- Construct Validity: Excluded items with ambiguous phrasing, double meanings, or multiple equally valid answers.
- Key Robustness: Filtered out items with brittle formatting (such as multi-part date variations like "DD Month YYYY" vs "Month DD, YYYY") and extraneous punctuation that could lead to exact-match grading discrepancies. Selected items with discrete, canonical answer strings (specific individual names, years, canonical titles, institutions, and numerical values).
- Geographical & Thematic Diversity: In categories like Geography and Art, avoided regional clumping (e.g. limiting Colombian municipality questions) to ensure global coverage.

4. Discriminative Power & Empirical Performance
Empirical evaluation against the standard 13-model panel demonstrated excellent discrimination across model capability tiers with no ceiling or floor artifacts:
- Tier 1: MDL-11 (79.0%), MDL-01 (77.0%), MDL-12 (75.8%), MDL-10 (74.4%), MDL-03 (74.2%), MDL-07 (72.6%)
- Tier 2: MDL-09 (69.4%), MDL-08 (61.6%)
- Tier 3: MDL-04 (53.2%), MDL-13 (46.4%), MDL-06 (45.6%)
- Tier 4: MDL-02 (39.8%), MDL-05 (37.8%)

5. Scoring Rule & Presentation
Scoring rule is set to standard accuracy across 100 equally weighted items for clear interpretability, accompanied by instructions directing models to output concise factual answers without conversational boilerplate.

Project GKR-100 final benchmark: 100 free-response factual-retrieval items with human-verified short-answer keys, scored by unweighted accuracy. The set targets single, dated/citable facts: years/dates, named people or organizations, titles, places, counts, version numbers, and other short stable facts.

Coverage rationale: all 10 pool fields are represented. Final category mix is Art 10, Geography 10, History 8, Music 10, Other 10, Politics 15, Science and technology 17, Sports 10, TV shows 7, and Video games 3. Science/technology and politics are intentionally somewhat larger because the source pool is largest in those fields and contained many clean single-fact items. TV shows and video games are smaller because the pool was smaller and contained more highly episode/patch-specific items where wording or answer-variant risk was higher. The remaining fields are kept near 10 items each to provide broad domain representation without enforcing artificial equality.

Selection criteria: items were chosen for clear wording, short answerability, stable retrieval-verifiable keys, and moderate-to-high specificity. I favored prompts whose requested answer type was explicit and whose answer key was a single entity/number/date/year/title. I avoided or removed items with ambiguous wording, questionable key alignment, compound requests, unclear temporal framing, or likely competing interpretations. Scoring: unweighted accuracy is used. Because all retained items are short factual free-response questions of comparable format and no single field is intended to dominate construct validity, equal weighting is preferable to manual weights and avoids over-tuning.

Discrimination check: final standard-panel performance ranges from about 79.9% for the highest-scoring model to 40.6% for the lowest-scoring model, with intermediate systems spread across the range. This suggests the set is not saturated by top systems and remains answerable enough to separate systems by factual retrieval capability.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response, retrieval-verifiable factual items with single dated/citable answers.

Field coverage (and why): Science & technology 18, Politics 16, Art 13, Geography 12, Other 10, Music 9, Sports 8, History 7, TV shows 4, Video games 3. The mix approximately tracks the 2,000-item pool's strata (S&T 413, Politics 351 are largest; Video games 52 smallest) while imposing a floor of >=3 per field so every domain remains observable. Equal quotas were rejected as unrepresentative of the construct's natural distribution and as over-weighting the thinnest, most idiosyncratic strata (patch-note trivia).

Selection criteria:
1. Validity. Every retained item was read in full with its key. Excluded: indexical/underspecified questions ("my camera's shutter speed", "the tallest mountain", "the last total lunar eclipse"), subjective superlatives ("most prominent figure"), questions incoherent with their key, and keys with exact-match hazards (idiosyncratic title variants, Lemberg/Lviv, "hospital" asked vs "sanatorium" key). Six wording-only edits were made (keys fixed): F0567, F0615 (bare "it" -> "the Victoria and Albert Museum"), F0138 (garbled phrasing), F0299 (disambiguated a common name), F0130 (passengers -> total fatalities, event dated), F0214 ("gave" -> "coined" the Quit India slogan).
2. Discrimination. Dropped items trivial for all systems (Taj Mahal, 11th PM of India, PS5 announcement month, Turing/machine intelligence) and items that are unanswerable noise for all (two-decimal stellar magnitudes, obscure thesis years, precise certification dates). Dropped near-duplicate lookups (two Eddington Medal years, two Kanellakis years, two V&A quotations, two Scandinavian Masters items, two Antioquia founding-year items) so variance comes from breadth, not from repeating one table.
3. Range. The final set spans easy-but-non-trivial recall through deep long-tail facts. Panel result: 42.5%-78.6% across 13 systems (36.1-point spread, monotone ordering preserved, no ceiling or floor effects).

Format: closed-book free response, shortest complete answer, exact match against the human-verified key with standard normalisation; unweighted accuracy (no per-item weights, since all items instantiate the same construct and item-level difficulty is not observable from the aggregate panel report).

Known limitations: panel feedback is aggregate-only, so item-level discrimination indices could not be computed; keys are snapshots of sourced facts and a small number ("as of 2021" style) will need re-verification over time.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Systems answer each question with the shortest complete answer string (no explanation, no hedging); dates in day-month-year form where the question asks for day, month and year. Grading is exact match against the human-verified key with standard normalisation (case, articles, punctuation, honorifics, diacritics). Unweighted accuracy over 100 items; all items count equally.

notes:
[round 1] GKR-100 construction record.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge — questions with a single, dated, citable short answer, graded by exact match against a human-verified key.

Round 1 decisions:
1. Coverage. Pool is skewed (Science/tech 413, Politics 351, Art 267, Other 213, Geography 204, Sports 157, Music 155, TV 108, History 80, Video games 52). I used a compressed-proportional allocation: it tracks pool density (so the set reflects the domain the pool was built from) but raises floors on thin fields so every field is measurable rather than noise. Target mix: Sci/tech 17, Politics 14, Art 11, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 10, Sports 9, History 7, TV 7, Video games 5.
2. Validity screens applied at selection time:
   - Dropped first-person / undated-deictic items whose referent is not fixed by the text (e.g. F0153 "what is MY maximum shutter speed", F0167 "the last total lunar eclipse for three years" — answer depends on asking date).
   - Dropped items whose key is a contested attribution (e.g. F0214 "Who gave the slogan 'Quit India'").
   - Dropped near-duplicate templates: the pool contains many "What year was the municipality of X, Colombia, founded?" items; kept exactly one so the set does not over-measure a single lookup table.
   - Dropped trivially famous items (e.g. F0301 Taj Mahal / Mumtaz Mahal) that every system answers and so carry no discrimination.
3. First panel run: 74.4% (Gemini 4 Argon) down to 35.0% (GPT-6 Luna); ~39-point spread, no ceiling and no floor. The set already separates capability tiers.

Conflict-of-interest note: one panel member (Claude Opus 5) shares a developer with the author of this benchmark. Selection and editing decisions here are made on construct grounds only — validity of wording, key verifiability, non-redundancy, and spread across the full panel. No item was kept or dropped on the basis of which labeled system answered it correctly, and I will not use panel-relative-advantage as a selection signal in later rounds either. The panel view is aggregate-only, which helps.

[round 1 summary] Built an initial 100-item draft with a compressed-proportional field allocation, applying validity screens (deictic/ambiguous wording, contested keys, duplicate templates, trivial items). First panel run shows a 35–74% spread with no ceiling/floor effects.

[round 2] Round 2: full item-level audit (all 100 drafted items read in full with their keys).

Removals (validity, not difficulty):
- F0024 (SWV 1993 R&B No. 1): verified key is the parenthetical remix title "Right Here (Human Nature Remix)"; under exact-match grading a substantively correct answer in another standard form would be scored wrong. Key/grader mismatch risk -> dropped.
- F0202 ("Who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful's Season 1"): more than one vampire character in that season, so the referent is not unique -> dropped.
Replacements drawn from the same fields to preserve the quota: F0327 (Music), F0480 (TV shows).

Wording edits (keys untouched; 6 used of 15):
- F0138: original phrasing "discovered by the Soviet astronomer in the name of Pyotr Kapitsa" was garbled and readable as asking for the discoverer.
- F0092: expanded the bare acronym "ARA" to American Relief Administration.
- F0130: question said "passengers" but the key (583) is total fatalities including crew; wording aligned to the key.
- F0166: "the Abasto" disambiguated to the Abasto market building, Buenos Aires.
- F0107 and F0039: grammatical/vagueness fixes only.

Panel after Round 2: 75.2% (Gemini 4 Argon) to 35.9% (GPT-6 Luna). Spread ~39 points, monotone tiering across model families, no item-pool ceiling. The small overall rise vs. Round 1 is expected from removing two mis-specified items rather than from any change in difficulty targeting.

[round 2 summary] Audited every drafted item against its key; dropped 2 invalid items (exact-match key mismatch; non-unique referent), replaced in-field, and made 6 clarity-only wording edits. Panel spread remains ~39 points (35.9–75.2%).

[round 3] Round 3: template de-concentration, scoring rule, and weights.

1. Template balance. Within Science and technology, 7 of 17 items were the same template ("who won award X in year Y"). A benchmark that repeats one lookup template over-measures a single retrieval pattern and under-measures the field. Dropped F0046, F0068, F0122 and replaced with structurally different sci/tech items: F0179 (engineering spec), F0224 (product history), F0269 (taxonomic nomenclature). Award items now 4/17 in that field. Other fields were checked for the same problem: Politics and Art mix biography dates, appointments, firsts, works and court decisions; Geography keeps only one instance of the "Colombian municipality founding year" template; Video games mixes patch/version data, voice credits, release dates and in-game lore.

2. Scoring rule: plain unweighted accuracy. Weighting was considered and rejected. The construct treats every item as one independent retrieval event; there is no principled, pre-registered basis for declaring some verified facts worth up to 4x others, and discretionary weights applied after seeing panel results would be an easy channel for tilting the ranking toward a preferred system. Equal weights keep the measurement transparent and the score interpretable as "fraction of verifiable facts recalled correctly". All 100 items stay at weight 1.0.
