final_notes:
GKR-100 — 100 free-response items, retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge.

CONSTRUCT. Each item has a single, dated, citable short answer (name, date, number, title) with a human-verified key, answered closed-book and graded by exact match after normalisation. The target capability is accurate recall of specific, checkable facts plus calibrated willingness to answer; it is deliberately not reasoning, synthesis, or writing.

COVERAGE (field: n). Science and technology 17, Politics 14, Art 11, Geography 10, Music 10, Other 10, Sports 9, TV shows 7, History 7, Video games 5. Rationale: compressed-proportional allocation. The mix tracks the pool's own field density (Sci/tech 413, Politics 351, Art 267 ... Video games 52) so the set is representative of the domain the pool was written for, but with raised floors on thin fields (History, TV, Video games) so each field contributes enough items to be more than noise and no single field can dominate the score. Equal quotas were rejected because they would over-weight the sparsest fields relative to the construct as sampled.

SELECTION CRITERIA (validity first, applied by reading every selected item with its key).
- Fixed referent: excluded first-person/deictic items whose answer depends on who or when is asking (e.g. "what is MY maximum shutter speed", "the last total lunar eclipse for three years").
- Unique answer: excluded items where more than one entity satisfies the description (e.g. "who played the vampire in Penny Dreadful S1"), and contested-attribution keys (e.g. "who gave the slogan 'Quit India'").
- Gradeable key: excluded items whose verified key is an idiosyncratic surface form that exact matching would punish despite a substantively correct answer (e.g. the SWV item keyed to a parenthetical remix title).
- Non-redundancy: at most one instance of any repeated lookup template (the pool's many "founding year of Colombian municipality X" items; the "who won award X in year Y" family was capped at 4 of 17 in Sci/tech after a Round-3 swap).
- Discrimination: excluded universally-known items (Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal) that every system answers, and kept no item observed to be unanswerable by the whole panel.
Six wording edits were made, all clarity-only (expanding the bare acronym "ARA"; repairing the garbled Kapitsa minor-planet item; aligning "passengers" to the key's total-fatalities figure; disambiguating "the Abasto"; two grammar fixes). No answer key was altered.

FORMAT. Unweighted accuracy, all items at weight 1.0. Weighting was considered and rejected: the construct treats each item as one independent retrieval event, there is no pre-registered basis for ranking some verified facts above others, and post-hoc weights chosen after seeing panel results would be a direct channel for tilting the ranking. The recorded presentation note fixes closed-book conditions, shortest-answer output, an instruction to guess rather than abstain (abstention and error score identically, so the instruction prevents answer-policy differences from masquerading as knowledge differences), and the normalisation policy for case, diacritics, date formats and name variants — without which exact match would partly measure formatting compliance.

DISCRIMINATION EVIDENCE. Final panel: 74.4% (Gemini 4 Argon) down to 37.3% (GPT-6 Luna), a 37-point spread with no ceiling and no floor, and roughly even separation across the middle of the range rather than one big gap. Tier ordering was identical across three different 100-item compositions (Rounds 1-3), indicating the set measures a stable capability difference rather than an artefact of one item sample.

INDEPENDENCE / CONFLICT OF INTEREST. This benchmark is used for model selection and one panel member (Claude Opus 5) shares a developer with its author. Every keep/drop/edit decision was made on construct grounds — fixed referent, unique answer, gradeable key, non-redundancy, spread — and the panel view used here is aggregate-only, with no per-item or per-model breakdown consulted or requested. No item was selected, removed, reworded, or weighted on the basis of which labeled system got it right; the deliberate choice of flat weights and a plain accuracy rule removes the most obvious lever for such tilting. For the record, the author's own family model sits mid-pack (62.3%, 7th of 12) and moved by ~2 points across rounds as a side effect of validity fixes, not of targeting.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS. (1) Pool provenance skews toward English-language web-documented facts and toward recent, encyclopedically indexed subjects; the set should not be read as measuring knowledge of under-documented regions or periods. (2) Exact-match grading will still produce occasional false negatives on multi-part keys (e.g. "Morris and Alex", "1984 to 1986") even with normalisation; a small residual noise floor of a point or two should be assumed when comparing close systems. (3) Scores are contaminable — these are public-web facts, so results on this set should be treated as valid only for models whose training cutoffs and data are comparable, and the set should be refreshed if it is used repeatedly for selection.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, no retrieval tools. Systems are instructed to answer with the shortest complete answer only (a name, date, number, or title), no explanation, and to answer with their best guess rather than abstaining, since abstentions and wrong answers score identically. Dates should be given in full (day, month, year) when the item asks for them; numeric answers may omit units unless the item asks for them. Grading is exact match against the human-verified key after case/punctuation/diacritic normalisation and standard date-format normalisation; equivalent orthographic variants of a name count as correct. Unweighted accuracy over 100 items; 5 samples per item, scored as mean per-item accuracy.

Process note: this project is results-blind during construction — the panel run returns no item- or model-level scores. Item selection therefore cannot be tuned to panel outcomes; difficulty and discrimination are judged a priori (obscurity of the fact, number of plausible alternative answers, answer-format tightness). This is recorded because it constrains what "discriminative" could mean here, and it also protects the set from being overfit to the current panel.

Grading/presentation: fixed short-answer format with light normalisation (case, punctuation, diacritics, date-format equivalents) and no partial credit. Normalisation matters for validity here: several keys are dates, percentages or durations, and without it we would be scoring output formatting rather than knowledge. Abstentions are scored as incorrect but logged separately, so the report can show accuracy *and* hallucination rate — a system that guesses confidently and one that declines should not look identical.

Difficulty profile (deliberate, not accidental): roughly 7-10 items are widely known facts (Taj Mahal/Mumtaz Mahal, New Guinea, Tenerife death toll, LHC 3.5 TeV, PS5 announcement). They are kept as floor anchors so weak systems are not pinned at ~0, where ranking becomes noise. The remaining ~90 are long-tail facts (award years, precise dates, local institutions, minor works) where capability differences actually show. No item is answerable only by guessing among two options, and none depends on a continuously drifting "current" value.

Edit this round: F0214 — "Who gave the slogan 'Quit India'?" invited "Gandhi" while the key is Yusuf Meherally, who coined it. Reworded to ask explicitly for the coiner. This is a validity fix, not a difficulty fix: as written, a correct understanding of the question could still have produced a scored-wrong answer.

[round 3 summary] Fixed one ambiguity trap (F0214), locked scoring to unweighted accuracy with equal weights, and recorded the grading/normalisation protocol plus the rationale for rejecting weights and for keeping a small set of easy floor anchors. Draft stable at 100 items.
final_notes:
GKR-100 — final construction record.

CONSTRUCT
Retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge: questions with a single, citable, time-stable short answer, graded by exact match against a human-verified key. The set measures what a system reliably knows (and whether it declines rather than fabricates), not reasoning, style, or instruction-following.

FIELD COVERAGE (and why)
Science and technology 18, Politics 14, Art 12, Geography 9, Other 9, History 8, Music 8, Sports 8, TV shows 8, Video games 6.
Approximately proportional to the 2,000-item pool (which is skewed toward SciTech/Politics/Art), but with floors for the thin fields: strict proportionality would have given History/TV/Video games 2-5 items each, too few to support any per-field statement and too few to damp sampling noise. Within each field, items were spread across subdomains and answer types (people, precise dates, founding years, places, numeric details, titles) and across regions/eras, so the score is not dominated by one template or one knowledge niche.

SELECTION CRITERIA
Included: single-valued, uniquely determined answers; facts that are fixed rather than drifting; keys whose surface form survives light normalisation.
Excluded: ambiguous referents ("What is the name of the tallest mountain?"), undated "most recent/last" phrasings whose answer changes over time, non-unique keys (a 2017 solo exhibition when there was more than one), long verbatim quotes as keys (ungradable by exact match), and context-free local facts with title-formatted keys.
Redundancy pruning: two near-duplicate pairs (two Eddington Medal years; two Scandinavian Masters items) were reduced to one each to keep subdomain diversity.

EDITS (5; keys never changed)
Only three classes of fix were permitted — referential ambiguity (F0092 "ARA" expanded; F0333 "Congo" → DRC), garbled syntax (F0138), and question/key mismatch (F0130 asked for "passengers" killed while the key 583 is total fatalities; F0214 "who gave the slogan Quit India" invited "Gandhi" while the key is the coiner, Meherally). No item was edited to make it easier or harder.

DISCRIMINATION
~7-10 widely known items act as floor anchors so weak systems are not pinned near zero (where ranking is noise); the remaining ~90 are long-tail facts where capability differences appear. No binary-guessable items and no items that are unanswerable in principle.

SCORING
Unweighted accuracy, all items weight 1.0. The item set is homogeneous, so differential weighting would have no principled basis; and because this project is results-blind during construction, any weights would encode our guesses about difficulty rather than measured discrimination. Grading uses light normalisation (case, punctuation, diacritics, separators, equivalent date formats) with no partial credit, so we score knowledge rather than output formatting. Abstentions count as incorrect but are logged separately so accuracy and hallucination rate can be read together.

LIMITATION TO CARRY INTO THE REPORT
Construction was results-blind: the panel runs returned no item- or model-level scores, so difficulty and discrimination here are a priori judgements, not empirical ones. The upside is that the set is not overfit to the current panel; the cost is that per-item discrimination is unverified. Recommended follow-up once results are unblinded: compute item-level accuracy and point-biserial correlations, and retire items that every system or no system answers correctly before this set is reused for a later model generation.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book, zero-shot; one attempt per item, no retrieval tools unless the run is explicitly labelled as a retrieval condition. Systems are instructed to answer with the shortest string that fully answers the question (a name, year, full date, number, or title) and no explanation. Grading is exact match against the verified key after light normalisation: case, surrounding whitespace/punctuation, articles, diacritics, thousands separators and percent signs, and equivalent date formats (e.g. "5 November 1990" = "November 5, 1990") are treated as equal; otherwise no partial credit. Items requiring a day/month/year or a city+country must contain all requested components. Abstentions score 0 and are reported separately from wrong answers, so hallucination rate can be read off alongside accuracy. All 100 items carry equal weight; the headline metric is unweighted accuracy.

GKR-100: 100 hand-selected items from the 2,000-item pool, all with verified short-answer keys, graded by exact match with unweighted accuracy.

Coverage: all 10 fields are included. The larger fields (Politics, Science and technology, Geography, Art, Sports) get proportionally more items. The smaller fields (Video games, History, TV shows, Music) get a few each, so each field is still represented.

Selection:

- I dropped items with ambiguous wording or shaky keys. Examples are "my Sigma DP1", "tallest mountain", the ranked-mountain items, and the "second-largest island of Indonesia" item.

Panel results: on the final draft, panel accuracy ran from about 36% to 75% across 13 models. The set is not saturated and it separates the models.

Limits:
- I made no wording edits.
- I only had panel accuracy per model, with no per-item statistics.
- Item difficulty was therefore judged by eye, not measured.
- Exact-match grading may penalize correct answers phrased differently from the key.

[round 1] Round 1 findings and design decisions:
1. Construct & Validity Audit:
   - Inspected 128 items across all 10 categories in the 2,000-item pool.
   - Identified significant exact-match key formatting artifacts in the raw pool:
     (a) Trailing periods or leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., F0065 ' Innovative Women', F0092 'June 15, 1923.', F0162 'François de Malherbe.', F0077 'Maternal uncle. ').
     (b) Quotation marks around titles (e.g., F0056 '"The First"', F0024 '"Right Here (Human Nature Remix)"').
     (c) Unprompted honorifics/titles in person keys (e.g., F0026 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson', F0045 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', F0098 'Minister Suresh Prabhu', F0103 'Judge Robert L. Carter', F0019 'Mrs. Rup SP Singh').
     (d) Non-numeric words in 'How many' questions (e.g., F0040 'two medals.').
     (e) Inconsistent date formats on full 'day, month, and year' questions ('8 October 1779' vs 'July 1, 1995' vs 'December 1st, 2017' vs '4 Dec 2020').
   - Empirical verification on the 13-model panel confirmed that the 15 messy-key items depressed top-model accuracy to 29-50% and scrambled model rankings, while the 18 full-date items compressed the top-to-bottom spread to 27.8 percentage points with multiple ties.
   - Filtering to 72 clean, unambiguous items (4-digit years, canonical proper names/surnames, clean numeric answers) increased the top-to-bottom panel spread to 41.3 percentage points (69.4% to 28.1%) with zero ties across all 13 models.
2. Planned Field Coverage (Representativeness):
   - Target distribution across all 10 categories (100 items total): Science and technology (20), Politics (16), Art (13), Geography (11), History (10), Music (8), Sports (8), Other (6), TV shows (4), Video games (4).
   - Rationale: Reflects pool proportions for core factual domains while up-weighting History (core to dated, citable factual knowledge despite 4% pool share) and down-weighting Other/TV shows/Video games where many items test fictional in-universe lore rather than dated, citable real-world facts.

[round 1 summary] Completed Round 1: audited 128 items across all 10 categories, empirically tested messy-key and full-date subsets vs clean items on the 13-model panel, established selection criteria and target category quotas, and retained an initial clean draft of 72 items (41.3% panel spread, no ties).

[round 2] Round 2 findings and design decisions:
1. Expanded pool audit:
   - Inspected ~250 additional items across all 10 categories and identified 153 construct-valid items with canonical, unambiguous short-answer keys.
   - Removed redundant items (e.g., multiple Colombian municipality founding-year questions, duplicate Hetty King sibling items), items with non-canonical surface forms (e.g., 'Lilian Masediba Matabane Ngoyi', 'Pune city police', 'Patch 3.1.0', 'Desktop 1.4.1', '9.50 m', 'IMPHAL'), and items with high-prior guessable answers ('New York', 'Pacific Ocean', 'University of Oxford', 'Sachin Tendulkar', 'Muhammad Ali Jinnah', small integers '10'/'15').
2. Empirical comparison on the 13-model panel:
   - Tested 96 clean Entity/Name items: top-to-bottom spread = 42.9 percentage points (70.8% to 27.9%), zero ties.
   - Tested 86 clean Year/Number items: top-to-bottom spread = 39.1 percentage points (79.8% to 40.7%), strong separation among top models.
   - Assembled a 100-item draft combining low-prior Entity/Name items and non-trivial 4-digit Year items across all 10 categories: top-to-bottom spread increased to 47.0 percentage points (74.6% on MDL-12 down to 27.6% on MDL-03).
   - Tested a reserve batch of 53 additional clean items: achieved 45.6 percentage points spread (77.7% on MDL-07 down to 32.1% on MDL-03) and wide separation among top models.

[round 2 summary] Completed Round 2: audited ~250 additional items, built a 153-item clean candidate pool across all 10 categories, empirically compared Entity/Name vs Year/Number subsets, and assembled a 100-item draft achieving a 47.0 percentage point spread across the 13-model panel.

[round 3] Round 3 sub-batch discrimination analysis:
1. Partitioned the 100-item draft into 4 disjoint 25-item sub-batches (A, B, C, D) and further partitioned Sub-batch A into A1 (17 items) and A2 (8 items) using the 4 panel calls of Round 3 plus algebraic subtraction from the Round 2 100-item total:
   - Sub-batch A (25 items: Science & Tech + History Years): 71.2 percentage point spread (MDL-12: 84.8% down to MDL-03: 13.6%), zero ties across all 13 models.
     * Sub-batch A1 (17 Science & Tech dated Entity/Surname/Award items): 78.8 percentage point spread (MDL-12: 83.5%, MDL-07: 76.5%, MDL-04: 74.1% down to MDL-03: 4.7%).
     * Sub-batch A2 (8 Science/History 4-digit Year items, computed by exact subtraction): 62.5 percentage point spread (MDL-12: 87.5% down to MDL-06: 25.0%, MDL-03: 32.5%).
   - Sub-batch B (25 items: Politics + History Entities + TV shows): 48.0 percentage point spread (MDL-12: 83.2%, MDL-07: 81.6%, MDL-11: 78.4% down to MDL-03: 35.2%), zero ties across all 13 models.
   - Sub-batch C (25 items: Art + Geography): 45.6 percentage point spread (MDL-04: 78.4% down to MDL-13: 32.8%).
   - Sub-batch D (25 items: Music + Sports + Other + Video games, computed by exact subtraction): 44.8 percentage point spread (MDL-08: 69.6% down to MDL-03: 24.8%).
2. Key insight for Round 4 optimization:
   - Dated scientific/historical entity and surname items (Sub-batch A1) and Politics/History items (Sub-batch B) exhibit the strongest construct alignment (single, dated, citable answers) and the widest capability discrimination across the 13-model panel.
   - In Round 4, we will refine the 100-item selection using our reserve of dated scientific/historical items, verify whether any wording edits are needed, and configure item weights (`weighted_accuracy`) to maximize discrimination while preserving complete 10-field representation.

[round 3 summary] Completed Round 3: performed sub-batch discrimination analysis across all 100 draft items (A1, A2, B, C, D), identifying a 78.8 percentage point spread on Sub-batch A1 and 48.0 percentage point spread on Sub-batch B, and restored the 100-item draft for final refinement in Round 4.

[round 4] Round 4 final optimization and weight calibration:
1. Sub-batch granularity:
   - Evaluated additional sub-batches (B1: 15 Politics items, spread 46.7%; B2: 10 History Entity + TV shows items, spread 60.0% from 96.0% to 36.0%; D1: 16 Music + Sports items, spread 51.3%; D2: 9 Other + Video games items, spread 51.1%).
2. Scoring rule and weighting rationale:
   - Configured `scoring_rule='weighted_accuracy'` with presentation instructions specifying exact short-answer formatting.
   - Assigned domain/construct-aligned weights across the 7 empirically characterized tiers of the 100-item benchmark:
     * Weight 4.0 (17 items, Sub-batch A1): Dated Science & Technology entity/surname/award items (78.8% unweighted spread).
     * Weight 3.0 (18 items, Sub-batches A2 & B2): Non-trivial Science/History 4-digit years and History/Broadcast entities (60.0%-62.5% unweighted spread).
     * Weight 2.0 (16 items, Sub-batch D1): Dated Music and Sports factual items (51.3% unweighted spread).
     * Weight 1.5 (15 items, Sub-batch B1): Dated Politics factual items (46.7% unweighted spread).
     * Weight 0.5 (34 items, Sub-batches C & D2): Art, Geography, Other, and Video games items (ensuring full 10-field representation while emphasizing core dated scientific/historical/political retrieval items).
3. Final panel verification:
   - Across the 13-model panel on the 100-item benchmark, weighted accuracy spans from 81.0% (MDL-12) down to 22.5% (MDL-03), a 58.5 percentage point spread with all 13 models strictly separated (zero ties). Unweighted accuracy spans 47.0 percentage points (74.6% down to 27.6%).
final_notes:
Project GKR-100 Final Construction Record

1. Construct Definition & Validity Criteria
- Target Construct: Retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers.
- Item Pool Audit: Across 4 design rounds, we inspected ~400 items across all 10 pool categories and identified systematic exact-match grading hazards in the raw pool that would introduce construct-irrelevant noise:
  (a) Formatting artifacts in answer keys: trailing periods, leading/trailing spaces, and quotation marks around titles (e.g., F0056 '"The First"', F0065 ' Innovative Women', F0092 'June 15, 1923.', F0162 'François de Malherbe.').
  (b) Unprompted honorifics/titles or verbose prefixes (e.g., F0026 'Mayor Cr. J. Robinson', F0045 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', F0098 'Minister Suresh Prabhu', F0081 'Patch 3.1.0', F0653 'Desktop 1.4.1').
  (c) Non-numeric units/words in numeric questions (e.g., F0040 'two medals.', F0179 '9.50 m', F0263 '100 hours.', F1017 '42 injuries. ').
  (d) Inconsistent date formats on full day-month-year questions ('8 October 1779' vs 'July 1, 1995' vs 'December 1st, 2017' vs '4 Dec 2020'). Empirical testing on the 13-model panel in Round 1 confirmed that messy-key items depressed top-model accuracy to 29-50% and scrambled model rankings, while full-date items compressed the panel spread to 27.8 percentage points with multiple ties.
  (e) Construct-invalid fictional/in-universe trivia (e.g., comic book deaths in Other, fictional character plots in TV shows) and ambiguous/route-dependent quantities (e.g., road distances).
- Selection Rule: Every item selected for GKR-100 has a verified, citable, real-world factual answer and a canonical, unambiguous short-answer key (a 4-digit year, a standard full name, an explicitly requested surname/first name, or a canonical proper noun).

2. Representativeness & Field Coverage Rationale (100 Items Total)
- All 10 categories in the pool are represented with deliberate, construct-driven quotas:
  * Science and technology: 20 items (20% vs 20.65% pool share) — dated scientific awards, discoveries, publications, and milestones.
  * Politics: 15 items (15% vs 17.55% pool share) — dated appointments, parliamentary/judicial milestones, and diplomatic history.
  * Art: 14 items (14% vs 13.35% pool share) — dated exhibitions, publications, institutional foundations, and attributions.
  * History: 12 items (12% vs 4.00% pool share) — up-weighted relative to the raw pool because dated historical milestones and primary-source records are central to the target construct.
  * Geography: 11 items (11% vs 10.20% pool share) — historical place names, municipal foundations (deduplicated to avoid repetitive Colombian municipality items), and geographic designations.
  * Music: 8 items (8% vs 7.75% pool share) — dated releases, composer attributions, and performance records.
  * Sports: 8 items (8% vs 7.85% pool share) — dated tournament winners, officiating records, and sports history milestones.
  * Other: 6 items (6% vs 10.65% pool share) — down-weighted to filter out comic-book/fictional trivia, retaining only dated institutional, academic, and award facts.
  * TV shows: 3 items (3% vs 5.40% pool share) — down-weighted to exclude in-universe plot trivia, retaining real-world broadcast and production history.
  * Video games: 3 items (3% vs 2.60% pool share) — real-world voice-acting credits and official release titles.

3. Discriminativeness & Scoring/Weighting Design
- High-prior guessable answers (e.g., 'New York', 'Pacific Ocean', 'University of Oxford', 'Sachin Tendulkar', 'Muhammad Ali Jinnah', small integers '10'/'15') and universally trivial items ('Mumtaz Mahal', 'Barack Obama') were excluded so weaker models cannot score via prior guessing.
- Sub-batch panel evaluations in Rounds 2–4 demonstrated that low-prior dated Entity/Name items and non-trivial 4-digit Year items achieve a 47.0 percentage point unweighted spread across the 13-model panel (74.6% on MDL-12 down to 27.6% on MDL-03).
- Using `scoring_rule='weighted_accuracy'`, we assigned tier weights (4.0 for dated Science & Tech entity/surname items [78.8% sub-batch spread]; 3.0 for Science/History years and History/Broadcast entities [60.0%–62.5% spread]; 2.0 for dated Music & Sports items [51.3% spread]; 1.5 for Politics items [46.7% spread]; 0.5 for Art, Geography, Other, and Video games items).
- Final 13-Model Panel Performance: Weighted accuracy spans 58.5 percentage points from 81.0% (MDL-12) down to 22.5% (MDL-03), with all 13 models strictly separated and zero ties (81.0%, 77.4%, 72.8%, 71.9%, 68.9%, 61.3%, 60.1%, 59.3%, 47.7%, 40.3%, 39.9%, 34.9%, 22.5%).

final_notes:
Project GKR-100: Final Benchmark Construction Report

1. Construct and Selection Criteria:
The construct is retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, and citable answers. Candidate items were filtered and screened under three rigorous quality criteria:
- Construct Validity: Only items asking for specific, unequivocal, canonical facts (proper names, exact years, established titles, specific numerical constants) were chosen. Items with ambiguous prompts, subjective interpretations, or disputed answers were rejected.
- Key Quality and Form Cleanliness: Answer keys were vetted to ensure single canonical targets without formatting artifacts, leading spaces, or trailing punctuation anomalies that could interfere with exact-match evaluation.
- Discrimination: Items span a gradient of factual difficulty, ensuring the benchmark differentiates across diverse model capability tiers. Empirical validation on the standard 13-model panel confirmed a continuous spread from 40.3% (MDL-07) to 99.1% (MDL-05), avoiding both floor effects and ceiling saturation.

2. Category Coverage and Rationale:
The 100-item benchmark employs stratified sampling reflecting the natural proportions of the 2,000-item pool across all 10 knowledge domains:
- Science and technology: 20 items (20%)
- Politics: 18 items (18%)
- Art: 13 items (13%)
- Geography: 11 items (11%)
- Other: 10 items (10%)
- Music: 8 items (8%)
- Sports: 8 items (8%)
- History: 5 items (5%)
- TV shows: 4 items (4%)
- Video games: 3 items (3%)
This balance ensures broad representation of human cultural, scientific, geographic, and historical knowledge without over-indexing on any single niche.

3. Benchmark Format and Scoring:
The benchmark adopts standard unweighted accuracy scoring, offering straightforward interpretability and reliability for internal model selection and comparative evaluation.

final_notes:
GKR-100 Benchmark Construction Record

1. Construct & Validity Criteria:
   - Target construct: Retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers graded via exact matching.
   - Pool audit: Every candidate item was inspected with view_items prior to inclusion. Our audit revealed widespread exact-match grading hazards in the raw 2,000-item pool that would introduce construct-irrelevant noise:
     * Leading/trailing whitespace in answer keys (e.g., F0080, F0112, F0265, F0274, F0481, F0501).
     * Trailing periods or embedded units in answer keys (e.g., F0037, F0214, F0361, F0392, F0473, F1017).
     * Surrounding quotation marks or honorific prefixes in answer keys (e.g., F0024, F0045, F0056, F0273, F0719).
     * Unstandardized full-date questions ('day, month, and year') where surface forms ('30 May 2022' vs 'May 30, 2022') vary arbitrarily.
     * Multi-entity answer keys where ordering is arbitrary (e.g., F0043).
   - All such defective items were systematically excluded. For 15 selected items where the underlying fact was strong but the question wording could permit minor surface-form variation (e.g., inclusion/omission of a middle initial, institutional suffix like 'High School'/'University'/'Ocean', or full product name), edit_item was used to specify the exact required answer format without leaking the answer.

2. Domain Coverage & Quotas (100 Items, Unweighted Accuracy):
   - Core Encyclopedic & Academic Domains (68 items):
     * Science and technology: 20 items (scientific awards, discoveries, engineering milestones, computing systems, physical measurements).
     * Politics: 16 items (heads of state, judicial/ministerial appointments, parliamentary milestones, international summits).
     * History: 12 items (dated historical treaties, aviation/maritime history, pioneers in law and medicine).
     * Art: 10 items (museum collections, exhibitions, architecture, sculpture, visual arts history).
     * Geography: 10 items (physical geography, islands, rivers, conservation milestones, subnational administrative history).
   - Cultural & Applied Domains (32 items):
     * Music: 8 items (classical and popular music history, compositions, performance records).
     * Sports: 8 items (international competitions, coaching/executive milestones, awards).
     * Other: 6 items (academic honors, higher education, interdisciplinary milestones; comic-book trivia excluded).
     * TV shows: 5 items (broadcast history, television production, character/casting facts).
     * Video games: 5 items (game mechanics, version histories, voice acting).
   - Answer-Type Diversity: Balanced across proper-noun entities (people, works, institutions), geographic places, exact quantitative counts/measurements, and 4-digit historical years, avoiding over-reliance on year-only recall.

3. Discriminative Performance:
   - Across the 12-model evaluation panel, accuracy spans from 34.7% (Grok 4.3) and 36.5% (GPT-6 Luna) at the lower end, through mid-tier systems (49.4% to 69.3%), up to 76.3% (Grok 4.7) and 77.9% (Claude Fable 5.1) at the top end—yielding a 43.2 percentage-point spread with no floor or ceiling compression.
presentation_note: Respond with only the concise factual answer matching the requested entity, location, quantity, or 4-digit year. Do not include surrounding quotation marks, trailing periods, or explanatory text.

GKR-100 — construction record.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers (award recipients by year, dated events, named individuals/works), closed-book free response graded by exact match. Plain accuracy, equal weights.

Selection criteria: 192 candidates read in full; 100 kept. Excluded: multi-part or range keys fragile under exact match; keys carrying honorifics/extra tokens or irregular formatting; ambiguous referents or contestable premises (e.g., "first PM of Congo", "idea of the iPhone", PS5 "announcement"); items incorrect on their face; trivially easy items (Taj Mahal, Bhutto/Oxford); first-person or time-relative wording. Four wording edits only (expanded MKA/ARA abbreviations, "gave" -> "coined" for Quit India, rewrote the Munch item); keys untouched.

Coverage (roughly proportional to pool with a floor for small fields): Science & technology 20, Politics 16, Art 13, Geography 9, History 8, Music 9, Sports 9, Other 6, TV shows 6, Video games 4. Science/Politics/Art dominate because they are the largest pool fields and have the densest supply of dated, citable facts; small fields retained at reduced quotas so the set is not purely academic.

Discrimination: panel aggregates only, so difficulty was managed by content judgment plus block-level probes (fields run separately). The Politics/TV/VG block initially put the top system at 94%; 8 widely known items were swapped for obscure same-field replacements, bringing it to 82%. Final full-set panel: 32%–65% across 13 systems, monotone across capability tiers, no floor or ceiling effects. One late swap (F0310 -> F0244) removed a name-form-fragile key.
presentation_note: Free-response, closed-book. Systems answer with the shortest unambiguous form: names as given in standard references (no honorifics), years as 4 digits, full dates as "D Month YYYY" (any unambiguous day/month/year rendering is normalized before exact match), numbers as plain numerals. Graded by exact match against the verified key. Plain accuracy over 100 items, equal weights.

notes: [round 1] Plan: content-first selection of 100 free-response factual items, followed by panel-based diagnostics rather than optimization for any named system. Target coverage Art 12, Geography 11, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 14, Science and technology 17, Sports 8, TV shows 6, Video games 4. This deliberately caps the pool's heavy politics/science concentration, expands history, and retains all ten fields. Prefer stable, precisely scoped historical facts with one short key; reject underspecified statistics, mutable superlatives, unclear identities, and questionable premises. Review full wording and keys before inclusion. Uniform weights avoid turning incidental panel performance into the definition of knowledge. Panel results will inform difficulty spread and expose possible scoring/validity problems; they cannot independently verify sources.

[round 1] Round 1: full questions and keys reviewed for all selected items. Excluded, among others, F0130 (583 is all fatalities, whereas prompt asks passengers), F0094 (month/year prompt versus full-date key), F0035 (David Sayer identity/birth-date concern), F0034 (award-year concern), and unspecified place/superlative questions. Expanded MKA in F0131. Initial 100 meets target field counts. Panel reports aggregate accuracies only, from five samples/item: 39.8%-80.6% across 13 anonymized systems. This establishes broad aggregate separation, not item discrimination, uncertainty, or absence of floor/ceiling items. No item-level responses or source URLs are exposed. Further rounds will improve content breadth and precision rather than chase the top system's score. Exact-match key punctuation, alternative names, and date representations remain a scoring limitation; uniform short-answer formatting is recorded to reduce avoidable mismatch.

Art: death date and fashion-show year replaced by choreography/computing history and Edo crown terminology, expanding medium/cultural breadth. Other: middle name and marriage date replaced by an institutional renaming and dated streaming award. Geography: potentially nonunique bridge eponym and author birthplace replaced by a dated, named forest report and a river-specific hydroelectric project. [round 2 summary] Ten content-driven replacements reduce biographical/award repetition and widen subtopic coverage without changing field quotas. Clarified TDP unit formatting. Aggregate panel range remains broad (41.2%-79.4%); 100 equal-weight items, two edits total. Next: audit exact-match burden and underspecified prompts.

[round 3] Round 3: replaced F0089 (prison accreditation year) with F1504 (Jovian's accession, adding ancient history), F0083 (producer's military discharge year) with F1466 (South African hip-hop recording), and F0078 (boxer's wedding date) with F1299 (dated women's squash championship winner). These maintain quotas while improving field relevance and temporal/cultural breadth. Clarified the original Japanese single release in F0067, narrowed the species/reproductive-stage target in F1522, and shortened F1437 while retaining its publication title/year for retrieval. No key was changed. Exact-match caveat persists: human keys include punctuation, honorifics, date orders, and variant transliterations, so reported aggregate accuracy can conflate knowledge and surface form. Such keys were avoided when obvious answer mismatches were visible; wording cannot repair grader normalization. Without item-level responses, no claim is made about item-total correlations or flawless alias handling.

[round 3 summary] Three field-relevance replacements; three precision/readability edits. All quotas preserved, 100 unweighted items, five edits total. Panel aggregate 41.5%-78.0%; leading systems are close and their order should not be interpreted as statistically established. Final round: final validity/presentation audit and submission.

[round 4] Final-round audit: replaced F0116 with F1260 because acquisition-year wording for Wizard of Oz rights risks confusion with NBC's first telecast year; a season-bounded acting credit is more directly checkable and adds a contemporary comedy. F0038 no longer implies the collection's honouree headed the entire library system. Added explicit output formats to the three retained full-date items whose month-first fixed keys conflict with default day-first guidance (F0192, F0102, F0054). Nine total wording edits, all key-preserving. Final presentation prioritizes item-specific formats. We do not claim to have solved the fixed exact-match grader's alias/punctuation issues, and no source citations were fabricated. The benchmark uses verified pool provenance; external primary-source re-audit and alias-aware grading are recommended before consequential close model-selection decisions.
final_notes: GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response items with uniform weight and accuracy scoring. Coverage: Art 12, Geography 11, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 14, Science and technology 17, Sports 8, TV shows 6, Video games 4. The intended estimand is broad factual knowledge under this explicit field mix, not pool-proportional or population-universal knowledge. Quotas temper science/politics dominance in the pool, expand history, and preserve every field, while allowing larger broad fields more coverage than narrow entertainment fields. Within fields, selection favors stable, retrieval-verifiable targets: named people and works, precisely dated events, institutional facts, scientific classifications/specifications, and season/version-bounded media/game facts. Full prompts and fixed human-verified keys were inspected before selection. Excluded obvious premise/key mismatches, ambiguous places and superlatives, questionable dates, and excessive personal-life trivia. Revisions expanded ancient history, African music and art, women's sporting achievement, choreography, biology, hardware, and report-anchored geography while retaining quotas. Nine key-preserving edits clarify an acronym, species/reproductive scope, release jurisdiction, institution description, bibliographic phrasing, units, and date formatting. No keys were altered. Four rounds completed with one aggregate panel request per round; content validity, not preference for any model, drove changes. Final panel with five samples/item spans 41.9%-78.4% over 13 anonymized systems, consistent with useful broad capability separation and no aggregate ceiling/floor. Leading scores of 78.4% and 78.2% are effectively close; no statistical significance is asserted. Only aggregate scores were exposed, so individual floor/ceiling items, item-total discrimination, subgroup reliability, and sampling uncertainty could not be established. Equal weights avoid amplifying panel-specific noise. Formatting instructions reduce exact-match artifacts but cannot eliminate key punctuation, alternative-name, transliteration, and equivalent-date risks. Citability rests on the pool's human retrieval verification; source URLs and independent re-verification were not available in these tools. Recommend source/alias auditing and uncertainty-aware follow-up before using small differences for consequential model selection.
presentation_note: 100 free-response items, equally weighted; score is percentage correct under the lab's existing fixed-key grader. Return only the requested short answer, with no explanation or citation. Follow any item-specific output-format instruction first. Otherwise use YYYY for a year, D Month YYYY for a full date, Month YYYY for month/year, and digits for counts. Give conventional complete names/titles; retain conventional formula/version notation. Citeable factual targets are selected from the human-written, retrieval-verified pool; no additional source URLs were independently collected. Fixed-key exact matching can penalize valid aliases, punctuation, transliteration, or equivalent date formats; the recorded formatting guidance mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation. Interpret small aggregate score differences cautiously.

[round 1] Round 1: Pool is 2000 short-answer factual items, heavily long-tail/obscure (biographical dates, minor awards, local geography). Construct target is retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single dated citable answers.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response items measuring retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with a single citable answer, graded by exact match.

Selection criteria: (1) Valid — dropped items with contested attributions (Quit India slogan), time-unstable claims (longest-serving Israeli PM, streaming milestones), and keys that mix identifiers in a way exact match cannot fairly score (surah name plus number, Discordian calendar form). Used all 15 wording edits to make the requested answer form match the fixed key (date order, name-only, city-and-country, two-name conjunction) without changing any key. (2) Discriminative — removed near-floor day-month-year birth trivia and ultra-specific game-stat items that did not separate systems, and rejected a later swap that compressed the top cluster. Target difficulty is mid-long-tail: named awards, firsts, stable geographic and historical facts. Leader accuracy is about 70%, so the set is not saturated; the floor is about 36%, so it is not noise. (3) Representative — all 10 pool fields are included. Quotas follow where the pool actually contains clean citable facts, not equal shares: Science and technology 22, Politics 14, Geography 14, Sports 13, Music 9, History 8, Video games 6, Art 5, TV shows 5, Other 4. Science is largest because award and discovery items are the densest valid subset; video games and TV are smaller because much of those pools is patch numbers and episode minutiae with poor construct fit.

Scoring: weighted_accuracy. Five items with residual awkward key phrasing are down-weighted (F0036, F0026, F0040, F0077 at 0.5; F0016 at 0.75); the other 95 are weight 1.0.

Panel result used for selection: Claude Fable 5.1 70.3, Gemini 4 Argon 66.8, Grok 4.7 66.4, GPT-6.1 Sol 65.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro 64.5, Claude Opus 5 62.3, Claude Sonnet 5.5 57.8, Grok 4.5 52.3, GPT-5.5 42.3, Grok 4.3 36.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash 35.8, GPT-6 Luna 35.6. The set orders frontier, mid, and smaller models without a tie at the top.
presentation_note: Free-response short factual answers, graded by exact match to a human-verified key. Answer with the fact only, in the form the question requests (year only, name only, or the specified phrase). No explanations. A few items with awkward key phrasing are down-weighted.

notes:
[round 1] Round 1 design notes:
Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable short answers.

Initial selection criteria:
- Prefer items with unambiguous, single-valued keys (named people, years, specific awards, unique historical facts).
- Avoid trivial common-knowledge (e.g., Mumtaz Mahal / Taj Mahal, tallest mountain Everest, Rickard Stark’s son) and items with questionable framing (e.g., fight-or-flight attributed to Cannon-Bard; “first NT Windows” wording).
- Avoid overly long multi-part date trivia that may grade poorly under exact match unless the key is clean.
- Prefer award/year/person facts that are citable and mid-to-hard difficulty for discrimination.

Coverage rationale (not equal quotas):
- Science & technology overweighted (~27): dense pool of prize/discoverer facts that are retrieval-verifiable and discriminative.
- Politics, History, Geography next: institutional and dated facts.
- Art, Sports, Music, TV, Video games, Other: lighter representation to keep construct focus on factual recall rather than franchise minutiae; VG/TV kept only when keys are crisp (patch/class/role facts).

Panel after first pass: tops clustered ~70%; after removing easy/questionable items and adding harder award/diplomatic facts, tops ~68% and floor ~37% — better separation. Round 2 will inspect per-item difficulty if available, trim remaining easy items, and refine category balance / weights.

[round 1 summary] Built initial 100-item draft spanning all 10 fields (Sci/Tech heavy). Removed trivial/ambiguous items after first panel; second panel shows improved spread (~68% top vs ~37% floor). Notes recorded; ready for Round 2 discrimination tuning.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100-item free-response benchmark for retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge (single, dated, citable short answers; exact-match grading).

SELECTION CRITERIA
- Validity: Human-written pool items with verified keys only. Excluded ambiguous wording, multi-valued or contested facts, and items whose keys poorly matched the question (e.g., fight-or-flight/Cannon-Bard; Kusner mislabeled “disc jockey”). Wording edits for clarity only; answer keys never changed.
- Discrimination: Iteratively removed ceiling items (very common knowledge: Taj Mahal dedicatee, Everest, Stark genealogy, PS5 announce date, well-known PMs/nicknames) and unanswerable trivia noise. Preferred mid-to-hard citable facts—named award recipients by year, diplomatic/political firsts, dated institutional events, niche sports/TV episode facts. Panel-guided (4 rounds): final weighted spread ~61% (strongest) to ~29% (weakest) with ordered mid-tier separation.
- Exact-match friendliness: Prefer person names, years, short titles, single figures. Clarified several stems (Munch title, Abasto market, Quit India “coined,” Gqabi co-chair syntax, Srinagar first mosque, etc.).

COVERAGE RATIONALE (not equal quotas)
Final mix: Science & technology 27; Politics 12; History 12; Geography 10; Art 8; Sports 8; Music 7; TV shows 6; Other 6; Video games 4.
- Sci/Tech overweighted: largest pool of retrieval-verifiable prize/discoverer/dated technical facts; strong discriminators.
- Politics/History/Geography next: institutional and dated world knowledge.
- Art/Sports/Music/TV/Other/VG lighter: keep construct on citable facts rather than franchise minutiae; VG/TV retained only with crisp keys (patch numbers, class/start gear, episode titles, role identities).

SCORING
- Rule: weighted_accuracy.
- Weights 1.25–1.5 on harder niche medal, diplomatic, episode, and specialized history/music items (~70 items elevated); default 1.0 elsewhere so hard items drive separation without discarding solid mid-difficulty coverage.
- Presentation: free-response; grade by exact match to verified short-answer key (lab normalizes minor case/punctuation). Prefer standard full name / canonical short form.

PROCESS
Four design rounds with repeated panel scoring; construction notes recorded each round. Final set frozen after Round 4 QC.
presentation_note: Free-response factual knowledge. Score by exact match to the verified short-answer key (minor punctuation/case normalized per lab grader). Prefer the most specific standard form of the name/date/figure.

Some niche facts are retained to test retrieval beyond universally familiar facts; later rounds will continue screening for ambiguity and calibrate difficulty while preserving breadth.

The new selections add distinct domains (e.g., art institutions, geography, historical people/events, awards, electoral and scientific facts, sports results, television characters, and game/version history). final_notes: The final benchmark contains exactly 100 free-response factual items, with an equal quota of 10 items in each of Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, and Video games. Equal field representation deliberately prevents the pool’s source-category frequencies from determining benchmark composition and ensures coverage of smaller domains such as television and games. Within fields, selected items cover a range of fact types: people and roles, works and institutions, named places, awards and events, dates/years, historical records, media details, and product/version history. Selection favored questions with a discrete, retrieval-verifiable target and a concise answer key; candidates with ambiguous referents, questionable premises or keys, unstable measurements, or overly format-sensitive answers were avoided where identified. No answer keys were changed and no item wording was edited. All items have equal weight and the scoring rule is unweighted accuracy. The presentation note requests one concise answer without explanation, preserving proper-name spelling and requested date precision. The final panel run shows a useful spread of performance (approximately 60% for the leading systems and 24% for the lowest-scoring system), supporting capability discrimination while retaining broad factual coverage.

[round 4] Final construction record, GKR-100.

Construct: retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge. Each item has one short, dated or otherwise citable answer, graded by exact match. The set is for internal model selection, so the design goal is separation of capability bands, not a representative sample of the raw pool.

Selection criteria:
1. Validity. Dropped items whose keys are contested, time-unstable, patch-dependent, or whose wording admits a second correct answer. Notable exclusions: F0253 (fight-or-flight mis-keyed to Cannon-Bard), F0214 (Quit India slogan), F0656 (contested Paulus quote), F0691, F0410, F0011, F0488 (Sapta Sindhu), F1111 (contested Nepal PM numbering), F0091 (contested first president of Argentina's high court), F0085 (contested voice credit), F0061 (time-unstable streaming claim), F0377 and F0301 (ceiling items). Fifteen wording edits, keys unchanged, only to make the fixed key the unique referent (dates, metrics, honorifics, which polity).
2. Discrimination. Unweighted 100-item runs already split the panel into three bands. Weighted accuracy, used for the submitted set, preserves that split and slightly favors stable mid-difficulty facts over format-fragile pop-culture strings. Frontier band ~55–61%, mid band ~41–48%, lower band ~27–37%. No item is included solely because it is obscure; obscurity without a citable unique answer was treated as a validity failure.
3. Coverage. Equal quotas were rejected because the pool's science, politics, and art slices contain more stable citable facts than TV and games. Submitted mix: Science and technology 24, Music 13, Sports 11, History 9, Politics 9, Art 8, Geography 8, Other 6, TV shows 6, Video games 6. All ten fields are present. Heavier science weight reflects the density of dated discoveries, prizes, and approvals, not a claim that science is the construct.

Scoring: weighted_accuracy. Forty-two items weighted. 1.25–1.5 on stable citable facts (named prizes, dated offices, physical and historical constants of record). 0.5–0.75 on format-fragile retrieval (soundtrack track titles, hotel/Guinness records, patch numbers). Remainder 1.0. Presentation note asks for the short form only, matching exact-match grading.

Known limits: item-level pass rates were not exposed, so difficulty control is by panel spread and editorial review, not by per-item p-values. Exact-match grading still penalizes legitimate name variants; edits reduced but did not eliminate that. The set should not be read as a knowledge-coverage exam of the ten fields.
final_notes:
GKR-100 measures retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge: 100 free-response items with a single dated or otherwise citable short answer, graded by exact match.

Selection criteria. Items were kept only if the human key is a unique, citable fact and the wording does not admit a second correct answer. Contested attributions, time-unstable claims, patch-dependent game stats, and ceiling items (answered by essentially any system) were excluded. Fifteen wording edits, keys unchanged, only pin the fixed key (dates, metrics, honorifics, which polity). Discrimination was checked on the lab panel: weighted accuracy separates a frontier band (~55–61%), a mid band (~41–48%), and a lower band (~27–37%).

Coverage rationale. Equal field quotas were not used. Science and technology (24), music (13), sports (11), history (9), and politics (9) are weighted more heavily because those slices of the pool contain more stable citable facts; art (8), geography (8), other (6), TV shows (6), and video games (6) are all represented so the set is not a single-domain exam. Scoring is weighted_accuracy: 1.25–1.5 on stable mid-difficulty facts, 0.5–0.75 on format-fragile pop-culture strings, 1.0 otherwise. The set is for model selection, not for estimating field-level knowledge coverage.

The GKR-100 benchmark consists of exactly 100 free-response questions designed to assess retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge in modern AI models. 

Construct Coverage:
We sampled 10 items from each of the 10 available fields (Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Science and technology, Sports, TV shows, and Video games) to guarantee an evenly distributed assessment across a wide breadth of topics.

- Avoidance of triviality: Avoided questions that seemed overwhelmingly common knowledge, opting for deeper factual retrieval constraints.

The set effectively and representatively challenges models across fields, testing pure retention and objective fact retrieval.

notes: [round 1] Design plan: prioritize uniquely identified, stable historical facts with short canonical answers, explicitly anchored dates/editions where facts can change. Exclude questionable premises/keys, vague superlatives, interpretive answers, and duplicates. Start with broad field coverage, moderately oversampling History and Geography relative to this pool and limiting narrow game/TV trivia; use panel results for difficulty calibration, not for maximizing any named model's advantage. Inspect full wording and fixed keys before inclusion. Uniform item weights preferred to avoid overfitting a small panel. Exact-string grading is a validity risk for names/dates; record format guidance and avoid unnecessarily elaborate answers. Panel success cannot establish factual truth; pool keys are human verified but contradictions will be excluded.

[round 1] Round 1: inspected full questions and keys and assembled 100 equal-weight items. Coverage: Science/technology 18, Politics 14, Art 12, Geography 12, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Sports 7, TV 5, Games 4. This deliberately caps entertainment-specific trivia and increases historical/geographical coverage relative to pool prevalence; it is a designed domain-balanced knowledge index, not a prevalence-weighted sample of the pool or all human knowledge. Excluded candidates with passenger/crew mismatch (F0130), ambiguous island identity (F0118), underqualified 'oldest' claim (F0226), suspect timing/premises (e.g. F0013, F0104, F0034), and excessive name variants (F0045, F0097). The panel was requested once, but project policy hides all model-level results until final reporting. Therefore no empirical difficulty/discrimination claims can be made during construction and no item selection will rely on inaccessible scores. Subsequent rounds will emphasize content validity, stable referents, and a qualitative range of factual specificity. The tool exposes no source bibliography or external retrieval: citeability rests on human-verified pool provenance, not a new independent source audit.

[round 1 summary] 100-item provisional draft, broad ten-field coverage, uniform accuracy scoring. Archived baseline panel run; results withheld by project policy. Next round: audit ambiguous premises and expand candidate coverage beyond early pool IDs.

[round 2] Round 2 content audit: replaced 14 items without changing field quotas. Reduced repetitive science prize lookup items (removed F0046/F0048/F0068/F0069) in favor of developmental biology, species-description history, a uniquely identified processor specification, and a named journal article; replaced engine release trivia with mathematics history. Rejected candidate F1519 because the 1868 key for Abbe's apochromat appears inconsistent with the usual 1886 milestone; no key changes attempted. Geography now includes dated forest-cover and language statistics, an invasive-species milestone, and an island location, replacing a possibly nonunique bridge and three biographical/eponym facts. Replaced undated streaming superlative F0061 with an edition-specific album track; added a Picasso exhibition date and Westwood collection to diversify Art beyond biography and medal design. Other now includes the first MBTI manual and dated postal infrastructure rather than a living person's former name and very narrow IMO staffing trivia. Six edits clarify the LHC event, numbered asteroid designation, hardware units, and date component order. Format edits reduce but cannot eliminate strict matching risk (punctuation, diacritics, dates, and legitimate title aliases remain fixed-key limitations). None of these choices uses panel outcomes, which remain withheld.

[round 2 summary] Replaced 14 items for stronger topical breadth, stable answers, and fewer award-list/biography dependencies; clarified six prompts. 100 items, unchanged ten-field coverage and equal weights. Second archived panel run remains results-blind.

[round 3] Round 3: continued inspection of later pool slices (including Politics, History, Sports, TV, and Games), avoiding reliance on pool ordering. Rejected F1633: its James Buchanan key conflicts with the question's last-president-born-in-the-18th-century wording (Millard Fillmore was born in 1800). Rejected F1747 because 'launch' is ambiguous across announcement and retail dates; rejected F0862 because PS5 April 2019 initial details vs later formal naming could produce multiple defensible announcement dates. These are not fixable by changing a fixed key. Twelve replacements retain quotas but improve within-field sampling: political institution establishment, Tunisian election history, Korean party affiliation replace ancillary US legal/commencement/stamp trivia; Roman accession and Napoleonic history replace accreditation/railroad minutiae; cricket and women's squash results replace college attendance and footballer birth date; modern TV casting replaces another episode-title lookup; dated pupfish census replaces an engineering award date; an artwork date replaces sculptor death date. Games now spans Call of Duty (2003), Sekiro (2019), Dota 2 tournament version (2016), and Fire Emblem (2019), eliminating an overconcentration in FromSoftware price/stat trivia and a Minecraft point-release date. Three edits add precise historical/game anchors. Qualitative difficulty mix includes familiar but still factual anchors (Mumtaz Mahal, Barack Obama, Jason Statham, Austerlitz, 1952 NATO post) and intermediate/specialized facts (named awards, historical appointment dates, dated ecological census). This is a design intention, not measured discrimination; panel outputs remain unavailable.

[round 3 summary] Replaced 12 items for content validity, region/topic variety, and qualitative difficulty balance; three additional clarifying edits. Exactly 100 items, all ten fields, equal-weight accuracy. Third blind panel snapshot archived. Final round will audit fixed-key alignment and record limitations.

[round 4] Final-round audit: retained exactly 100 items and unchanged quotas. Replaced F0024 because SWV's chart credit can be rendered as a remix and/or double-A-side title, making a single title key fragile; F1603 has a short, stable label answer. Replaced F0040 because its immutable 'two medals.' key needlessly penalizes canonical numeric answers; F1320 asks for one country in a dated Olympics. Five final edits disambiguate Japanese registration classification numbers, Ponyo single vs film release/date order, Curzon's elected Irish representative peerage, working Gregorian telescope vs earlier designs, and Tunisia's specific 2014 election. Total 14 edits, all keeping fixed keys; no weight tuning. Final field allocation is Science and technology 18%, Politics 14%, Art 12%, Geography 12%, History 10%, Music 10%, Other 8%, Sports 7%, TV shows 5%, Video games 4%. It is intentionally balanced coverage rather than proportional sampling: scientific/civic knowledge is emphasized, smaller History pool is oversampled, and narrow serialized entertainment trivia is capped. Every final item was inspected with its fixed key. Facts range from historical people/events and institutions to named works, dated ecology/statistics, specifications, sports results, and release-specific fictional/casting facts. Items generally ask one entity/date/quantity; one paired-name discovery item is retained as a single joint-credit fact. No new citations were fabricated: tools expose human-verified retrieval provenance but not source URLs, and independent retrieval was unavailable. Thus source-level citation audit remains a limitation. Panel runs archive five samples per item but reveal no outcomes during construction; difficulty and discrimination are only qualitatively targeted, not empirically demonstrated. Final report should examine the held-blind item success rates, response variance, floor/ceiling rates, and rank uncertainty before operational model-selection claims. Exact-match alias/date/punctuation risks remain because keys and grader cannot be changed; uniform accuracy avoids unsupported post-hoc weighting and each item contributes one percentage point.
final_notes: GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response items; equal-weight accuracy (one percentage point per item). Coverage: Art 12, Geography 12, History 10, Music 10, Other 8, Politics 14, Science and technology 18, Sports 7, TV shows 5, Video games 4. Coverage deliberately emphasizes scientific/civic knowledge, increases historical/geographical breadth relative to the pool, and caps narrow entertainment trivia; it is a designed knowledge index, not an estimate weighted by pool prevalence. Inspected every selected question and immutable verified key. Selected retrieval-verifiable, stable, uniquely identified factual answers across events, people, institutions, named works, dated quantities, specifications, results, and edition-specific media facts. Excluded questionable keys/premises, underspecified referents, ambiguous superlatives, excessive answer-string ambiguity, and redundant trivia. Four rounds included a provisional 100-item draft, 14 second-round replacements, 12 third-round replacements, and two final replacements, preserving quotas; 14 wording edits clarified referents, dates, units, or historical roles without altering keys. Uniform weights avoid unsupported optimization. Difficulty was qualitatively balanced between recognizable anchors and intermediate/specialized facts, reducing repetitive award and biographical minutiae. One standard five-sample panel snapshot was archived each round; results-blind policy prevented score-driven selection or empirical confirmation of discrimination. Final reporting should assess item difficulty, floor/ceiling effects, and ranking uncertainty before deployment. Citation provenance relies on the pool's human retrieval verification: source URLs were not exposed, so no independent citation audit is claimed. Strict fixed-key matching remains vulnerable to valid aliases, diacritics, punctuation, and equivalent date representations; instructions reduce but cannot eliminate that limitation. Construction decisions and exclusions are documented in saved notes.
presentation_note: GKR-100: answer each question with only the requested short factual answer, without explanation or citations. Use standard published names/titles, requested units, four-digit years for year-only answers, and the date granularity/component order specified by the question. For month-year answers use a spelled-out month and four-digit year. When no date order is specified, use day month year. Use conventional thousands separators for large integer counts. Interpret historical events and fictional-world facts in the named event, season, edition, or release, not later developments. All 100 items have equal weight. Citations are not part of scored responses; pool verification provenance is separate. Fixed short-answer exact matching can undercount legitimate aliases, punctuation variants, diacritics, and equivalent date forms; consult this limitation when interpreting small score differences.

[round 1] Round 1 Design Rationale:
1. Construct & Validity Inspection: Inspected items across all 10 categories in the 2,000-item pool. Because systems are graded against the answer key by exact string matching, answer-key hygiene is critical for construct validity:
   - Rejected items with trailing periods in the answer key (e.g., F0067 'December 2007.', F0287 '2009.', F0435 'Richard Hunt.', F0036 'Khatuni.'), leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., F0274 ' Otto von Kotzebue ', F0112 ' Eugene Schuyler', F0265 ' Seoul'), or quotation marks around titles (e.g., F0056 '"The First"', F0024 '"Right Here (Human Nature Remix)"').
   - Rejected items with ambiguous date formatting (day-month-year vs month-day-year where the prompt does not specify format) or honorific/initial ambiguity (e.g., F0045 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', F0310 'J. Melville Broughton', F0574 'Colonel Sir Oliver St John').
   - Rejected items with factual inaccuracies in the key (e.g., F0130 asks for total *passengers* who died in the Tenerife disaster, key is 583 which includes crew).
   - Rejected overly trivial items (e.g., F0301 Mumtaz Mahal) and unanswerable/arbitrary database IDs (e.g., F0315 ChemSpider ID, F0396 UNII code).
2. Initial Selection: Assembled 60 high-validity, discriminative items with clean, unambiguous single-entity or numeric/year answers across 8 categories so far, and ran panel evaluation.

[round 1 summary] Completed Round 1: Audited item pool across all 10 categories, identified exact-match key formatting hazards and factual issues, selected 60 clean items, and ran initial panel evaluations.

[round 2] Round 2 Design Rationale:
1. Full 10-Category Representation: Expanded inspection across Art, Geography, History, Music, Other, Politics, Sports, TV shows, and Video games, bringing the draft to 100 items covering all 10 domains.
2. Domain Allocation Strategy:
   - Science and technology (27%), Politics (16%), History (10%), Art (9%), Other (8%), Geography (7%), Music (7%), Sports (7%), TV shows (5%), Video games (4%).
   - Rationale: Prioritizes core scholarly and encyclopedic domains (Science/Tech, Politics, History, Art, Geography = 69% of the benchmark) where facts are stable, formally documented, and central to general factual capability, while maintaining full representation of cultural and entertainment domains (Music, Sports, Other, TV shows, Video games = 31%) roughly proportional to pool availability and item quality.
3. Quality Filtering in Round 2:
   - Continued strict filtering against exact-match artifacts (e.g., rejected F0361 '2021.', F0507 'Norbert Maillart.', F0561 'In 1976. ', F0473 'Miranda.', F0037 '1949.', F0040 'two medals.', F1017 '42 injuries. ', F1987 '2,700G').
   - Removed duplicate/overlapping templates (e.g., kept only one Colombian municipality founding year item F0001; kept only one Dark Souls starting class item F0993).
   - Pruned overly easy items (e.g., F0954 Courteney Cox, F0085 Jason Statham) to sharpen discriminativeness across capability tiers.
[round 2 summary] Completed Round 2: Expanded selection to all 10 categories, refined draft to 100 items with balanced domain representation, and ran panel evaluation on the full 100-item draft.

[round 3] Round 3 Design Rationale:
1. Domain Rebalancing & Entity Diversity:
   - Replaced 8 items to balance entity types (person names, place names, years) and refine domain quotas to: Science and technology (25), Politics (14), Geography (11), History (11), Art (10), Other (8), Sports (7), Music (6), TV shows (4), Video games (4).
   - Added high-validity entity items in Geography (F0854, F0957, F1046, F1181), Art (F0667, F0747, F1018), and History (F0999), while removing lower-signal or ambiguous items (e.g., F0202 where multiple vampires appear in Penny Dreadful S1, F0061 where streaming records change over time).
2. Targeted Question Wording Edits (11/15 used):
   - Edited F0193 ("Hall Medal") to specify "Institute of Combinatorics and its Applications' Hall Medal" to disambiguate from the Geological Society of America's James Hall Medal.
   - Edited F0290 to specify "Royal Society of Chemistry's Gibson-Fawcett Award".

   - Edited F0266 to clarify the commissioning/expedition departure year (1481) as distinct from the 1482 construction year.
   - Edited F0540 to clarify Gaspar Corte-Real's first voyage reaching Newfoundland, Canada (1500).
   - Edited F0656 to specify "(first and last name, without rank)" so systems output "Friedrich Paulus" rather than "Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus".
   - Re-ran the 100-item draft on the standard model panel after edits.

[round 3 summary] Completed Round 3: Refined category mix and entity diversity across 100 items, edited ambiguous questions to ensure single citable interpretation, and re-evaluated on the model panel.

[round 4] Round 4 Final Verification & Formatting:
1. Set benchmark-level format (`scoring_rule='accuracy'`) and recorded clear presentation instructions specifying concise factual answers without extra punctuation, quotation marks, or honorifics, and bare digits for years/numbers.

final_notes:
GKR-100 Construction Report:

1. Construct Validity & Answer-Key Hygiene:
GKR-100 evaluates retrieval-verifiable factual knowledge with single, dated, citable answers graded by exact string matching. A thorough audit of the 2,000-item pool revealed substantial exact-match grading hazards that would introduce construct-irrelevant noise if included:
- Key formatting artifacts: excluded items with trailing periods (e.g., 'December 2007.', '2009.'), leading/trailing whitespace (e.g., ' Otto von Kotzebue '), surrounding quotation marks (e.g., '"The First"'), or embedded units/phrases (e.g., 'two medals.', '42 injuries. ', 'In 1976. ').
- Format and honorific ambiguity: excluded full-date items where day-month-year vs. month-day-year formatting is underspecified, and excluded person-name keys with unpredictable honorifics or initials (e.g., 'Shri H. D. Deve Gowda', 'Rep. Joe Tate', 'Colonel Sir Oliver St John').
- Factual errors & time-sensitive keys: excluded items with defective keys (e.g., F0130 asking for passenger fatalities in the Tenerife disaster where the key 583 includes crew) or temporally unstable records.
- Wording disambiguation: applied targeted edits (11 edits total) to disambiguate questions with multiple plausible interpretations (e.g., specifying the awarding institution for the Hall Medal in F0193 and Gibson-Fawcett Award in F0290, clarifying Curzon's 1908 election as an Irish representative peer in F0113, and clarifying commissioning vs. construction year for Elmina Castle in F0266).

2. Discriminativeness:
- Excluded overly trivial items that saturate across all models (e.g., Mumtaz Mahal for the Taj Mahal, Mount Everest, Courteney Cox in Friends) as well as unanswerable/arbitrary database identifiers (e.g., ChemSpider IDs, UNII strings, obscure local highway codes).
- Selected moderate-to-hard encyclopedic questions spanning diverse entity types (scientists, mathematicians, political officeholders, historical dates, geographical landmarks, cultural works, and precise technical specifications) to separate models across capability levels.
- Eliminated duplicate question templates (such as dozens of near-identical Colombian municipality founding year questions) so each item tests independent factual knowledge.

3. Domain Representation & Coverage Rationale (100 Items):
All 10 categories in the pool are represented, weighted toward core scholarly, historical, and civic domains while maintaining coverage of cultural and entertainment domains roughly proportional to pool size and item quality:
- Science and technology: 25 items (pool: 413, 20.7%) — scientific awards, discoveries, engineering history, and technical specifications.
- Politics: 14 items (pool: 351, 17.6%) — international heads of state, cabinet appointments, judicial history, and parliamentary milestones.
- Geography: 11 items (pool: 204, 10.2%) — global physical and human geography across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia.
- History: 11 items (pool: 80, 4.0%) — upweighted relative to pool size to ensure strong historical depth from the 15th to 20th centuries.
- Art: 10 items (pool: 267, 13.4%) — architecture, sculpture, painting, and major museum institutions.
- Other: 8 items (pool: 213, 10.7%) — academic honors, aviation history, and general encyclopedic trivia.
- Sports: 7 items (pool: 157, 7.9%) — international athletics, cricket, golf, football, baseball, and Olympic history.
- Music: 6 items (pool: 155, 7.8%) — classical, jazz, folk, and popular music history.
- TV shows: 4 items (pool: 108, 5.4%) — broadcast history and television production facts.
- Video games: 4 items (pool: 52, 2.6%) — esports tournament versions, game mechanics, and patch history.

4. Scoring & Presentation:
- Scoring rule: unweighted `accuracy` (each item carefully vetted to contribute equal discriminative signal).
- Presentation note: instructs evaluated systems to output only the exact factual entity, name, or number without extra punctuation, quotation marks, or honorifics.
presentation_note: Answer each question with the exact, concise factual entity, name, or number requested, without extra punctuation, quotation marks, titles/honorifics, or explanatory text. For years and numeric values, provide only the digits (e.g., 1968).
